A MAN UNDER HER BED.
THE BLACK RASCAL TRAPPED BY
A PLUCKY WOMAN.
He is Believed to be One of the Incendiaries Who Started the Big Fire at Thomson Recently—He Implicates a Dozen Other Negroes and Three Are Arrested.

AUGUSTA, GA., May 29.—For a long time there has been systematic thieving going on in the thriving little town of Thomson, on the Georgia road. Some six or eight residences have been burglarized during the past month or so. The visits were nearly always paid to homes where the men were absent and the work showed familiarity on the part of the perpetrators with the lay of the land. Almost the entire business portion of the town was burned about Christmas, and the fire was believed to be due to an incendary.

Last night Mrs. Burnside, of this city, who was visiting her mother at that place, heard a noise as if some one was entering her room. The lamp, which she had left buring, was out, and a window that was shut when she retired stood open.

A PLUCKY WOMAN.

She felt sure from the sound that the party had lodged beneath her bed. She went into the room of her sister, Mrs. Bossford, and placing her hand over her mouth so that she could not cry out, told her there was a man under her bed, and to dress and go out and bring in some neighbors, telling her in a loud voice for the benefit of the hidden party, to go out and get some cool water for her child, which was ill. Mrs. Bossford hurried to the home of D. T. Irving and brought him and C. K. Williamson back with her. Mrs. Burnside was during the interval cooing and talking to her infant.

THE CULPRIT.

When the negro was secured he proved to be a worthless fellow named Allen Sturgess. He was whipped after he told how he had entered the house. He had been in the house, he said, about twenty-five minutes. Allen confessed that he was a member of a gang organized for burglary and he implicates ten or twelve of his companions, giving their names. Three of the men were arrested and are now in jail. Threats of lynching were freely indulged in-to-day on the streets as the men in jail are thought to have had a hand in burning the town. Sensational developments are expected.

allen-sturgis-thompson-1888-06-03.A2:
A LYNCHING AT THOMPSON.
Allen Sturgis Taken from Jail at Night and Hanged.
THOMSON, GA., June 3. Allen Sturgis
Night and Hanged.

THOMSON, GA., June 3.—Allen Sturgis, a negro about 21 years of age, was taken from the jail at this place during last night and lynchel. The jail door, which is very strong, being sheet iron on the outside, was broken open with a sledge hammer. The locks were first broken, and then the door battered in. The work was done with a very few blows, as the signs of only five can be seen. The lock on the cell door was broken, and Sturgis was taken about half a mile from the jail, just outside the corporate limits, and hung to a large oak, 15 feet from the public road leading from Wrightsboro to this place. His arms were tied behind him and his legs were tied together. The rope was thrown over a large limb projecting out toward the road a securely fastened to the body of the tree. His feet were about four feet from the ground after he fell. The rope was securely tied around his neck in a knot something like a hangman's knot.

HIS NECK BROKEN.

His neck was broken. It was a set of determined men that did the work, and they were very quiet, as no one heard any noise at the jail or saw any suspicious crowd during the night. The people of the town were greatly excited this morning when they learned of the lynching, and large crowds were soon going to and from the scene of the hanging. The body was left hanging to the tree till the Coroner, James P. Johnson, was notified, which was about 11 o'clock, when a jury was impaneled, and the following verdict rendered: "We, the jury, find that Allen Sturgis came to his death on Saturday night, June 2, 1888, by hanging, by parties to us unknown."

Allen was an unmitigated rascal, and, although quite young, he had served two terms in the chain gang.

THE CRIME THAT COST HIS LIFE.

On the night of April 26 a negro opened the window of the room of a very prominent young lady of this place for the purpose of committing an outrage, and, being detected before getting in, threatened to shoot her if she moved or made a noise. Since that time several attempts have been made to break in houses, and always houses occupied by ladies alone. On Monday night, May 28, he was caught in the room of Mrs. Brassford, a widow lady. Since his incarceration in jail he admitted that he was the man who tried to commit the outrage first mentioned.

While the more conservative of the citizens prefer seeing the law take its course yet everybody is agreed that it is no more than what he deserved. Even the colored people approve of the step taken and say he only had justice meted out to him.

HIS BODY REFUSED BY HIS MOTHER.

The mother of Sturgis would have nothing to do with the body and would not even let it be carried to her house. The other negroes also refused to have anything to do with it. It is now in the hands of the Coroner and constable and they are in communication with the Medical College at Augusta, preparatory to turning the body over to that institution in accordance with the provisions of the law. This is the first lynching that ever took place in McDuffie county. As a rule the people are conservative and law-abiding and it was only a repetition of the attempts to commit these pernicious outrages that caused the people to lose their patience and resort to lynch law.
allen-sturgis-thompson-1888-06-03.A3:
Hanged by a Mob.
ATLANTA, GA., June 3.—On Friday night Allen Sturgis was pulled from under a lady's bed at Thompson, the lady having given an alarm in time, and he was jailed. Last night a mob broke into the jail and hung the miscreant to a tree.

allen-sturgis-thompson-1888-06-03.A8:
STURGIS STRETCHED.
THOMSON, Ga., June 3.—[Special.]—For some time the citizens of this place have been much annoyed by a series of burglaries and attempts to enter houses, which baffled their most strenuous efforts to discover the perpetrators.

About a year ago some one entered the residence of Miss Jennie Collins, on White Oak street, and took therefrom a sum of money. Later Mr. W. C. Worrill's house was entered and his daughter robbed of about $30.

About two weeks ago, Mr. A. L. McLean's residence was entered. The would-be burglaries entered the room of a young lady visitor, and upon her awakening, threatened her life if she gave the alarm. She screamed, and they

JUMPED THROUGH THE OPEN WINDOW, and made good their escape. The next day, a negro, by the name of Mack Bacon, was arrested on suspicion, but the evidence was not conclusive enough and he was released. He was soon afterward whipped and ordered to leave town.

Late at night last week some one tried to enter the room occupied by two young ladies at Dr. W. M. Pitts's residence. They were discovered, and the doctor promptly went to the window, but the scoundrels had gone.

A few nights later the residence of Judge E. S. Harris was visited. They went to the window of the room occupied by his two daughters, but no attempt was made to enter.

Other residences were visited by these daring burglars, and the whole town has been in a state of excitement.

PULLED FROM UNDER A BED.

On Monday night the daring scoundrels were at last cornered, and the manner in which it was accomplished is best told by the following excerpt from the McDuffie Journal:

Mrs. Willie Burnside, of Augusta, is visiting her mother, Mrs. Basford, in this place. About 1 o'clock on Monday night she awoke, and was surprised to find that the lamp she had left burning had been extinguished, and a window was open. She arose quietly, lighted the lamp and discovered a pair of feet and legs under her bed. With remarkable nerve and coolness she went into another room, awoke her sister, and sent for assistance, for the ladies and children of the family were alone in the house, while she herself returned to her room and, with heroic courage, sat down on the bed within a few inches of the hidden burglar. In a few minutes Messrs. D. F. Irving, Campbell Williamson and John Arrington arrived and promptly pulled the scoundrel from his hiding place. He proved to be Allen Sturgis, colored, about 20 years old, and the most hardened theft ever known in the county. Being questioned, he confessed to being one of a gang of negroes in Thomson and vicinity, who were banded together for the purpose of committing any sort of rascality. He said that himself and his gang had committed all of the crimes we have named, and gave the names of his accomplices.

Allen was placed in jail and warrants issued for the following: John Ramsey, Charlie McNair, Allford Reese and Sam Jones.

THE COMMITMENT TRIAL.

A commitment trial was held on Wednesday last, and all were bailed out except Allen Sturgis, who was bound over to the fall term of the superior court.

There has been much diversity of opinion as to the proper course to be pursued in the matter. Some were in favor of taking the law in their own hands and making an example of Allen, while others favored allowing the law to take its course.

Since the commitment trial, Allen has confessed to going to the rooms of several young ladies, and watching them disrobe for the night. It is hard to say exactly what his motives was for entering Mrs. Basford's residence. Whether he only went as a sneak thief or contemplated some more serious crime, is a question, and from his own confession it is natural to suppose he had in view something more than the mere stealing of money.

DANGLING TO A LIMB.

Everything has moved along very quietly, and most people were surprised on awaking this June Sunday morning to learn that a band of determined men had silently come into the quietly sleeping town, and, after breaking into the jail, taken Allen Sturgis and hanged him to an oak tree just on the outskirts of the town. The place where he was found hanging is on a little eminence, just beyond the colored Baptist church, by the side of the public road.

Everything was done with so much system and done so quietly that even the night marshal was not aware of it. There is no excitement here over the occurrence, and every one one seems to be satisfied that Allen has been dealt with as best suited his crime.

A great many many persons have visited the scene this morning, and many many more will go to see him hanging there today.

The coroner was notified and held an inquest on the body. Following is the verdict:

We, the jury, find that Allen Sturgis came to his death on Saturday night, June 2d, 1888, by hanging, by parties unknown to us.

While it is quite often the case case that lynching parties are rather hasty, in this instance they seem to have deliberated well over the matter and acted with discretion. There is no doubt of Allen's guilt, and there is no doubt but that his dead body hanging by the public road this Sabbath morning hanging will prove a good warning to both white and black that the men of Thomson and McDuffie know how to act when the emergency arises. If the negro had have been allowed to stand a trial by jury there is not the shadow of a doubt but what he would have been sent to the penitentiary. But what good would have been accomplished? Practically nothing, as his class of criminals, white or black, care no more for serving a term in the penitentiary than they would for the bite of a mosquito.

Even the colored people approve of the step taken, and say he only had justice meted out to him. The mother of this negro would have nothing to do with the body, and would not even let it be carried to her house. The negroes will have absolutely nothing to do with it. It is now in the hands of the coroner and constable, and they are in communication with the medical college of Augusta, preparatory to turning the body over to that fraternity, in accordance with the law, which provides in such cases. This is the first lynching that ever took place in McDuffie county. As a rule our people are conservative and law abiding, and it was only a repetition of attempts to commit these peculiar outrages that caused our people to lose their heads, and resort to lynch law.

SERVED WITH A SHORT SHRIFT.
A Negro Ruffian Found Under a Woman's Bed Is Lynched.
A Negro Ruffian Found Under a Woman's Bed Is Lynched.

An Augusta (Ga.) special says: "A few nights ago Allen Sturgis, a burly negro, was found by Mrs. Burnsides, of Thomson, Ga., under her bed. She effected his arrest by sending her little sister for aid under the pretense of going for a glass of water. When arrested Sturgis confessed that he was a member of an organized band of incendiaries and robbers who have committed outrages in that vicinity. Several of his associates have been arrested. Two disastrous conflagrations have occurred in Thomson in the last few months, and several attempts have been made to assault defenseless women. Last night the men of Thomson determined to make an example of Sturgis, and he was taken from jail and hanged to a tree in the public street."

The death of James B. Hayes, Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Idaho, occurred at Boise City on the 1st, at the age of forty-eight years.

Frothers were reported on the 1st from East Towas and Tustin, Mich., as having damaged vines, clover and fruit, and a severe hail-storm from Springfield, Mo., that injured all crops and ruined some wheat and corn fields.

In the lumber-yards at Gull river, near Brainerd, Minn., a fire on the 1st consumed over fourteen million feet of lumber.

A FUNNEL-SHAPED cloud passed southeast of Springfield, Mo., on the 1st, doing great damage to crops and buildings.

On the 1st Andrew Grandstaff, a young desperado, was arrested for the recent murder of Renben Drake and his wife and two grandchildren near Viroqua, Wis., and confessed the crime, and soon afterward was taken from jail by a mob and hanged to a tree.

Cowboys took possession of the town of Stewart, Col., on the 2d, demolished the post-office and took what they wanted.

By the sinking of a row-boat Prof. Anderson, principal of the Spencer high school at Vincennes, Ind., and Clara and Lillie Hornady were drowned in White river on the 2d.

Allen Hurois, in jail at Thompson, Ga., for robbery and incendiarism, was taken out on the 3d by a gang of masked men and lynched.

Reports of the 2d from Illinois, In liana and Missouri, crops showed a general improvement in the condition of winter wheat.

The record of the base-ball clubs in the National League for the week ended on the 2d was as follows: Chicago (games won), 27; Boston, 22; New York, 19; Detroit, 19; Philadelphia, 15; Pittsburgh, 12; Indianapolis, 10; Washington, 8. The American Association clubs stood: Brooklyn (games won), 27; St. Louis, 20; Cincinnati, 23; Philadelphia, 15; Baltimore, 15; Cleveland, 11; Kansas City, 9; Louisville, 19. In the Western Association the following was the order: Des Moines (games won), 14; Omaha, 15; Kansas City, 15; Milwaukee, 11; St. Paul, 11; St. Louis, 12; Chicago, 7; Minneapolis, 9.

On the 2d the steamship Etruria arrived in New York from Queenstown, having made the trip in five days and twenty-two hours, the fastest time on record across the ocean.

JEFFERSON DAVIS celebrated his eightieth birthday in a quiet manner on the 3d at his home in Beauvoir, Miss.

At Helena, M. T., a fire on the 2d destroyed Zeigler's livery stable, and one man and twenty-seven horses were cremated.

Half of the village of Fairville, Mo., was destroyed by fire on the 4th.

The Supreme Court of Missouri on the 4th sentenced Hugh Maxwell, alias Brooks, the murderer of Preller, in St. Louis, to hang July 13.

On the 4th all but two of the business houses at Wakenda, Mo., were destroyed by fire, including the newspaper office.

HERMANN (Rep.) was elected Congressman by 1,500 majority in the Oregon election on the 4th, and the Republicans would have from 10 to 14 majority on joint ballot in the Legislature.

EARLY on the morning of the 4th the Mandine Hotel at Rockdale, Tex., was burned, and the following persons perished in the flames: Mrs. W. A. Brooks, wife of the proprietor of the hotel, and her four sons, aged four, six, nine and fifteen years; J. T. Briscoes, wife and two little children; Isaac Crown, and Pemberton Pierce, a traveling salesman.

A CYCLONE passed near Hilton, N. C., a few days ago, extending over a track twenty-five miles long and five hundred yards wide. The damage was enormous, as it swept through a fine farming section and every thing in its track was completely destroyed. No loss of life was reported.

In Wisconsin forest fires were doing great damage on the 4th. At Thirty-Mile siding the post-office, three houses, thirty cars, five thousand ties and three thousand posts have been burned.

From the West and Southwest crop reports of the 4th showed a marked improvement in the wheat prospects, and corn would be an average crop, although a little late in harvesting.
Edward Shepherd in a quarrel at Pekin, Ill., on the 4th with John Jennings bit off the latter's nose. Both are under nineteen years of age.

Amsley O'Dell Fatally Shoots James M.
Powell at Greenville, Ohio.
GREENVILLE O. Oct. 30 — After a Demo.
Amsley O'Dell Fatally Shoots James M.
Powell at Greenville, Ohio.
GREENVILLE, O., Oct. 30—After a Democ-
ratic political meeting Saturday night, and
while a delegation from Dayton were at
the station waiting for a train, Amsley
O'Dell, a Republican, got into a fight with
some one in the crowd. O'Dell fired three-
shots, one of them striking James M. Powell,
of Dayton, a by-stander, in the groin, inflicting a fatal wound.
The Dayton men then became frantic with
rage and were determined to lynch O'Dell.
He took refuge in the depot, several officers
and citizens trying to protect him. The in-
furiated mob attacked the depot, and while
some on the inside held the doors and windows,
others took O'Dell and secreted him in the
cellar, where he was afterward taken and
placed in jail.
The mob wrecked the lower part of the
building, the panels of the door and window
sashes being smashed in. O'Dell is badly
used up, but he would have been torn to
pieces had he not escaped from the crowd.
Powell had nothing to do with the flight and
much sympathy is expressed for him, as he
has a wife and four small children. His
wife is here with him.

THE new Stock Exchange of Philadelphia was formally opened on the 27th. Representatives of the various exchanges of New York, Boston, Baltimore and Chicago were present.

MRS. JACKSON and Miss Nellie Norris, of Cleveland, O., poured gasoline on the kitchen floor, on the 28th, to kill roaches. In the explosion which followed, both women were severely burned. Miss Norris will die.

A DISPATCH from Heidelberg, Germany, on the 29th, said that Mr. James C. Flood was improving.

QUEEN NATALIE, of Servia, declined receive the document notifying her of the divorce obtained by her husband, which was carried to her a special messenger.

In a political fight, after a mass meeting, at Dayton, O., on the 27th, James M. Powell, a bystander, was fatally shot by Amsley Odell. The crowd then attempted to lynch Odell, but he was spirited away and saved by officers and citizens.

NATHANIEL WATTS, of Baltimore, Md., aged ninety-three years, died on the 28th. He was an "Old Defender," one of the gallant little band of patriots who, on September 14, 1814, repulsed the British attack upon Baltimore. James C. Morford is now the sole survivor of the defenders of 1814.

EX-MINISTER LOTHROP says it is a great mistake to imagine that the people of Russia live under perpetual restraint, or that they are in constant danger of arrest and imprisonment for fancied offenses.

JAMES C. WEMERS, an Omaha grocer, was found hanging from the banisters of the stairway leading to the second floor of his home, on the 28th. His neck was broken, and it is supposed that death resulted instantly.

WM. FAIRES brought suit, on the 29th, against the National Fair Grounds Association of Washington for $15,000 damages for the death of his horse Paragon, resulting, as he claims, from injuries attributable to the unsafe condition of the Ivy City track.

THIRTY THOUSAND men employed in the Derbyshire (England) collieries were conceded an advance of ten per cent. in wages on the 29th.

The Union base-ball grounds at Boston have been sold to the State of Massachusetts for $80,000. An armory for the First Regiment and Boston Light Artillery is to be erected there at a cost of $250,000.

The steamer Kingfisher, engaged in fishing, went ashore near the iron pier at Coney Island on the 29th. The crew was saved. The Kingfisher was of 125 tons burden and valued at $50,000.

Two well-defined shocks of earthquake were felt in New Bedford, Mass., on the night of the 28th.

SECRETARY OF WAR ENDICOTT returned to Washington from New York on the 28th.

REPRESENTATIVE McMILLEN, of Tennessee, left Washington, on the 29th, for Indiana, to make campaign speeches.

A CIRCULAR letter, alleged to have been sent out by a firm of brewers of Wabash, Ind., to their customers, urges saloon men to fight the Republican party.

The Clyde Line steamer Saginaw, while loading at her dock in the East river, New York, on the 29th, for the West Indies, listed and sank. No lives were lost. The vessel will be raised.

STATE NEWS ITEMS.
Wm. Black committed suicide by shooting himself, at Cincinnati.

Alex. Kissinger, who was shot election night, died at Dayton, a few days ago.

Henry Beahr was found dead in bed at Cincinnati.

Mrs. Jas. Fleming, a young mother, of Springfield, died from blood poisoning caused by decayed teeth. A year ago she had diphtheria, after which her teeth began to decay until her gums became so mortified as to cause blood poisoning. She died in great agony.

B. F. Bauers, a brakeman, was seriously injured by the cars at Carlyle.

The tally-sheet case against Allen O. Myers will be tried at London December 10.

James Garret was struck by a train at Frazeysburg and instantly killed.

Miss Maria Warner, of Green Springs, near Tiffin, aged fifty, who has been a cripple and an invalid for many years, in a fit of despondency crawled from her bed to a cistern and committed suicide by drowning.

John Sekes was run over by the cars at Lima and horribly mangled.
JOHN SEKES was run over by the cars at Lima and horribly mangled.

EDWARD UHL was murdered by a colored man named Napper at Marion.

EDDIE RISBRINKER, an eight-year-old boy, was drowned at Cincinnati.

CHARLES WEEST, a brakeman, was fatally injured by the cars at Atwood Station.

FOUR pickpockets were bound over to court at Athens.

Two well-dressed strangers, the names they gave being no doubt fictitious, went into Bill Hoffman's saloon, opposite the Ft. Wayne depot, at Massillon, between one and two o'clock the other morning, locked the door after entering, pointed a brace of revolvers at the proprietor and demanded the contents of the till and any other money in the house. Hoffman made at them with a huge cheese-knife, and the stand-and-deliver gentlemen retreated. They were caught next evening and locked up. It is believed they are professional burglars or thieves, as they were heard wrangling about the division of booty, and are well supplied with money.

A FREE-FOR-ALL fight, participated in by at least a dozen persons, took place at McConnellsville.

JERRY HEMMINGER, a thirteen-year-old boy, had his leg cut off by a Bee Line train at Delaware.

While an old man named Garrett was walking on the Pan-Handle track fifteen miles east of Newark, he was struck by fast line passenger No. 9 and killed instantly, his brains being scattered some distance and his body horribly mangled. He leaves a wife and two children.

A young man aged eighteen years, named Len Wilson, living about four miles east of Cambridge, was instantly killed by the accidental discharge of a gun.

The three-year-old daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Pat Carroll, of Springfield, was playing with a button hook and in some way got it caught in an eyelid. The mother did not know it was hooked in the flesh and grabbed the child by the arm to take the hook from it. This act caused the hook to actually tear off the lower lid of the eye.

One person was killed and several injured in a freight collision on the B. & O.
ONE person was killed and several injured in a freight collision on the B. & O. railroad, near Zanesville.

MAJOR F. H. BRAGGINS, a prominent citizen of Cleveland, was arrested for forgery. He confessed his guilt.

LEVI and Robert Stevenson, wealthy farmers of Richland County, have been sued for slander.

As George Seese, a laborer in Lyth's Pottery, Wellsville, was walking under a trestle a piece of clay weighing one hundred and fifty pounds fell on him, crushing his skull in a fatal manner.

JAMES M. POWELL, who was shot in Greenville, at the D. and U. Depot by Almsley Odell, of Arcanum, during the riot on the night of October 27, died of his wounds November 9. The deceased was taken to his late home, near Dayton, for burial. Young Odell is under $2,000 bond to answer to the next grand jury.

JOHN SMITH, one of the oldest passenger engineers on the Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton road, was stricken with paralysis as he was in the act of boarding his engine to take out a train, at Lima, and on the 9th was in a very critical condition.

ALBERT BLACK was seriously injured by the cars at Tiffin.

MICHAEL GRAF, arrested at Cincinnati for abusing his family, attempted to commit suicide by taking laudanum.

JOHN REED was run over by the cars near Circleville and seriously injured.

FINDLAY is shipping articles of glassware to Europe.

THE Fanny Furnace at Shawnee is again in blast after an idleness of five months. Every mine in that locality is running full time.

THE county commissioners of Clarke County have offered a reward of $1,000 for the perpetrator of the recent assault upon General Bushnell.

MRS. ELLEN NEWHALL, aged fifty years, fell down stairs at Cincinnati while under the influence of liquor, and sustained serious injury.

HENRY PERDY died, near Ashland, from the effects of aconite, taken by mistake for whisky.

JAS. McCOMBS, of Cincinnati, fell down stairs while drunk, and fractured his skull.

JOHN HACKE fell from a scaffold, at Cincinnati, and sustained serious internal injuries. THOS. REED, who fell under the wheels of a moving train at Kingston, the other evening, and had his legs so badly crushed, died of his injuries at his home.

ben-brand-salem-1888-09.A1:
Lynch Law in Salem.
Lynch Law in Salem. We are informed that Ben Brand, a negro, was found dead, hanging to a limb of a tree, last week, near Douglass swamp in Salem. Brand went to a white man's house in that neighborhood, three weeks ago, and obtained permission to spend the night. During the night he attempted some undue liberties in the house, for which he was severely whipped, and ordered to leave the county, on penalty of death for failing to do so. He didn't leave, and the result is as above given.

The wind and floods have destroyed considerable corn and tobacco in lower Indiana.

FREDERICK SCHUNEMAN, a rich Chicago brewer, was murdered by foot pads while returning home from business.

The Democracy of Iowa met in Convention at Des Moines and nominated a State ticket, with the exception of candidates for Governor and Lieutenant-Governor. P. W. VAN ANTWERP, a Cincinnati officer, attempted to arrest Frank Kline, a notorious train robber, in Chicago, when Kline killed him by crushing his skull with some blunt weapon and escaped.

WIFE murderer Burke Mitchell, colored, has been hanged at Houston, Texas.

WIDESPREAD prairie fires have devastated the pasture ranges of Northern Montana, between Maria's River and Sweet Grass Hills.

GEORGE W. Cox has been hanged at San Andreas, Cal., for the murder of his son-in-law, Henry G. Cook, last November. Cox manifested the utmost indifference as to his fate.

The valley in which Hot Springs, Ark., is situated was swept by a mighty tidal wave, which destroyed six lives and inflicted damage to the extent of $100,000.
ben-brand-salem-1888-09.A3:
LATER NEWS.
DR. H. R. MINER, a prominent physician of Chester, Penn., committed suicide by shooting himself through the head. He had been despondent since the death of his wife, which occurred a year ago.

JOSEPH BREED, the Assistant Cashier of the Hartford (Conn.) National Bank, committed suicide by cutting his throat with a razor in the bank hallway. He was an embezzler of trust funds to the amount of $20,000.

The Democracy of Iowa met in Convention at Des Moines and nominated a State ticket, with the exception of candidates for Governor and Lieutenant-Governor. The platform adopted indorses President Cleveland and the Mills bill, and condemns prohibition as injurious to business interests and the cause of temperance.

BEN BRAND, a desperado who had been detected in a burglary at Salem, S. C., was taken from his captors and hanged by a mob.

Over one hundred cases of typhoid fever have occurred recently at Caldwell, Ohio, with twenty-five deaths.

The Nebraska Democratic State Convention met at Lincoln and nominated John A. McShane for Governor and Frank Folda for Lieutenant-Governor.

The Senate has confirmed the following nominations: L. Austin Spalding, at Brunswick; J. Russell Parsons, Jr., Aix la Chapelle; Charles Deblanc, at Puerto Cabello; and Ernest W. Smith, at Mozambique.

PRESIDENT CLEVELAND has sent the following nominations to the Senate: William Gaston Allen, of South Carolina, to be United States Consul at Kingston, Jamaica; Vincente M. Baca, of New Mexico, to be Consul at Piedras Negras, and J. G. Cisco, of Tennessee, to be Consul at Nuevo Laredo, Mexico.

A HEAVY rain, accompanied by a gale, recently prevailed over England, doing additional damages to crops. As a result of the expected shortage in breadstuffs the bakers have raised the price of bread.

Five hundred dervishes attacked an Egyptian fort near Wady Halfa and captured a portion of it. The Egyptians received reinforcements from Wady Halfa and finally succeeded in driving out the dervishes, killing more than one hundred of them. The Egyptian loss was sixteen killed and twenty-seven wounded.
ben-brand-salem-1888-09.A6:
Was not a Case of Lynching.
Our Bethlehem correspondent, writes us, under date of Sep. 5th: I have investigated the reported hanging by Klu Klux in Salem of one Ben Brand, alias Ben Evans, recently reported in the Times, and find there is no truth whatever in it. Brand or rather Evans was publicly whipped in the day time by a party of unmasked citizens, white and colored, and ordered to leave the county for grossly insulting a married white woman. He left, and I am reliably informed is picking cotton on the Fulwood place in Sumter county.

ben-cunningham-1888-06.A1:
SWIFT VENGEANCE TAKEN.
A South Carolina Desperado's Terrible Crime.
COLUMBIA, S. C., May 27.—[Special.]—Great excitement is reported to exist in the upper portion of Union county, this state, in consequence of the brutal murder of Gunnings Byers, a white youth of sixteen years, by a negro named Ben Cunningham. This negro had previously had a difficulty with Byers's father, on whose farm he was a tenant, swearing vengeance against the whole Byers family. Cunningham took it on the first member he met unprotected. Meeting young Byers alone in the woods he dealt him a mortal blow on the head with an ax and then fled. A party are already in pursuit, and it is not likely that Cunningham can escape. There is much talk of lynching him, and unless he falls into the hands of the authorities before the pursuers take him he will doubtless never come to trial.

The finest private collection of old almanacs in America is said to be owned by one of the justices of the supreme court of the United States. The rarest almanac in the country probably is one published by William Bradford in 1686. It is in the collection of the Historical society, of Pennsylvania and is valued at $350.
ben-cunningham-1888-06.A2:
SOUTH CAROLINA NEWS.
Mrs. M. E. Keys, proprietress of the Keys Hotel, Anderson, S. C., has been accused of being an accomplice to the numerous fires that have occurred there, but has been declared innocent by a committee of inquiry. Mrs. Keys is a daughter of Mrs. Cochran, formerly a popular hotel proprietress in Anderson.

In the United States Court at Charleston, last Thursday, judgment for $10,000 was given by a jury against the bondsmen of Chas. E. Bartlett, cashier of the Sumter national bank, who absconded after stealing the entire capital of the bank. There is no knowledge of Bartlett's whereabouts. He has not been heard from since his departure. The bondsmen will accept the judgment without appeal.

On Tuesday of last week, while Theron Earle, son of the Rev. T. J. Earle, of Gowensville, in Spartanburg county, and his sister, Miss Juliet Earle, were attempting to cross North Tyger river at Turner's mills, the buggy and occupants were swept down the stream by the flood and drifted over the mill dam. Miss Earle fell on the rocks, and her skull being fractured, she sank and never reappeared until her dead body was found the next morning. Young Mr. Earle was separated from his sister and was saved in a half drowned condition by the miller, who had seen the accident and had gone to the rescue.

Calvin Williams and Allen Smith, both white farmers living near Greenville, were drowned last Saturday in Reedy river at Fork Shoals mill. A large fishing party had collected there, and Williams and Smith were drawing the seine. Williams was taken with cramps, when Smith tried to save him, and both were drowned. Among the fishing party were Mayor Townes and several lawyers from Greenville. Mr. J. A Mooney, a young lawyer, plunged into the river and tried to save the drowning men, but failed. Each of the drowned men leaves a family.

— About 11 o'clock on Monday morning of last week, says the Greenville News, a little eight-year-old son of Samuel Brown, the miller at Richardson's mills, two miles from Piedmont, was fishing in the stream near by the water wheel of the mill. There was an upright shaft near which was revolving rapidly. The little fellow jerked his fishing rod for a bite, when the line was caught around the revolving shaft and was twisted around the shaft and around the boy's arm at the same time. The tough cord refused to break, and the terrible result was the cutting off of the unfortunate little fellow's arm about three inches from the shoulder. The limb was cut off as smoothly and as sharply as if by a knife, and almost before the victim could realize his position.

— A few weeks ago, Joe James, a citizen of Darlington county, was assassinated and killed by being shot under circumstances of atrocity that startled the people in that community. Investigation leads to the belief that his son, Joe James, Jr., procured two negroes to commit the deed, agreeing to pay them $500 each to murder his father. He and two negro men are in jail charged with the crime, or being accessory thereto, but Bob Arthur, colored, who is thought to be the one who fired the shot, has evaded arrest up to the present time. Young James is chained down in the dungeon, and the trial justice who committed him refuses him a preliminary hearing, although his counsel has repeatedly demanded it. It is possible and indeed probable, that the sheriff is in possession of some very strong evidence which he does not care to have made public before the case goes to trial.

— A terrible tragedy occurred near Wilkinsville, in Union county, last Thursday evening. It appears that Mr. William Byers, one of the largest planters in that part of the county, had a difficulty a few days ago with one of his tenants, a negro man named Ben Cunningham, which so enraged the negro that he swore vengeance against the whole Byers family; and on Friday, meeting young Gunning Byers, son of Mr. William Byers, aged about 16 years, attacked him with an axe, striking him in the head, inflicting a wound which will prove fatal. The negro made his escape and had not been captured at last accounts. The foregoing is from the Greenville News of Sunday. The News and Courier of Monday has a dispatch from Spartanburg dated Sunday, which says: "Yesterday Mr. Byers was resting quietly and was rational. The negro was arrested at noon yesterday. He was hiding out several miles from home. The officers have started towards the Court House with him."

THE CROPS OF THE COUNTRY.—The South Carolina weather service furnishes the following concerning the effect of the weather on the various crops in the State for the week ending last Saturday:

The rainfall for the past week has been above the average, and for the same period the temperature has been below the average, with but little sunshine.

In the northern counties, the weather for the last seven days has been injurious to crops. Heavy rains have fallen, Spartanburg reporting over four and a half inches in two and a half days; also that cotton had been washed out and that farmers will have to replant. Others report wheat blown down, or land too wet to work. In the middle counties the cool wet weather has been unfavorable for cotton and corn; other crops are doing well. Bottom land inundated, but no washing or pounding has been reported. Three days of farm work has been lost by rain. Fairfield, Kershaw and Darlington report over two inches of rainfall, Newberry and Sumter over three inches, and Orangeburg and Barnwell over four

inches. The southern counties have had too much rain for cotton and corn. During the week three days have been too wet to plough.

The National weather crop bulletin for the week ending Saturday says:

"The weather has been generally favorable in the States of the Mississippi Valley, resulting in the general improvement of the crop conditions. Local storms have caused some damage in Arkansas and in Louisiana, rendering it necessary to replant cotton in some sections. The deficiency of rainfall in Mississippi is reported as having unfavorably affected crops in that section. The continued rains during the past week have retarded farm work in the Middle Atlantic States, but the condition of wheat, rye, oats and grass have been improved.

For the Yorkville Enquirer.

BETHESDA FARMERS' CLUB.

GUTHRIESVILLE, May 28.—On last Saturday afternoon, the Bethesda Farmers' Club met and reorganized, electing W. N. Elder, President; Capt. E. A. Crawford, C. L. Percival and J. R. Logan, Vice-Presidents; and Alfred Moore, Secretary.

J. F. Hinson offered the following resolutions, which, after some discussion, were unanimously adopted:

1st. Resolved, That this club approves the policy contained in the address issued by the executive committee of the Farmers' State Association.

2nd. That the farmers of this club demand the acceptance of the Clemson bequest by the State, and that the Legislature make the appropriation necessary for the establishment of an agricultural college.

3rd. This club respectfully requests all candidates for nomination to either branch of the General Assembly, to express their views through the county papers and in the canvass, upon the establishment of a separate agricultural college and the reduction of salaries in the executive and judiciary departments.

4th. That farmers should vote in the primary for no candidate who will not fully pledge himself to vote and work for the establishment of a separate agricultural college and the application of the land script fund, the Hatch fund and the privilege tax for the maintenance of said institution, and for a reduction of salaries in the executive and judiciary departments.

5th. We deprecate any party division, recognizing the fact that the Democratic party of the State is the resultant of the mutual concession among men of different sentiments, and that upon unity depends the perpetuation of good government.

ben-cunningham-1888-06.A5:
There will be an effort made to send from Edgefield to the Congressional Convention twelve delegates who will support a Cleveland-Mills bill Democrat to represent the Second district in the next Congress.

A difficulty between Mr. J. Frank Kellar, white, and Thornton Hughey, colored, occurred Thursday on the outskirts of Greenwood, in which Hughey was dangerously shot by Kellar in the thigh and face.

The Rev. J. Thomas Pate, pastor of the Southern Methodist church at Florence, has recently declined a tempting offer from a large Northern publishing house to take charge of its business in the Southern States.

Barney Garrett, son of the widow of Thos. G. Garrett, died at Greenville, suddenly, a few days ago, of neuralgia, superinduced by an aching tooth. Some suppose the young man died of an overdose of an anesthetic taken to allay the pain.

A son of R. G. Sims, of Lancaster county, was recently walking through his father's fields, and while not looking he stepped on a snake. He was bitten twice before he could jump out of the way, but fortunately nothing more serious than swelling resulted.

While a party of gentlemen were seining in Reedy river, near Greenville, a few days ago, Allen Smith got into water over his head, and was drowning, when Calvin Williams swam to his rescue, and Smith clinching him around the neck, both were drowned.

The Rev. J. W. Welling, formerly of the South Carolina Conference of the Southern Methodist church, who has been spending the past several years in Brazil as a missionary, has been forced to resign his position on account of bad health, and is now en route home.

Mrs. Lewis Wingo, near Wellford, was killed by lightning Tuesday afternoon while she was sitting near the fireplace. Two children were in the room at the time, but were not hurt. The husband and the other children were in the field at work, and had taken refuge in an out-house.

The following are the nineteen varieties of cotton with which experiments are being made at the Darlington station: Williamson, McIver, Peterkin, Allen long staple, Truitt, Chambers, Rogers, Southern Hope, Crawford, Miles, McCall, Dearing, Jeff Welburn, Excelsior, Crossland, Winters, Herlong, Eureka, and Black Prolific.

State Treasurer Bamberg announces that the floating of the $400,000 of the new 4%
c
State Treasurer Bamberg announces that the floating of the $400,000 of the new 4½ per cent. bonds is practically completed. Sufficient bids have been received to cover the whole amount, but bids will still be received for $15,000 or $20,000 more in case some of those who have already bid for the bonds may fail to comply.

The commencement exercises of the Newberry College will take place on June 17-19. The address to the graduates of the Theological Seminary will be delivered by the Rev. H. S. Wingard. The alumni address will be delivered by Burr James Ramage, of New York city. Prof. F. C. Woodward, of Wofford College, will deliver the literary address.

A terrible tragedy occurred a day or two since near Wilkinsville, in Union county. A negro man named Ben Cunningham was working on the farm of William Byers, one of the largest planters in that section, and, becoming enraged with Mr. Byers, swore he would exterminate the whole family. Next day, meeting young William Byers, the 16-year-old son of his employer, he hit him in the head with an ax, killing him.

On Oct. 31, 1880, there were 78 companies of State volunteer troops upon the rolls; a year later there were 900,000 of the United States regulation uniform, obtained at cost from the War Department, will be about $500. At the present rate of assistance rendered by the general government, all the South Carolina companies as yet unprovided for will be fully uniformed in the course of a couple of years without cost to the State, provided they adopt the United States army uniform. This, it seems probable, will be done. The militia now have a very fair equipment of arms.

A case of fatality from the use of faith cure is reported from Darlington county. Some weeks ago Annette, the daughter of W. M. Maness, a well-to-do white farmer, was stricken with dysentery, but the disease soon yielded to the treatment of a regular physician. In the meantime a corps of the
W. M. Maness, a well-to-do white farmer, was strenken with dysentery, but the disease soon yielded to the treatment of a regular physician. In the meantime a corps of the Salvation Army came along, and with it Miss Mattie Gordon, a faith cure physician. Miss Gordon appeared at the girl's bedside, and soon induced her to leave off the doctor's medicine and adopt the faith remedy. The mother protested, but the child was firm in her convictions, and refused to take the doctor's medicine. As a consequence the disease took a firmer hold, and with nothing to check it raged with more violence than ever. Day after day it sapped the substance of the victim, and with nothing but faith to sustain the system, she continued to sink. Finally, the physician was recalled, and he called in other doctors in consultation, but all their efforts were fruitless, and the victim of the faith cure doctrine breathed her last.
ben-cunningham-1888-06.A6:
Correspondence of the Yorkville Enquirer. NOTES FROM UNION COUNTY.
ETTA JANE, June 4.—The abundant rain-fall of last week did great damage to the farming lands. Tuesday's rains washed the land more than any rain that has fallen this year in this section. On Capt. S. S. Walker's plantation, below the mouth of Thickety creek, the hail was heavy. It riddled the corn blades and beat down and otherwise injured his oats. There was but little wind during the storm.

Farmers are more or less disheartened about their wheat crops. The "scab" has made its appearance, which, with rust in some places, makes it entirely worthless. Oats are not so good as might be expected; too much rain for them.

An account of the wounding of Gunning Byers, by Jerry Cunningham, colored, has already reached your readers. Some of the published statements are quite erroneous—particularly that of the Atlanta Constitution. It is a lamentable fact that many newspaper reporters look upon the history of Ananias and Sapphira as a mere myth.

Of the difficulty that led to the wounding of young Byers, it is not our purpose to speak. The stone shown us as the one the negro threw and struck him with, will, we think, weigh about four pounds. The distance he threw it is claimed to be twenty-eight yards. The stone struck him above the left eye near the edge of the hair. After he was wounded the young man walked several hundred yards to his home, going a zig-zag course, unable to follow the path. Dr. M. J. Walker, who lives within a few hundred yards of Mr. Byers, was called immediately. Fortunately the messenger met the Doctor near the edge of Mr. Byers' yard, on his way to see another patient. In a few minutes he had examined the wound and removed twenty-four pieces of the fractured skull,

which were more or less imbedded in the brain. A considerable portion of the brain substance oozed out. One spicula of bone, much deeper than the others, pressed on the optic nerve. After its removal the patient regained consciousness, and has remained so ever since. The wound is suppurating freely, and at each dressing particles of injured brain are being removed. At last accounts the patient was doing well. We have studiously avoided giving the details, as the matter will undergo a legal investigation. The difficulty took place on Mr. Byers' plantation.

We regret to say that Mr. Henry Wilkinson, of Hopewell, is lying quite sick. He has been suffering for a long time with consumption. His children are mostly girls. We hope his kind neighbors will assist his wife and children in working their crop.

Miss Rebecca Davidson, whose affliction we reported some time ago, has recovered the use of her limbs. Her mind is still much impaired.

Rev. J. W. Query will preach at Salem next Sunday, 10th instant. SIGMA.

bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A1:
GUILTY AS CHARGED.
Rayalton's Murderer Remanded to Jail Until Next March.
LITTLE FALLS, Dec. 3.—The examination of Albert Bulow, for the murder of Frank Eich, near Royalton, Nov. 24, which was postponed from last Friday, took place in the county jail this morning before Justice Honde. Bulow pleaded not guilty, waived examination and was remanded to jail to await the action of the grand jury next March.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A2:
beercrushed.
Confession of Murder.
widows of French Fiefs.
The murderer of Frank Eich of Royalton was arrested at Verndale, Minn., by S. S. Parmeter, village marshal. He was spotted when he first drove into town with the team. The man gives his name as Albert Bulow. He attempted to borrow money from both banks on the team, but without success. He gave his name as Dassell and claimed to live at Aldrich. When arrested he offered no resistance. He subsequently made the following statement to the officers:

My name is Albert Bulow. I was born in England and am twenty-six years old. I worked for Eich a year ago and did not get my pay. I met Eich at Royalton and asked him for my pay. He owed me $60. He said he could not pay it. I asked to ride into the country with him. When about two miles north of Royalton I asked him for money again. We quarreled and I shot him with a revolver through the head. I took all the money I could find, about $5, and threw the body into the bushes, took the team and skipped. I am satisfied the way things turned out and do not care what they do with me.

Bulow does not look like a hardened character, but does not express any sorrow for having committed the terrible deed.

A Little calls telegram says: The sheriff went to Verndale and will return with the murderer of Eich and place him in the jail at this place. People in the southern part of the county, near the scene of the crime, have threatened to lynch the man when caught, but the county and city authorities here are determined that the man will be kept from a mob, and the city spared the disgrace of an unlawful execution. There is no serious danger of trouble, but a force has been organized that will support Sheriff Rasicot at all hazzards, and no attempt to lynch the prisoner can possibly succeed.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A3:
SAVED BY THE SHERIFF.
A Mob Raids the Jail at Little Falls With the Intention of Lynching Bulow.
LITTLE FALLS, Dec. 5. — Yesterday an unusual influx of strangers and citizens from adjoining towns was noticed in this city that augured ill to the murderers, Bulow and Randall, who were confined in the county jail. Warned by a telegram, Sheriff Rasicot and Deputy William Rasicot took Bulow, the murderer of Frank Eich. and Randall, the murderer of Ziegler, from the jail, shackeled them together, put them into a carriage and drove rapidly away, at about 6 o'clock last evening. This morning at 4:30 a crowd of people numbering about 150, assembled at the jail and demanded admittance of Deputy Sheriff John Sands, who informed them that the prisoners were not there. The crowd refused to believe the deputy's story, and the jailer, in order to satisfy the would-be lynchers, admitted a delegation of ten, who searched the jail only to find that the prisoners had flown. The disappointed crowd then retired. There were

TWENTY-SIX WAGONLOADS of them, from St. Cloud, St. Wendel, Buckman and other towns of Morrison, Benton and Stearns counties. Sheriff Rasicot's movements were conducted with such secrecy that not a person in the crowd even suspected this morning that the prisoners were miles away. To what point the prisoners were taken is unknown, but no doubt they are in a safe place somewhere in the state. The sheriff proved himself too sharp for the would-be lynchers, and the judge of that court failed to secure his victims. It is rumored this morning that the murderers are in St. Paul. Sheriff Rasicot will probably keep their whereabouts a secret for the present. If the prisoners had been found justice would have been summarily meted out to Bulow. It is not understood that Randall was wanted, Bulow being the special object of vengeance.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A4:
Found the Rope.
ditor of the Globe
Found the Rope.
To the Editor of the Globe.
LITTLE FALLS, Dec. 6.—It has been discovered that Sheriff Rasicot took Bulow and Randall, the two murderers, to Brainerd jail for safe keeping. Young Randall will be returned to this city as soon as the excitement subsides. Bulow will probably be taken to Fergus Falls. The sheriff has secured the rope with which the crowd proposed to hang Bulow, alias Myers. It had a slip knot in it and looked as though it had been used some time for tying cattle.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A5:
TO AVOID A LYNCHING.
AINERD Minn. Dee & Tom.
BRAINERD, Minn., Dec. 6.—To escape a mob the sheriff of Morrison county this morning brought to Brainerd jail Bulow, the Royalton murderer, and Frank Randall, the Little Falls Berry murderer. The latter will be returned today to Little Falls as his life is not wanted and the other will be left here. Bulow was scared almost to death. The flight from Little Falls was made by team across the country during the night.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A8:
HIS NAME IS HASSEL.
"Bulow" Turns Out a Well-Known Railway Man.
BRAINERD, Minn., Dec. 9.—The murderer known heretofore as Bulow was to-day started on another trip, perhaps a return to Little Falls, though Sheriff Rascott, of that place, who came for him, was reticent as to his destination, but he left with the prisoner heavily ironed on the noon train. The past day or two parties have been suspiciously reconnoitering the jail, one party from Royalton and certain citizens here, who were friends of the murdered man, all of which gave rise to a feeling of uneasiness, and Sheriff Spalding is glad to be rid of the man. Bulow, since coming here, has been identified as Charles Hassel, a former railroad man, employed on the Northern Pacific a year ago here as a fireman running with Engineers Greene, Jones and others.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A9:
Still Talk of Lynching.
Special to the Globe.

LITTLE FALLS, Dec. 11.—Sheriff Rasicot took Bulow from the jail at Brainerd yesterday, and he is now in a safe place and no amount of bull-dozing can bring to light his whereabouts. Parties are ready to lynch him if opportunity presents, but Sheriff Rasicot is too many for the lynching crowd, and law will prevail. Great excitement exists in this city.
bulow-little-falls-1888-12-06.A10:
MINNESOTA NEWS NOTES
The West Duluth Street Car company has filed articles of incorporation Capital $100,000.

Archbishop Ireland confirmed a class of 130 at Lewiston.

Twenty miles of grading beyond Cloquet on the Duluth and Winnipeg road are ready for the rails. About 3,000 men are at work.

A valuable deposit of slate and coal has been discovered in Carleton county. A company has been formed to develop the mineral.

James Sullivan and Joseph Fautz were drowned at Big Stone lake Thanksgiving day by an ice boat on which they were riding plunging into an air hole.

The diphtheria epidemic at Aitkin is raging, and all exposed persons are put under quarantine. It is impossible to secure nurses, and the local physicians are unable to cope with the ravages of the disease.

It is said that parties hunting near Lake Itasca discovered a new source of the Mississippi that leaves Lake Glazier out in the cold. It is a number of springs that pour from the mountain about three miles southeast of Itasca.

St. Paul and Minneapolis have contributed $932 to the Parnell defense fund.

A. J. Blethen, of Minneapolis, is reported as about to invest in a Duluth newspaper.

The Woman's Relief corps at Adrian have donated $50 for the Soldiers' Home at Minnehaha.

The Minnesota Valley Medical association held its semi-annual meeting at Mankato and elected officers for the ensuing year.

J. W. Root, a Windom merchant, deliberately committed suicide by laying down on the railroad track and letting a freight train pass over him. Deceased had been wounded in the head during the war, and that with business cares overbalanced his mind.

The senior class in the Duluth high school over a month ago held a meeting to which Superintendent R. E. Denfield was invited. The class members related their wrongs and refused to recite any further to Principal G. H. R. Plumb. The board of education is undecided what to do.

Ole G. Dahl, of Albert Lea, died recently, leaving a family in very destitute circumstances. Subscriptions were taken for his wife, one paper being circulated by Ole Jensen. He collected $16 and taking it to the widow, informed her that he had endorsed a note for her deceased husband and would keep the money until his claim was liquidated. The family were thereupon taken in charge by the city. Chief of Police Merchant made complaint before Judge Stacy, and Jensen was arrested for embezzlement.

Arrangements are being made at Winona for a steamboat excursion on Christmas.

Winona will have a grand musical carnival this winter.

Sauk Center's new Sawyer elevator holds 300,000 bushels.

St. Paul butchers are meeting sharp competition, and surloin steak sells at 10 cents.

A gasoline stove exploded in Baker's restaurant at Brainerd, destroying the contents of the building.

The Sawyer elevator at Sauk Center is about completed, and will add 300,000 bushels to the elevator capacity of the town.

J. W. Root, of Windom, laid his head on a rail in front of a freight train and was beheaded. He was an old soldier and was in bad health.

The Fergus Falls council and the gas company are at war over the gas contract. The city made a ten-year contract five years ago, and now wish to annul the contract and use electricity.

George Schriber had a preliminary examination at Litchfield for the killing of Elza Haskins last October, and was discharged. The two were out hunting and Haskins was accidentally shot by Schriber.

The railroad and warehouse commission has received replies from Vice President Manvel, of the Manitoba road, and President Oakes, of the Northern Pacific, to the recent circular touching the question of steam heating for passenger cars. The opinion of both gentlemen is to the effect that steam heating of passenger cars in Minnesota is not practicable, owing to cold weather causing the steam pipes to freeze.

Lake Benton schools have closed on account of measles.

The new $40,000 hotel at Little Falls will be opened with great ceremonies Jan. 1.

The question of a park commission and a series of public parks has been revived at Winona.

The capital stock of the Austin Pressed Brick company has been increased from $100,000 to $200,000.

Rog Hernwig, aged 9, and Frank Middaugh, aged 11, were drowned in the Straight river at Owatonna while skating.

Winona's board of trade will get out an edition of 10,000 copies of a pamphlet setting forth the advantages and industries of Winona.

The contract for the brick work on the Riverside company's 800-barrel flouring mill at Little Falls has been let to a St. Paul contractor.

St. Peter merchants are getting up a stock company for the purpose of building a creamery with a daily capacity of 2,000 pounds of butter.

In 1877 the buildings of Duluth cost $2,901,000 and numbered 775, beside alterations; this year they will cost $8,150,-000 and number nearly 1,100.

Twenty-six wagon loads of lynchers from St. Cloud, St. Wendel, Buckman and other places went to the jail at Little Falls and demanded Bulow, the murderer. The sheriff had secreted him and he could not be found.

At St. Cloud an indictment was found against Barbara Wagner, of Avon, for the murder of her husband, Felix Wagner, June 14. He died under suspicious circumstances, and an investigation showed that he had been poisoned with strychnine.

The big cut of lumber in the Duluth district is exciting comment. In St. Louis and Carlton counties and in Douglas county, Wis., it amounts for 1885 to 230,000,000 feet.

calvin-moody-moulton-1888-07-01.A1:
Alabama's First Lynching.
Special to the Globe
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 3.—At Moulton, Lawrence county, Sunday night, Calvin Moody, colored, was lynched for the murder of his wife last Friday night. The lynching was done by a mob of 200 negroes, and is the first case of the kind in this state.
calvin-moody-moulton-1888-07-01.A2:
A Negro Brute Lynched.
HILLSBORO, Ala., July 3. —Calvin Moody, colored, of Moulta, Ala., dragged his pregnant wife to a piece of woods two miles distant, Friday night last, crushed in her skull and cut her throat. Jealousy was the cause. He was arrested and jailed on suspicion. A mob of 200 colored men overpowered the jailer Sunday night, took him out and hung him. He confessed. The mob was orderly.

An Exclusively Black Lynching
RINGHAM, Ala., July 4-
BIRMINGHAM, Ala., July 4.—The first lynching of a negro by men of his own race in this state, occurred Sunday night at Moulton, Lawrence county. Last Friday Calvin Moody, colored, quarreled with his wife about a trifling matter. He struck her on the head with a club, knocking her down, and then stabbed her several times with a knife. He then dragged her into the woods near his house, where she bled to death. After she was dead he returned and covered her body with leaves. Moody was arrested on suspicion Saturday morning and that afternoon his wife's body was found. Saturday night about 200 armed negroes surrounded the jail. The sheriff and a special guard were overpowered and Moody was soon in the hands of the mob. They carried him a short distance out of town and hanged him to a tree. When the rope was thrown over the limb he asked for a chance to talk. It was granted, and he made a full confession of his crime.

RACE TROUBLES IN LOUISIANA.
E. P. Smith, a Civil Engineer, Killed by Negroes.
A dispatch from New Iberia, La. says:
A dispatch from New Iberia, La., says: "Information by courier has just been received of the killing of Mr. E. P. Smith, civil engineer, at Freetown, a negro village ten miles northwest of New Iberia. Rumors have been coming in for several days that the negroes were collecting at Freetown and arming for the purpose of avenging their supposed wrongs in Abbeville and St. Martinsville. The exiles of these latter places have taken refuge in Freetown, and have excited the negro element there. It seems that a collision took place there yesterday between the whites and blacks, resulting in the death of Mr. Smith. Rumors are to the effect that another white man has been wounded. The reports and meagre details have caused great alarm here. Mr. Smith's brother at Chicago has been apprised of the affair. His body was brought into New Iberia to night under escort of a squad of armed men. Iberia is a parish in which the blacks largely outnumber the whites, and at the last election chose several of their color as town officers. They have since been called upon to resign by a citizens' committee, and they complied with the demand under protest, and white men were appointed by Governor Nicholls. In the adjoining parish of Vermillion the regulators have been riding about nights whipping vagrants. On Saturday night the regulators visited a house where a negro was living with a white woman, and were fired on and wounded by the woman. A mass-meeting of whites and blacks then appointed a committee of twelve of both colors to look after the whipping of bad characters, but the only victim was a white man.

A WAR OF RACES.
Indignant Whites and Disreputable Blacks Clash and Many Fatalities Result.
Indignant Whites and Disreputable Blacks Clash and Many Fatalities Result.

Special Cable to the Globe.

NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 17.—A dispatch from New Iberia says that E. F. Smith was buried with military and civic honors. Yesterday's trouble grew out of a demand by the respectable white element of the county that the disreputable class of negroes who had gathered and armed themselves at Freetown should lay down their arms and disperse. The leading negroes were in a certain house. The whites gave them twenty minutes to surrender. Before the time was up the negroes burst out of the house and began firing. The first volley wounded a horse. The firing then became general. The negroes again shut themselves up in the house and fired from the windows. The whites returned the fire. The shooting lasted an hour and a half. At the end of this time E. P. Smith made a dash for the house and was shot dead while forcing in the door. Only one man had the courage or foolhardiness to accompany him in his attack. This man escaped and retreated. The negroes now became frightened and fled from the house. Thirteen of them were killed, eight in the house and five outside. Some accounts say three or four more were killed. None of the negroes escaped, except those who surrendered before the fight. An inquest will be held.

A RACE WAR RAGING Thirteen Colored Men Killed for Refusing to Surrender Arms. STORMING A RESIDENCE. A Desperate Pitched Battle Between White Citizens and an Armed Body of Colored Men in Iberia Parish, Louisiana.
NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 20.—News was received here of the killing by negroes at Freetown. or Cadiz station, in Iberia Parish, of E. Payson Smith, of New Iberia. Some time ago several negroes, who were reported to be organizing the negroes for some purpose or other, were ordered away from New Iberia, because they were believed to be instigating disorder among the colored people. They retired to Freetown, eleven miles from New Iberia, and were supposed to be continuing their objectionable operations.

On Monday the 12th, reports reached New Iberia that the negroes were arming and congregating at Freetown. Their number was estimated at fro 1500 to 600 strong, mounted. Tuesday they had received re-inforcements sufficient to fully double their numbers, and, feeling their strength, they assumed a threatening attitude, boldly declaring the refugees should not leaves the parish and should not be molested. On Wednesday the numbers were further increased and the people of the surrounding country began to feel some alarm lest these negroes, overstimating their strength, should attempt deeds of violence.

On Thursday matters had not improved up to noon. By this time the residents and property owners of that section began to collect at a point a short distance from Freetown. The citizens rode into Freetown and found, as rumored, a large number of negroes quartered there. They asked its meaning, and the negroes were silent. They then demanded a surrender of the colored men's arms, with the promise that when the negroes learned to behave themselves they would be returned, and that the negroes should at once disperse. The great majority of the colored men accepted the terms of the party and surrendered their arms, which were found, without exception, to be loaded with ball or buckshot.

Rev. H. Nora, a colored minister, left Freetown in the morning to attend a conference of ministers at New Iberia, and during his absence his residence was taken possession of by a number of the armed negroes. The negroes in that house refused to surrender. The whites sent a second messenger to the house, saying they would give the inmates twenty minutes in which to lay down their weapons. The negroes again refused.

In this house, situated a short distance from the main road, or street, were quartered some twelve or fifteen negroes, among the number their leaders. A squad of mounted white citizens were some 150 yards from the house, waiting the expiration of the twenty minutes, and before the given time had expired a door of the house was thrown open and a volley fired at them. One horse was wounded. This was a surprise to all, and immediately the firing became general. The door of the house was again closed, but a constant fire was kept up from the windows and doors, partly open, for quite an interval. Later the fire was carried on by spurts by both sides, lasting in all for nearly an hour and a half.

At this time Mr. Smith broke from his lines and made for the house. His comrades implored him to return, but deaf to their entreaties he went on. The house was reached, the door was forced, and he fell. At his side was a comrade who had followed him on his fatal errand, but when Mr. Smith fell his comrade retreated backwards, keeping up a constant fire from a repeating rifle, and escaped unhurt.

At this stage of the fight the negroes became panic stricken and attempted to flee from the house, and the deadly work was soon brought to a close. After the fight closed the bodies of eight negroes wer. sound in the house and five others outside. Others say three or four more were killed. It is thought by some that a few made their escape, while others who were at the scene deny this. One of the negroes who shot Mr. Smith was named Smith, and was recognized among the crowd by Mr. Smith's comrade.
f-p-smith-freetown-1888-08-16.A23:
The Bloody Shirt.
Chicago Inter-Ocean: Some four hundred loyal, law-abiding citizens of Iberville, Louisiana, being "scandalized by immoralities" of certain colored people, met and appointed "a committee of 100" to wait upon them. They did it in the usual way, with shot guns and Winchester rifles. The negroes had the impudence to go into a house instead of waiting to be shot down in the open air; and, what was worse, they were accused of "opening up a regular fusilde." The result was, "twenty negroes killed and a large number wounded." Of the attacking party one man was killed, but as he was reported "from Chicago recently," he did not count. With two or three exceptions the southern press have treated the affair as a very small matter. Even the associated press at New Orleans forgot all about reporting it. Had it not been for the reporters for the "united press" and special correspondents the north would have known nothing of the facts.

It is perhaps natural for the associated press and the newspapers of the south to side with the poor abused and
colated press and the newspapers of the south to side with the poor abused and wronged white population, who are so shocked over "immoralities" in the blacks that they are willing to become assassins in a wholesale sort of way that would shame the barbarians of any part of the earth. It is pleasing to be told that "one negro shammed death until one of the [civilized] white men welted his back with a raw hide, and he jumped and ran." But the account pleasantly states, "he was riddled with bullets and fell dead."

If telling the truth about such outrages and denouncing the perpetrators as dastardly assassins is "waving the bloody shirt," let Mr. Watterson and the rest of the democratic speakers make the most of it. Cain answered, "I am not my brother's keeper." Nevertheless, his brother's blood continued to cry out against him, and in due time the punishment came. The time will come when there will be an end of such infamous crimes against humanity, the law, and the constitution, as the one above referred to. The republic can not always live and let such assassins go unwhipped of justice. If there must be a gallows, it is the fit place for such as these.
f-p-smith-freetown-1888-08-16.A25:
THE NEW IBERIA RIOT.
Twenty Negroes and One White Man Killed.
Brief mention was made in last Saturday's Telegraph of the riot near New Iberia between the whites and negroes. The lateness of the arrival of the news before that issue of the Telegraph was published prevented our giving full details. Appended is a full and fair account of the affair taken from the Pica-yune:

LAFAYETTE, La., Aug. 17.—The riot briefly reported from this point at a late hour last night, as occurring at Cade's station, really occurred about six miles southwest of that point at Freetown, which is located in the corner of Iberia parish, and only a short distance from St. Martins, Lafayette and Vermillion parishes. This section is more properly located four miles southwest of Burk station, on the Morgan road, and about ten miles from New Iberia.

FREETOWN IS A LITTLE TOWN OF NFo GROES
but more of a neighborhood, as it covers about four square miles with fifteen families living in small but-like houses from 100 to 400 yards apart, with small fields attached from which they are supposed to make a living, and these houses and fields usually belong to the family using them.

About the centre of the settlement is a store kept by a negro, a Baptist church and a schoolhouse. But few white families live in the range of this neighborhood. There are but few houses there which could be called comfortable negro houses.

It is understood that for some years considerable

FORAGING AND DEPREDATIONS in stealing of cattle, corn and cotton on the outlying white neighborhood has been carried on, and supposed to have been done by some of those at Free-town. This is said to have been known to be true of Andy Smith and one or two of Tom Simon's sons. Several of these negroes are reported to have been whipped for it, but it was not possible to detect the ringleader, Andy Smith.

It is said that a few days since the regulators of that neighborhood sent him word that they were going to whip him. He immediately drew around him sixteen to eighteen

NEGROES OF THE NEIGHBORHOOD, all of whom were armed with Winchester rifles, old muskets and doublebarreled shotguns, numbers of the latter of recent purchase in New Iberia. This was but a few days since. He then sent word to the white people to come on, that he and his friends were ready for them, and, it is said, threatened the lives of four or five white men near by.

Andy Smith, the leader of the blacks in this trouble, has shot two or three white men in the past five years, and is known to be of desperate courage and meanness.

The four or five whites receiving this defiant message
BELIEVED THEIR LIVES WERE IN DANGER,
and sent a few messengers to New Iberia and Abbeville, across the line, and into Lafayette, to the effect that they would be killed and appealed for help.
In response to this call about 150 to 500 men from these three sections reached Freetown after the dinner hour of yestarday. They found these armed negroes, about eighteen in number,
BARRICADED
in a new four-room frame house, built by their pastor, Rev. Celeste Noop, who was at the time in New Iberia, holding a protracted meeting among his people. These negroes had sent Noop's wife away and were its sole occupants at the time.
The house was surrounded by the whites, and a half-hour's delay occurred in a parley on the part of the whites who assured Smith and his crowd that it was peace if it was desired and not violence, and if the negroes would surrender their arms the whites would take them away for the present but at a subsequent time when peace was fully established they should be returned to their owners, and

GUARANTEE NO VIOLENCE to any of the party.

In the interest of this purpose, the whites secured the services of old man Tom Simmons, father-in-law of Smith, and father of Louis and Edward Simmons, two of the occupants of the house, and also old man Sam Cohit, each of whom besought the barricaded negroes to comply with the request to surrender their arms and prevent any one from being hurt. Surly silence was the only response. The pacifying efforts were ineffectual. The whites were about twenty feet from the house

PAYSON SMITH AND ALFRED LASELLE, of the whites, approached the house, and as Laseile opened one of the doors

FOUR HUNDRED TO FIVE HUNDRED SHOTS

fired, and when the battle was over the walls from four inches to five feet above the floor were riddled with bullet holes. Several of the negroes during the fight escaped and were shot while running, but most of them fell when they opened battle in the house.

It is understood when the battle was ended there were over twenty guns found in the house.

In addition to the killing of Payson Smith the white forces suffered a slight wound in the wrist of Mr. Mauard, a young Creole from New Iberia station.

From a negro from Freetown, who was to-day at Cade's station: He says that there were originally

in the church, but that five were carried away, and that Tom Simmons, the unknown negro who died last night, and the school teacher would make sixteen, and the four missing would make a total of twenty.

In addition to the names of the dead first given the negro informant gives those of Edward Simon, son of old man Tom Simon, and brother-in-law of Andy Smith; Edward Vallier, Jr., Alex Vallier and T. P. Pochelle.
f-p-smith-freetown-1888-08-16.A28:
NEGRO MURDERING IN THE SOUTH.
There is no denying the fact that in some parts of the South the negroes are treated in such a manner as will bring disgrace on the entire American nation if such treatment continues. THE CITIZEN does not take up this matter of negromurdering for partisan purposes, but simply for the sake of humanity. If the States in which those horrible outrages are committed cannot or will not hinder them, or bring their perpetrators to punishment, then every law of nature and of humanity calls on the national government to step in and put a stop to those inhuman outrages.

Louisiana seems to be the State in which the worst and most wanton of these murders are committed. Here is a telegraphic despatch from New Orleans, dated August 18. It can be found in Democratic as well as in Republican papers; no one has contradicted it, and there cannot be any doubt of its authenticity:

"Reports from Freetown and from other sources indicate that more than

twenty negroes were killed on Thursday by regulators, and that several others were severely wounded. E. Payson Smith, a civil engineer of Chicago, is said to be among the killed. Several persons who had been whipped in Abbeville sought shelter in Freetown, a small negro village near the junction of New Iberia, Vermillion and Lafayette parishes, and stirred up the inhabitants against the white regulators. They all armed themselves, and upon being called on to surrender their arms by Capt. C. T. Cole, of the Atta Kapas Rangers, who had with him a large posse, they fired. Several attempts were made to break into the houses of the negroes, but they failed, owing to the incessant firing. It was during one of these attempts that Smith was killed. The posse then centered its fire on the house in which Smith was killed. Several of the occupants attempted to escape, but were promptly killed. A negro preacher, finally gained admittance and, coming back, reported Smith and all the occupants dead. The bodies were brought out, and it was found that one negro was shamming. Someone hit him with a rawhide, whereupon he jumped to his feet with a yell and started to run, but was riddled before he could take a step. Smith was buried with military honors in New Iberia."

It is a dead certainty that not a hair of any white man's head will ever be injured on account of those murders, that is, if the punishment is left to the authorities of the State of Louisiana. Such murders could not take place in a time of profound peace in any other civilized country under the sun, and the perpetrators of them left unpunished. But how are they going to be punished? That is a question for the United States authorities.
