OPEN ADDRESS.
Colored Citizens of Louisiana Appeal For Redress.
The following is the conclusion of the Address to the people of the United States recently issued from New Orleans in the name of the colored people of Louisiana;—

The latest wholesale murder, rivaling the most horrifying brutalities of the Comanehes, took place only a few nights ago, near Cade station, in the parish of Iberia, in the Negro village of Freetown. This place is owned exclusively by colored people who were conceded to be industrious and respectable. They were charged with hiding and protecting in their midst some Negroes from other parts of the parish whom the regu lator wanted to whip. When this news was spread abroad a sheriff, farudu'ently installed, with his men, without any warrant or shadow of law, at the hour of midnight invaded the quiet village, attacked a house wherein a number of Negroes expecting the assault had gathered for self-defence, and deliberately slaughtered the inmates. No arrests will follow. The civil authorities are in sympathy with, and applaud the crime.

The Governor has shown no disposition to afford our people any protection, because of this and other kindred wrongs, and our sad experience leads us to expect no redress from that source.

The papers daily record lynchings, whippings, and murders of people on various pretences, such as are not considered sufficient cause for lynch law for whites under the like circumstances, and tidnings pour in upon us like a flood of brutalities the record of which is suppressed from the public print because of the supposed political effect they would have upon the Presidential and Congaessional campaigns in Northern States.

South and West.
Megamom of the Kicks
CHIEF MESCOTT of the Kickapoos, his squaw and five children, have been killed by lightning, in his cabin, on the reservation near Netawaka, Kansas.

SIMON WALLACE, aged thirty-one years, and his mother, aged fifty-five, were burned to death at Charleston, W. Va.

RACE troubles led to a terrible fight in Freetown, La. The colored men armed and ensconced themselves in a house, and after a fight lasting an hour or two, thirteen of them were killed. None of the white men lost his life and none is reported missing.

A SAWMILL at Blooming Valley, Mich. exploded, killing Engineer C. L. Dodge and Orson Robb and fatally injuring Mr. Prosser, the owner.

In a railroad accident near Wilmington, N. C., two persons were killed and three injured.

MRS. REED, wife of N. M. Reed, a prominent farmer of Alexander City, Ala., was found in bed strangled to death. The husband has been arrested.

General Lew Wallace, the distinguished author of "Ben Hur" and life-long friend of General Harrison, has just completed an authorized biography of him. W. U. Hensel, a staunch leader in national councils of the Democratic party, has just completed an admirable biography of Cleveland, with a bright sketch of Thurman.

HEAVY rains have fallen in Southern Louisiana flooding many cotton and sugar fields and submerging the railroad tracks.

BILLY COLE, the desperado who recently emptied a revolver into a dancing party at Guiding Rock, Neb., wounding two persons, has been lynched.

GREAT damage has been done in New Orleans along the river front by a gale, accompanied by heavy rains. Several buildings were unroofed, trees were uprooted, and the coal fleet of the Pittsburg and Southern combine suffered severely. Fifty boats are known to have been lost. They were valued at $5000 each. Great damage has been done to the rice and sugar cane crop. Telegraph wires were prostrated in every direction.

A TORNADO demolished many buildings in Marquette, Mich.

Just before Professor Bartholomew was to ascend in his balloon and make a parachute jump at La Grange, Mich., the pole, twenty-five feet high, fell into the crowd, killing two boys, Charles Graftmiller, aged nine years, and Gilbert Appleman, aged fifteen years.

CAPTAIN N. KINNEY, the founder and chief of the infamous Bald Knobbers, has been shot and killed at Ozark, Mo., by Bill Miles, an anti-Bald Knobber.

In attempting to get down from a load of hay a farmer near Zanesville, Ohio, slipped and fell on a four-pronged fork, three of which entered his breast. He pulled the prongs out, walked around the wagon to where his wife was standing, fell into her arms and died.

CATHERINE WILLEM, of Cincinnati, aged thirty-one, assisted to prepare the wedding feast for her young sister's marriage, and then went up-stairs and committed suicide by cutting her throat. She declared that she killed herself because she feared she was doomed to lead the life of an old maid.

DOUBLE LYNCHING IN WYOMING.
Game-Butchers who Burned a Ranchman's House for Revenge Hanged.
CHEYENNE, Wyo., Oct. 22.—A cowboy from the
Game-Butchers who Burned a Ranchman's House for Revenge Hanged.

CHEYENNE, WY., Oct. 22.—A cowboy from the Snake River country brings news of the lynching of F. W. Adams and a companion known in these parts as "Dutchy," two hunters, who maliciously burned the house of a ranchman, a few miles north of the Snake. The pair started out with horses and Winchester to kill elk and deer. They found game in abundance and began wholesale slaughter of the animals. They were not hunting for venison, but for hides and horns. Tom Johnson, a ranchman, met them Thursday and demonstrated with them. He said they were violating the game laws of the territory, and he threatened to have them arrested if they did not cease the useless slaughter. This threat enraged Adams, and that night, accompanied by his partner, he rode down to Johnson's ranch and set fire to his house. He did not attempt to avoid detection, and instead of riding away he hovered around the burning building until Johnson came out carrying his wife and little girl in his arms. Adams rode over to the ranchman with a cocked revolver in either hand and smilingly told him that he was going to kill all the elk in Corbin County. "And," he added, "if you interfere with me again,

I'll KILL YOU, TOO."

A short time afterward Adams rode away, accompanied by his partner, and then Johnson, leaving his wife and child in a barn, set out for a little settlement on the Snake to alarm his friends. He reached the settlement about daylight, and within an hour he gathered a force of forty men who were eager to join him in the chase. The pursuers rode until noon, when they came upon a little dinner camp of which the hunters were the only occupants. Adams saw the approaching squadron first and instinctively grasped his Winchester and raised it to his shoulder, but he lowered it when he saw the long line of gleaming six-shooters that suddenly sprang into view. The two hunters were made prisoners, and after being tied securely to their own horses were started back to the settlement, where they were confined in an adobe hut. That night 100 men took them out and hung them to the limb of a tree. When a cowboy who brought the news left the Snake the bodies were still swinging in the air.

He reached the settlement about daylight, and within an hour he had gathered a force of forty men who were eager to join him in the chase after the vandal hunter. The pursuers separated into squads and started in a northerly and western direction. They rode on until noon without discovering any trace of their men, but a short time after that hour an old trapper, who belonged to the party, found a trail that led in a southerly direction. Fresh imprints of horses' hoofs could be traced distinctly in the clay, and every member of the party who saw this agreed with the trapper that they were made by the bronchos of Adams and "Dutchy." Such proved to be the case, for the trail had not been followed an hour when the prisoners rode down upon a little dinner camp, of which the hunters were the only occupants. The two hunters were made prisoners, and after being tied securely to their own horses were started back for the settlement. They reached there about 7 o'clock Friday night and were placed in an old adobe hut for safe keeping. Armed men guarded the only entrance. Their orders were to shoot the first head that showed outside of the mud prison. About 10 o'clock that night, while a furious thunderstorm was raging, a hundred men whose faces were hidden by crude masks, surrounded the doby, their leader, a tall man, who carried a six-shooter in his right hand, commanded the guards to fall back and return to their homes. The command was obeyed without a murmur, and the tall man, followed by half a dozen of his companions, sprang through the narrow entrance of the hut. Those who were on the outside heard a chorus of angry yells and curses, sounds of a fierce struggle, finally a single shot. When the masked men who entered the hut reappeared they were carrying Adams and "Dutchy," both of whom were bound hand and foot.

"What ye going to do with us?" growled Adams as he looked around the strange assemblage.

"Hang ye, ye varmints," said the leader in a low voice. "Boys," he added, "take them to the red tree and let 'em both dance from the same limb."

The "boys" responded with a cheer. Adams and "Dutchy" were seized by a score of hands and carried swiftly in the direction of the river. Neither of the doomed men uttered a word, though he knew he had only a few minutes to live, and when the noose of a lariat was adjusted around Adams' neck he smiled as if he rather liked the touch of the leather. Presently the red tree was reached. The knots and nooses were readjusted, the ends of the ropes were thrown over the lower branch and seized by as many hands as could find a hold.

"Have you anything to say?" the tall leader demanded as he eyed the two victims sternly.

Adams shook his head but "Dutchy" did not move a muscle. The leader raised his pistol, cocked it, and after counting one—two—three as deliberately as possible, fired a shot in the air. This was the signal the men who held the lariats were waiting for. The instant they heard the detonation they gave a great shout, and two writhing bodies sprang into the air. The Double Wyoming Lynching.
DENOUNCED BY SOME CITIZENS AND THE OSTER
The Double Wyoming Lynching.
DENOUNCED BY SOME CITIZENS AND THE GOVERNOR ASKED TO PUNISH THE LYNCHERS.
CHEYENNE, WYOMING, Oct. 30.--Further particulars of the double lynching on Snake River, Carbon County, last week have reacher here. The bodies of Adams and "Dutchy," the victims, were discovered by a settler named Davis Phelps, who followed the trail of the masked horsemen from the improvised jail to the place of execution. The mounts of Adams and "Dutchy" were killed, as also was their hunting dog. A coat worn by one of the vigilants was found near the bodies, and the owner may be identified. A coroner's jury is investigating the case. During the inquiry it has been learned that "Dutchy's" name was Chas. Lutzier. Robert McIntosh, an old-timer in that region, has notified the governor of Wyoming of the occurrence, and urges that the lynchers be punished. He says the hanging of the men was a brutal, cowardly and outrageous murder. Adams was a veteran, and came from Illinois, where he has a brother and sister and an aged mother. In examining his effects it was learned that he was soon to come into possession of a legacy valued at $40,000.
f-w-adams-snake-river-settlement-1888-10.A20: Two hunters, named "Dutchie" and Adams, were lynched near Snake river, Colorado. The men had been for several weeks killing elk and deer for the hides and had been warned by the settlers to desist on the pain of death. f-w-adams-snake-river-settlement-1888-10.A28:
HIS BROTHER WAS LYNCHED.
A Resident of Fargo Will Inaugurate a Vendetta.
Special to the Globe.
* FARGO, Dak, Nov 1

FARGO, Dak., Nov. 1.—J. P. Adams, of this city, is a brother of Adams, who with "Dutchie," was lynched in Wyoming the 21st by cowsboys. Adams is an engineer in the roller mills here. He saps that some time after the offense was committed by Adams and "Dutchie" he received a letter from his brother stating that he feared some move of the kind was on foot. The letter contained an inventory of all his personal effects and requested that upon hearing of his death to come at once and take possession of and sell them, the proceeds to be devoted in ferretting out murderers and bringing them to justice. Seeing a special in the GLOBE from Cheyenne to the effect that the governor had been appealed to in the matter, Mr. Adams to-day forwarded him the letter mentioned, together with one mailed by his brother just before the lynching occurred. Mr. Adams has two sons here with him, and states that as soon as possible he and his sons will proceed as per directions in the letter, to carry out the request of his brother, if not with the assistance of the authorities, then without them.

Shot Himself Rather Than Testify About the Double Lynching Affair.
Later particulars of the recent lynching on Snake river show it to have been one of the most atrocious outrages ever committed in Wyoming territory. The bodies of the men, when cut down after they had been hanging for a week, were found to be shockingly mutilated. Their faces were pounded to a jelly with the butt of a pistol, the eyes knocked from their sockets and their noses broken. The brutality of the self-appointed executioners beggars description. The horses of the men were killed near the spot where they were hung.

Three men named Harper, Joe Miller and Henry Cantlin were subpoenaed to testify before the coroner's jury. But Miller and Cantlin skipped the country and their whereabouts are unknown.

Harper took a dose of poison with suicidal intent, but his life was saved by a prompt use of emetics. As soon as he was able to move he disappeared, and a week later his dead body was found with a bullet hole through the head. He had killed himself sooner than tell what he knew of the disgraceful affair.

A coat found at the scene of the hanging has been identified as belonging to Joe Miller, and it is known that he had a hand in the outrage. His wife passed through this city, and is thought to be on her way to join her husband. She would not be interviewed. John P. Adams, a brother of one of the murdered men, who resides at Fargo, Dakota, is on his way to this city to investigate the matter and bring the guilty parties to justice.—Rawlins Special to Snn.

THEY WERE RELEASED.
Old-Time Judicial Proceedings Out On Snake River.
A humorous incident growing out of the atrocious lynching of two men on Snake river some time ago is given to the world by THE LEADER.

Three settlers were arrested on suspicion of being implicated in the brutal outrage. There wasn't a limb of the law in the well timbered valley, but John M. Finley, a killer, who who was once official reporter for the territorial legislature, and subsequently constable at Rawlins, volunteered to defend the alleged strangers.

Finley barely knows the difference between a mittamus and a bill of sale, and thought he had very cleverly clogged the wheels of justice when he moved for a change of venue. Old timers say that Hughes, the law dispenser for Snake river precinct, used to be a vigilantee and will stand no foolishness. He patiently listened to Finley's argument on the motion and frequently delayed the harangue by arguing points with John. He finally took the matter under advisement and after two days' consideration concluded to send to Rawlins for Justice Dodge and Prosecuting Attorney Dixon. Knowing Hughes neither official paid any attention to the summons.

After three days of grace had expired Finley demanded the release of his client, when Hughes calmly declared that in the absence of Dodge and Dixon he would preside at the hearing.

In vain the amateur attorney protested. The judge was firm. A few drinks were taken as the debate progressed. In due course of events Hughes gave Finley the lie, and when the latter reached for his six shooter knocked him down for contempt of court. Several fights ensued, and whiskey was imbibed between rounds.

The upshot of the queer proceedings was that the entire party celebrated in hilarious style, the prisoners were released and the hearing never did take place.

The foregoing is vouched for by a gentleman who visited the region since the double hanging. A reward of $500 has been offered for the apprehension of the murderers, but it is doubtful if they will ever be captured.
f-w-adams-snake-river-settlement-1888-10.A39:
THE DOUBLE LYNCHING.
An Interview with an Officer from Snake Riyer.
In an interview Friday evening J. M. Finley, constable at Snake river, Carbon county, spoke freely of the atrocious double lynching which occurred in that locality some three months since. In the first place he says that Adams and Dutchie, the victims, were pretty bad men, in fact thorough scoundrels, but public sentiment against their cowardly murder is not mitigated on this account. They slaughtered game ruthlessly and burned the property of a helpless old man, but this did not warrant their murder, which, by the way, Finley declares is not so brutal as has been reported. He says that their faces were not bruised at all, that they were simply hanged. There have been a number of sudden emigrations since the institution of a legal investigation and it looks as though the guilty ones would escape. In fact there is no possibility of the apprehension of the lynchers unless one of their number turns state's evidence, and this will hardly occur.

Finley, who has been on an unsuccessful hunt after suspected lynchers, says that THE LEADER's account of the very informal preliminary hearing of some of the accused was correct in the main but inaccurate in one or two particulars. For instance, he denies that Justice Hughes knocked him down.

STRUNG UP THREE TIMES.
A Man Who Was Almost Lynched Tells How He Felt. Ohio State Journal.
Ohio State Journal. are several prisoners

There are several prisoners in the penitentiary who know only too well what it is to be drawn up slowly by a rope around their necks for a time. Several of these were called and related some of their thrilling experiences for the benefit of the State Journal and others. The most interesting case was that of Frank B. Mason, the paroled prisoner, who was brought from West Virginia last week by Mr. Cheerington.

It will be remembered that he was "strung" up three times by a mob in the wilds of West Virginia, about forty miles from any railroad. He was suspected of stealing $43 from a store in Calhoun county, and was captured in Roane county by a "posse" of horsemen, who leveled their guns on him just as he was entering a cornfield. He was then subjected to a variety of inhuman treatment, which would make a Hercules shudder, with a view to making him confess.

He said: "At dusk I was taken out of the jail to a beech tree about fifty rods away. They threw the rope over a limb and swung me off over a little embankment. The pain at first was terrible, but soon stars flitted before my eyes. There were more than a million of them it seemed to me, moving in every direction. Then I began to see all the different colors imaginable, blending in the most beautiful and fantastic outlines. I tell you, if you had a thousand paint brushes and all the paints in the world you could not make so many pretty colors. This sensation was very pleasant, and I thought I was in a dream. I don't know how long I hung, but my most severe pain was just as I was coming to my senses again. I shook violently, and it seemed as though it would kill me. The third time they let me down they flourished revolvers in my face and said: 'We'll shoot the _____ and not let his friends cut him down again.' I thought all the time that they intended to hang me for good, and I sent a farewell word to my mother. I thought they would hang me if I confessed. After this they bound me tightly with ropes and took me five miles in the rain. The ropes were contracted by the water so much that they left black and blue prints all over my body and arms."

Mason was sent up from Noble county on a seven-year sentence for burglary and was paroled April 29, 1888. Deputy Cheerington confirmed his statement about his treatment in West Virginia.

A QUERY. Mr Editor: -In Mr. Crawford's fine defensive letter, that gentleman makes a remark about a "poor editor." Can any one tell what is meant by such a term? Will some one competent rise and explain? CITIZEN. BULL-DOZING. Three Negroes Whipped and One Killed.
Considerable excitement prevails in the southeastern portion of this county, on account of the recent exploits of several men, who seem to delight in creating disturbances.

From the best information we could obtain, it appears that these men disliked certain of their colored neighbors, named Hardy Kaigler, Ben Kaigler and Joseph Prescott and have for some time, endeavored to get information that would necessitate "regulating" them.

On Friday night they arrested Frank Warner, a negro boy, about fifteen years old, and beat him unmercifully, with a view of making him tell something against the above named negro men, but without success. On Sunday night they caught Frank again and treated him even worse than before. They asked direct questions in regard to the Kaigler's and Prescott, and when the boy said that he knew nothing against them, a rope was placed around his neck and he was told that he would be hung unless he answered the questions put to him in the affirmative. Seeing that there was no other way to save his own life, the poor boy told that the aforesaid negro men had attempted to break into a store at Dillon's Bridge. This was all they wanted and immediately started for the respective abodes of the unsuspecting negroes—taking the boy along with them. The two Kaigler's were caught and placed under guard and then they proceeded to the house of Joseph Prescott, on Mr. Richard Fortimberry's plantation, and called him out. It was then past mid-night. As soon as the negro ascertained what they wanted with him, he jerked loose from them and ran off. Several shots was fired at him by the crowd—only one of which took effect. The ball entered the right side just above the hip and penetrating the bowels, produced a wound from which he died on Monday. The assassins then returned and whipped the two Knigler's in a most brutal manner—one of whom they left for dead by the road-side, but they still live and if their lives are spared will be important witnesses against their assailants.

An inquest was held Tuesday, over the body of Joseph Prescott and the Coroner's Jury returned a verdict in accordance with the above facts, charging twenty-four white men with the crime.

Warrants for their arrest were placed in the hands of Capt A. A. Boyd, Sheriff, who summoned a posse of twelve men and after riding all night succeeded in arresting seventeen of the persons named in the verdict. The accused were brought before Mr. I. M. Ellzey, Justice of the Peace, Wednesday morning and had the preliminary trial set for Thursday.

Religious Discord.

Religious Discord.

MONTREAL, April 17.—[Special Telegram to the BEE.]—This unfortunate city, so often the scene of bloody religious conflicts, is again divided on strictly religious lines, over proposals made by a number of leading Catholic citizens asking the city council for a site in the center of Mount Royal park on which to erect a mammoth statue of the Virgin Mary. The proposal has called forth the most vehement protests from the Protestant population, and on Sunday in all churches stirring references were made to it and Protestants were urged, irrespective of denomination, to combat the scheme. After services, petitions to the council not to allow the diversion of public parks to such purposes, were signed by many thousands of laymen and clergymen, and last night a united meeting of the Evangelical alliance and ministers in the association discussed the project in no halting language. Extremists threaten, that if the statue is erected it will be blown up, and in such an event there is no saying what would be the

result. The incident has renewed all smoldering fires of radical and religious discord, and the city is divided against itself.

A STATEMENT
DILLON, Miss., April 28., '88.

EDITOR GAZETTE—We, the undersigned citizens of the southeastern portion this county, wish to correct a statement in your paper of April 14, headed, "Bull-Dozing—Two Negroes Whipped and One Killed." In justice to our community and those who are accused, we think it just and proper, that the true facts in the case should be stated. The parties accused, so far as we can ascertain, were not, and never have been, only on the best of terms with the two Kaiglers' and Joseph Prescott, and we most emphatically deny that these parties have been endeavoring to get information that would necessitate "regulating" them, as was stated in the issue of April 14. Nor can we find any proof, or even one, who had heard of Frank Warner being arrested and brutally beaten on Friday night, in view of making him tell something on the above named parties, until published. It was indeed a great surprise to the people of this section, and we think it very unfair and an injustice to our community to have such reports circulated, unless they were true. Neither was Frank caught on Sunday night and treated worse than before, a rope being placed around his neck, and told to answer questions put to him in the affirmative; as he will state himself, that such was not the case. On Monday, April 9th, some two or three gentlemen went to the field where Frank was working, had a lengthy conversation with him, then one of them placed him on a horse, and carried him to place of Inquest. On the same day, two went and took another boy out of the field and carried him to the place of Inquest, but unfortunately he could not give any information. and was allowed to return home. We have been informed that there was some little display of fire-arms at the inquest, which is indeed quite a surprise. In our weak judgments we thought at inquests and places of like character the citizens met quietly and peaceably, with a firm resolve to try and find out the perpetrators of such crimes and to bring the guilty parties to justice and to hold the same publicly and openly so as to let the public shed as much light on the case as possible, and not hold the same secretly as was done in this case. Nor can we understand why the testimony of the dying negro was ignored, which must have been the case as no attempt has been made to arrest those he recognized. Joseph Prescott made a state

ment before his death that he knew six of the parties who were instrumental in causing his death, four of whom reside in Louisiana and two in this State, who up to this time have not been arrested or molested. From the best information we can obtain the Coroner's jury did not charge the twenty-four white men with the murder of Joe Prescott; if so what authority did those men have in releasing those six men charged with the crime without any examination whatever, as such was the case? We have always understood that where a Coroner's jury charged a man or a set of men with a crime (especially murder) that they were compelled to stand an examination before they could be released. There was a young man fourteen or fifteen years of age arrested charged with the murder, who is not of sound mind and understanding. What the object was for having this young man arrested we do not know, unless they thought he could give some information. As was previously stated the inquest was held strictly secret no information whatever being given to the public. In face of the facts we can not see the necessity of putting a man on horseback and sending him to Magnolia after Capt. Boyd, sheriff—and several volunteered their services, together with their shot guns—to go at the hour of midnight to arrest a lot of men innocent of the existence of warrants for their arrest. We cannot give any reason why they preferred to go at night unless they knew it would be more pleasant traveling and wished to avoid the hot, cruel rays of old Phœbus.

Resolved, That this alliance deplore the action of the Governor of this State in the interview with the State Alliance Committee, and that we regard it as a blow struck against the existence of our order.

Resolved, That we, as an alliance, will not support Robert Lowry for any office of trust, proft or honor, and ask other alliances to do the same.

frank-warner-magnolia-1888-04-08.A7:
A DARK CORNER.
PIKE COUNTY, Miss., April 28, '88.

EDITOR SENTINEL: Dear Sir—The communication of the 27th inst., in the Osyka Two States, from Josiah Brumfield and others, of the vicinity of Dillons, headed a "Correction" in refutation of certain charges made by the editor of the MAGNOLIA GAZETTE, of April 14th inst., is of interest to the people of our county. It clearly shows the treachery of parties interested in these crimes. The editor of the Gazerre stated the facts as current in the vicinity of the crime, as will be seen when compared to the testimony of the witnesses for the State; with respect to the gentlemen whose names are to the communication, they have unquestionably put their names to an article written by one of the Bull-leezers, as the article itself clearly shows. Notwithstanding they have denied the statements in the Gazette and would have the public to believe that parties from a different direction committed the murder of Joe Prescott, the matter to the satisfaction of all rest closer to our doors than on parties away in Louisiana, as they would have you believe. In all these crimes, parties take different views as to who are the perpetrators. Some think one thing and some another, but in this case the evidence is conclusive, and settles the matter in one direction upon the parties sworn to by witnesses; however all are innocent, and yet crime after crime, blood and midnight terorizing is the order of the day. We do not censure people of one section more than we do another, but to say the least, there are different squads of these desperadoes in different localities and evidently have for their leaders some men who should be above suspicion in such crimes. They organized about two years ago. Their motive is, so far as can be ascertained, to drive from our county the colored population, doubtless to reduce farmers and merchants of high ability, to a common level. a species of anarchy, and should be suppressed at all hazards. To perpetrate these crimes, requires the basest element of human nature to be aroused, and only requires to be muttered and braced up by such men, as are lending the organization a helping hand, for it to ruin our otherwise prosperous county. We do hope that all good people will lend a helping hand to the speedy suppression of this state of affairs. Men who have not read newspapers since the war should not be leaders of organizations of any kind, more especially bull-dozing. [Anti-Bulldozer, in Summit Sentinel.

Special Dispatch to the Intelligencer.

CHARLESTON, W. VA., Sept. 21.—Geo, Simpson, colored, who attempted an indecent assault upon a respectable married white lady near Echo, Friday, and failed in his purpose, was jailed at Fayetteville. KILLED A MARSHAL
And Emptied a Revolver Into a Crowd Fears of Lynching. Special Dispatch to the Appeal.
And Emptied a Revolver Into a Crowd—Fears of Lynching.
Special Dispatch to the Appeal.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., May 1.—Late this afternoon George Martin was drunk and raised a row in front of a saloon in Warrior when Owen Kelly, acting marshal of the place, undertook to arrest him, whereupon Martin drew a pistol and shot the officer dead, then turned and ran, a crowd pursuing him. He turned and fired at them as he ran, emptying his revolver, but hitting no one. He was caught on the edge of town and taken back and locked up along with his brother, William, who is concerned in the original racket, and tonight it is feared an attempt will be made to lynch him. The mayor has telegraphed Sheriff Truss for help to protect him, and Truss is preparing to send several men and a lot of rifles up on the midnight train.

Perry Steel, a grown negro, was brought in from Oxmoor tonight and jailed on the somewhat remarkable charge of raping a girl of his own color. The alleged victim is Hattie Mitchell, a twelve-year-old.
george-martin-warrior-1888-05-01.A2:
MURDAR AND LYNCHING.
Tragic End of a Fight Between Two Miners at Warrior.
Miners at Warrior.

BIRMINGHAM, ALA., May 1.—Two miners created an affray at Warrior, in this county to-night. One of them named George Martin shot and instantly killed Deputy Marshal Kelly. Martin was arrested, and the officers smuggled him aboard the caboose car of a freight train bound for this city, but a mob cut the caboose loose from the train, captured Martin, and hanged him, and filled his body with bullets. Martin's brother, who was with the lynched man in the row, is yet alive and will be brought here.
george-martin-warrior-1888-05-01.A4:
A NERVY MAN

Lynched by a Mob Near Birmingham.

The Train Which Carries Him Is Held Up by the Vigilantes.
He Asks One of the Guards for a Gun to Protect Himself.
This is Refused, and He Walks Right Into the Howling Mob.
He is Hanged to a Tree After Asking the Lynchers to Do No Harm to His Brother, Who is With Him.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.
Special Dispatch to The Appeal.

BIRMINGHAM, Ala., May 2.—Sheriff Truss made ready last night with three deputies to go to Warrior, twenty miles north of here, on the midnight train to help defend from mob law George Martin, who in the afternoon, while resisting arrest, had shot and killed Acting Town Marsnal Owen Kelley. Just before their train came through Truss received a telegram saying Martin had been safely placed aboard a freight train and would be brought here, then a little later came another telegram saying the train was detained by a mob, and upon its arrival here at 2:30 o'clock it brought news of Martin's fate at the hands of the latter. The officers had thought to get ahead of the would-be lynchers, but they heard the prisoner was about to be shipped. They made a rush for the train and captured it, and while some of them stood guard over the engineer and fireman others uncoupled the caboose in which were Martin, his brother William and the officers, and pushed it several rods up the track where they took Martin from the officers and hung him to a tree, then half a dozen of them emptied the contents of their guns and pistols into his body, killing him almost instantly. He already had one pistol wound which was given by one of his pursuers yesterday. There were four guards in the car with Martin. He walked to the door of the car and addressing the mob told them that he alone had committed the murder, and his brother should not be held responsible for it. He then returned to the guards and asked them for a gun, remarking that if they were not able to protect him he would protect himself. The request being refused, Martin deliberately walked out into the crowd and told them to take him, but to spare his brother William Martin, who was arrested for the same brawl for which Kelley wanted George.

William was left in the hands of the officers, and by them brought to the city, bespattered with his brother's blood, and jailed. Owen Kelley had not served as marshal twenty-four hours. He was filling the place of his kinsman, Marshal John Kelley, who left the night before for Knoxville to bring back William Dodd, who killed a man in a fight at Warrior about two weeks ago, and barely escaped a mob.
george-martin-warrior-1888-05-01.A12:
WARRIOR.
Murder and Jude Lynch Busy.
Warrior, Ala., May 2, '88.
1. BREEDING.
Secretary protem.

Yesterday the peace of our quiet town was broken by another terrible crime—another murder—a soul sent all unprepared before its maker.

George and Will Martin were drunk and disorderly. Acting Town Marshall, Owen Kelly, interfered in behalf of law and order, where upon Geo, Martin sent a leaden missile into the officer, murdering him outright.

The Martins fled into the country but were captured and lodged in the Guard House. Lynching being feared, the officers tried to slip the prisoners to Birmingham on a freight train.

A mob of several hundred men put in an appearance and taking George Martin carried him about a hundred yards and hanged him to a limb; afterward riddling his body with bullets. His body was left dangling in the air.

Here is another temperance lecture. Whiskey is at the bottom of nine-tenths of the evils of the day Down with the whiskey monster and hoist the Prohibition banner high over the country. W. J. C.

TELEGRAPHIC BREVITIES.
Melon, O., had a fire which destroyed $100,000 worth of property.

The Standard Oil hearing by Congress is closed for the present.

Seven people were cremated in a barn at Arlington, Neb., Saturday.

The Methodist bishops in conference at New York are still debating the eligibility of women as lay delegates.

A company with a capital stock of $1,000,000 has been organized at Birmingham, Ala., to manufacture steel by a new process.

A severe windstorm at Laconia, Io., unroofed several buildings and blew down one, burrying in the ruins a farmer named Leonard Wilson.

C. J. Rutgers, a prominent Trenton, (N. J.) lawyer, committed suicide Saturday by hanging himself with a handkerchief.

John L. and Samuel Black, brothers, in business at Virginia City, Nev., got into a quarrel in which Samuel killed his brother.

The Army of the Potomac Saturday petitioned Congress for $23,000 to help along the reunion of that army and the Army of Virginia.

The Democratic members of congress presented a gold lock and key to Mr. Enloe for his efforts in breaking the deadlock on the direct tax bill.

Three stills and five moonshiners were captured in the last raid of United States revenue officers in the Clay and Cleburne Counties, Ala.

The farmers near Owensboro, Ky., were called from their houses by a mob and whipped severely, and then warned to leave the county.

Jose Martin, living at Albuquerque, N. M., was shot and killed by a man named Vincente Armijo, for trying to gain entrance into a room where Armijo was, with some others.

William Carson, a son of the famous "Kit" Carson, shot and killed a man at Fort Garland, Colo., in self-defence, the man attacking him with a bowne-knife.

George Martin, while resisting arrest at Warrior, Ala., Thursday, killed the Deputy Marshal, Owen Kelly. At 11 o'clock he was swung from a tree by a mob. This makes the third lynching in that county within a month.

William Herman, living near Leavenworth, Kan., while unhitching a team of mules on his return from the funeral of a member of his family was kicked by one of the mules and died from the injuries.

A desperate fight took place in Chinatown, San Francisco. Friday between four Chinamen, members of rival highbinder societies. By the time the police reached the scene three of the men were fatally wounded.

A case which is puzzling the doctors is that of a 16-year-old boy named Frierson at Columbia, S. C., who had his head laid open by machinery, exposing a portion of his brain. He still lives and may recover.

Mrs. Charlotte Smith of the Woman's industrial League has preferred charges before a Senate Committee against the Chief Clerk of the Treasury Department on the ground that he does not "eat the chairwomen fairly.

Frederick Siedel, a three-year convict in the Ohio prison, and who has been acting as engineer for some time, got caught in the huge fly-wheel of his engine and was literally torn to pieces, parts of his body being found scattered all about the engine-room.

Morgan Hunter, who was under indictment at Chattanooga, Tenn., for the murder of Frank Dearman, at Dayton, Tenn., jumped his $5,000 bond and escaped. After his escape his wife re-lated a horrible story of the crime and how she was forced to be a witness to it.

Henry Pope, colored, was lynched ed at Summerville, Ga., on a charge of assulting a 16-year-old girl. The girl stated positively that he was the man, although several prominent citizens swore that he was fifty miles away at the time the crime was committed.

Gen. Wirt Adams, Postmaster, of Jackson, Miss., and a well-known Mississippi statesman, fought a duel with John H. Martin, Editor of the New Mississippi. At Bennettsville, S. C., Dock Dargar, a negro boy, deliberately shot with a gun and instantly killed a white boy, W. E. Coxe, Jr. All the parties lived near Bennettsville. The negro is in jail there. Several attempts have been made to lynch him. The sheriff keeps the jail guarded. A number of enraged men shot into the house of Essex Dargar, the father of the murderer, and killed a three year old child. The entire section is aroused.

The announcement that Col. W. L. Scruggs would accept the editorship of the prohibition weekly at Atlanta seems to have premature. It is now said that Col. John William Jones, the historian, will be selected to fill the position. Col. Scruggs is a regular contributor to the North American Review, but on account of his being a Republican it was thought best not to select him. The first issue of the paper is expected to appear on May 8th.

Two miners engaged in an affray at Warrior, Ala., a few days ago. One of them, George Martin, shot and instantly killed Deputy Marshal Kelly. He was arrested. The mayor of Warrior telegraphed the sheriff to come quickly with a posse to resist the mob and miners and protect the prisoner. The officers smuggled Martin aboard a freight train. A MAN ACCUSED OF BURGLARY STRUNG UP TO MAKE
HIM CONFESS.
CHICAGO, Feb. 3.—A special from Decatur, Tex..
CHICAGO, Feb. 3.—A special from Decatur, Tex., says Jas. Anderson and Henry Harvey were arrested at Chico, Wise County, yesterday, charged with burglary. The constable started for Decatur, taking Anderson with him and leaving Harvey with a guard at Chico. Late last night a party of twelve men took Harvey from the guard and strung him up twice. After he had been up some time he was cut down, nearer dead than alive. Harvey stoutly maintained his innocence, asking time to pray, after which he said he was ready to die. The county authorities will investigate the affair.

the Reported Lynching of Joe Hovey is True in every Particular—More Gold Talk

Special to the Gazette.

DECATUR, TEX., Feb. 4.—The special sent from Decatur about the lynching of the party, Joe Hovey, at Chico, Tuesday night, was literally true as stated. It is deeply regretted and condemned by the good people of the Chico country, as that scotton had been the most law-abiding neighborhood in Wise county heretofore, and the great majority look with horror upon mob law and summary justice. Clara Foltz, the lady lawyer, political orator and ex-editress, has filed an affidavit with the San Diego (Cal.) county clerk, stating that she is entitled to vote, and requests that her name be placed on the great register. It is understood that she will make a test case of it at the fall election.

A naval guard on the Prussian model is being organized at all South Russian sea ports. The object is to reinforce the mariners and to supply crews to merchant ships equipped for war. The German and Italian governments have each ordered the construction of two torpedo boats at Elbind, Prussia.

The London police are endeavoring to prevent the fight between Sullivan and Mitchell, and have been keeping a close watch on Sullivan's quarters at the Windsor. Wednesday they were astounded to find that Sullivan had disappeared. It is not known where he has gone. The police are completely baffled.

It is rumored at Mount Pleasant that Homer Hart and Oliver Hart, father and son, who were arrested Friday on the charge of assaulting the 5-year-old daughter of the last named, have been lynched. He was in charge of an engine when Roxy and others approached the engine and endeavored to take charge of it. An altercation ensued and Roxy drew a pistol. Bostwick then shot him in self-defense.

St. Joseph, Mo., Jan. 29.—[Special Telegram to the BEE.]—A parallel of the cold-blooded wife murder of last April in this city, for which a Bohemian named Hronek is now in the Buchanan county jail under death sentence, occurred to-day in the murder of Mrs. Flora Bulling by her husband, Louis Bulling.

Bulling is twenty-five years old and a son of sixteen years old and a son
desperate struggle to escape but was captured and taken away by the police.
A howling mob was soon on their heels, discovering which the police secreted Bulling.
There is no question but if he can be found to night he will be swung to the nearest lamp-post without ceremony.
Bulling has nothing to say about his crime.
He is one of the most desperate ruffians in the city, and for several years has terrorized South St. Joseph. While engaged in a fight about two years ago with a country fellow Bulling had his left ear bitten off. This ear he carries in his vest pocket as a "mascot."
In shaking dice at saloon counters he frequently pulled the bit of shriveled flesh out of his pocket and put it upon the counter beside him. A couple of weeks ago he tried to force his way into Tootle's opera house on the representation that he was a policeman and it took a half dozen men to remove him. The family to which Bulling belongs is a large and wealthy one. It exerts considerable influence politically and altogether is one of the most prominent in this community, and his father and uncles have held numerous offices in the city and county.

A Batch of Crime From St. Joe, Mo., Which is Appalling.

ST. JOSEPH MO.
Special to the Globe.

ST. JOSEPH, Mo., Jan. 30.—Buchanan county added another to her list of murders last night. The coroner was still examining witnesses in the Bulling wife murder case when the news was brought to him by telegram that a murder had been committed at Wallace's, eighteen miles from this city. The names and particulars were not learned till to-day. William Ester, eighteen years old, shot and instantly killed William Blakely, also aged eighteen years, at 7:30 last night. The murder took place at the front of the Christian church. Young Blakely was keeping company with Ester's sister, a sixteen-year-old girl, to which the brother and father objected. A few weeks ago old man Ester flogged the girl because she refused to drop Blakely, whereupon she left home, living since with a friend. Last night she and Blakely were at church together. At the close of services old man Ester went to his daughter and had some words with her. Blakely then offered to turn her over to her father, and advised her to go home with him. This she refused to do, and went out of church with her lover. A few yards beyond the door the two met young Ester, the girl's brother, who at once drew a revolver and began firing. The fellow had been to church, and it is supposed left before the services were over in order to get his revolver. The first shot struck Blakely on the lower lip, knocking out two of his front teeth and lodging in the back part of the head. He then drew his revolver and returned the fire without effect. The father of the girl, who had been watching the affray, at this juncture drew a revolver and began shooting at Blakely. The latter turned from the son to the old man and, firing, wounded him in the shoulder. This left Blakely at the mercy of young Ester, who stepped up close and sent a bullet through his heart. Wallace is greatly excited over the murder. Blakely belonged to one of the best families of this county and was above reproach in every way. No reason, except personal grounds, could have been urged against him keeping company with the young lady. The Ester family does not stand so well. The younger Ester is a hard case and has been in several scrapes. Both father and son would have been lynched last night could they have been found.

THE BULLING MURDER.

Mrs. John Bulling, the mother of Joseph Bulling, who murdered his wife at the Herbert house yesterday afternoon, stated that the immediate cause of the murder was a fancy masquerade ball which Flora, the wife, attended on Saturday evening. Bulling was forced to marry his wife about four years ago and since that time has fallen desperately in love with her. The woman is remarkably pretty and has a number of admirers, among them a young man in town who represents one of the best families. It is this young man of whom Bulling was jealous, and for whom he claimed his wife forsook him. He is now trying to come the insanity dodge. Last night he was put in Cell No. 8, the one occupied by Peter Hoonck, the Bohemian, who murdered his wife about eighteen months ago. When the deputy sheriff opened the cell door this morning Bulling was sitting up with several blankets wrapped around him, pretending to be shivering with cold. He wanted to know if he would lose his job. Later on he was informed that his wife was buried at 3 o'clock this afternoon, and he requested that he be allowed to attend the funeral, which was refused him. There is no little excitement and talk of lynching.

SHOT HIMSELF.

Frank Gesthauser, son of a wealthy farmer living near the town of Platte River, this county, shot himself through the body while hunting Saturday and died this morning from the effect of the wound.

YORKVILLE, S. C. :
WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 8, 1888.
MERE-MENTION.
President and Mrs. Cleveland have concluded to pay a flying visit to the Subtropical Exposition in Jacksonville, Fla., during the latter part of this month. The Senate has confirmed the nomination of Beckford Mackey to be consul at Paso del Norte. He is a son of ex-Judge Mackey, and is credited to South Carolina. The Republican State Convention of Mississippi has been called to meet in Jackson tomorrow for the purpose of electing delegates to the national convention. Mr. and Mrs. Brunner, of Aurora, Mo., who recently inherited $70,000 from a relative, have mysteriously disappeared. It is supposed that they were murdered for their money, which was kept in their house at that place. J. W. Miller, a painter who left Union, S. C., recently, was found frozen to death in Decatur, Ala. His wife is living at Union. Woman suffrage has been defeated in Wisconsin. The City Council of Santa Rosa, California, has passed an ordinance making it a criminal offence to sell cigarettes to boys under sixteen years of age. It has also prohibited boys from smoking cigarettes upon the streets or in public places. Greene Henderson, a colored man, has been arrested in Atlanta for selling the body of his dead wife to the medical college. Florida strawberries are selling in New York at $2.50 a quart. John Greenwood was arrested at Livingston, Tenn., Friday morning, on a charge of murder. He is accused of killing Andrew Wilson seventeen years ago. It is estimated that the Chinese merchants of New York pay the United States government over $2,500,000 per year for duties on imported goods. The ten cents special delivery stamp has proved a financial failure. There is a proposition before the people of Rhode Island to so amend the constitution of the State as to abolish all property qualifications for voters in its elections. The Catholic convent property in Hickory, N. C., has been sold to the Ohio Lutheran Synod. It will be converted into a school under the auspices of the Lutheran church. The National Democratic Executive Committee will meet in Washington on the 22nd instant to decide upon a place of meeting for the nominating convention. The women living in the southeastern part of St. Joseph, Mo., are circulating a petition to have Hoonick and Buelling, two men in jail charged with wife murder, lynched. Lent comes earlier this season than for many years past. It begins on February 15th. Easter Sunday is on April 1. The Governor of Georgia has commuted the sentence of Eliza Randall, who was to have been hanged in Clay county last Friday, to imprisonment for life. Eliza is a young white girl, who deliberately murdered her father a few months ago because he wanted her to attend church. Public sentiment against the infliction of capital punishment on a woman was what saved her from the gallows. Under a legal decision in the Iowa Courts that permits to sell liquor for legal purposes can be used only by the persons to whom issued, the stock of every wholesale liquor firm in Des Moines was seized last Wednesday. Each firm does business under the company title, and the Judge's ruling forbids such latitude. Statistics of life insurance show that there are now 820,000 policies in this country, representing an aggregate insurance of $2,100,-000,000. Governor McEnery, of Louisiana, has called a convention to meet in New Orleans on March 5 to encourage immigration into the State. The Mississippi House of Representatives has adopted a memorial to Congress, protesting against the passage of the Senate bill having for its object the prevention of the use of cotton seed oil as a substitute for hog's lard. Chicago speculators propose to buy the old Libby Confederate prison in Richmond and remove it to Chicago. According to statistics gathered by the Railroad Gazette, there were in December last ninety-two railroad collisions, eighty-three derailments and seven other accidents, making 182 in all; in which seventy-one persons were killed and 211 injured. At Newcastle, Cal., there is a famous fig tree. One foot from the ground it measures eight feet four inches in circumference, and its branches cover 2,500 feet of surface. Revenue officers in Alabama captured several stills, 16,000 gallons of whisky and seven moonshiners last Friday. There are twenty-one iron furnaces idle in Pennsylvania in consequence of strikes. A band of strolling gypsies, arrested at Providence, R. I., a day or two ago, were found to have $9,000 in gold tied up in rags with them. Earthquakes have been felt recently in Vermont, New Hampshire and Maine. At Birmingham, Ala., last Saturday evening, Tom Ellis, editor of the Hornet, was shot and mortally wounded by a detective named Sullivan. Ellis published a statement in his paper concerning Sullivan which the latter regarded as libelous. Wm. Showers, of Lebanon, Pa., who murdered his two grandchildren, has been sentenced to be hanged. Business failures occurring throughout the country during last week number for the United States 247, Canada 32; total 279, against 217 the preceding week.

MISSOURI STATE NEWS.
Governor Morehouse has pardoned Albert McIntosh, sentenced to the penitentiary for fifteen years in 1887. He is in the last stages of consumption.

Governor Morehouse has pardoned Albert Hawkins, serving a sixty-days' sentence in Jackson County for receiving stolen goods.

Josiah White, aged thirty-five, was working over a lard tank in Fowler's packing-house at Kansas City. a few days ago, when his foot slipped on the oily board and he plunged headlong into the boiling grease. Before he could be rescued he was dead. Every particle of flesh on his head, arms and shoulders was cooked off and his chest was burned through to the lungs, the bones crumbling away under the touch.

The dead body of August Jansen, whose mysterious disappearance created a great stir at Lexington recently, was found against a tree on the Carroll County side of the river below Lexington. He had evidently wandered away while in an intoxicated condition, and being overcome by the cold, was frozen to death. The finding of the body clears up the suspicion of murder which prevailed among his friends.

The St. Louis police force is at present made up of a chief, six captains, forty-five sergeants, ten detectives, forty mounted men and 400 footmen.

Joseph Crouch, of St. Joseph, deserted his wife and family recently and went to Kansas on an evangelizing tour as a Baptist preacher. Mrs. Crouch was furnished a ticket to Corning Kas., and proceeded there to corner her recreant spouse.

The receiver of the defunct Fifth National Bank of St. Louis is paying a first dividend of fifty per cent. to the depositors of the institution.

A stranger, supposed to be Franz Mueller, from Buffalo, N. Y., committed suicide in St. Louis a few days ago by shooting himself in the mouth with a pistol.

Herman Kamp, assistant book-keeper in Gildehaus, Wulfing & Co.'s wholesale grocery house in St. Louis, committed suicide a few days since by shooting himself in the left breast. His accounts with the firm were all right, but he had expended $865 intrusted to him to deposit for safe-keeping by a Mrs. Bamberger, in paying his own debts. He was twenty-five years of age and unmarried, his parents living in Germany.

The miners in the Lexington coal mines have agreed to a reduction in wages for six months.

The name of the post-office at Bradley, Carroll County, has been changed to Bosworth, and the site removed two and a half miles southeast.

The post-office at Elks Grove, Caldwell County, is discontinued, and the mail will go to Black Oak.

The open season on quail, ruffled grouse, prairie chickens, doves and wild turkey is closed, and it is now a violation of the law to shoot this species of game in the State.

At a recent meeting of the Kansas City police commissioners, Patrolmen Rademacher and Ryan were dismissed for leaving their boats while on duty, and Fitspatrick for being found asleep on duty.

The arrest of Mrs. Saloma Mattingly, on a charge of poisoning two fine horses belonging to H. C. White, has created excitement in Aurora and vicinity. She is well known, and is the mother of an interesting family and stood well in social circles. Many believe her entirely innocent.

Collector Lancaster of St. Louis, in his report of customs collections for the month of January, shows a large and steady increase over the same month for the past four years. In proof of this he submitted the following figures, showing the receipts for January since 1885: January, 1888, $122,009; January, 1887, $100,-133; January, 1886, $90,846; January, 1885, $58,241. Increase for January, 1888, over 1887, $21,870.50; over 1886, $31,160; over 1885, $63,768.

The groundhog cautiously emerged from his hole on Candlemas Day and peered around on all sides to look for his shadow. The obscured sun left the little animal shadowless, so he showed his teeth, which is his way of smiling. Finding the sky overclouded he boldly set out on a tour of the country surrounding his hole, and as the day wore off and the sun failed to put in an appearance, he gave up the idea of going back into his retreat. It is, therefore, certain that winter is ever, and that spring will soon make its appearance even before the appointed time.

The transactions of the State Treasurer for the month ending January 31, 1888, as reported by Treasurer J. M. Seibert, are as follows: Balance on hand January 1, 1888, $479,986.18; receipts during January, $1,054,377.51; disbursements during January, $227,516.51; balance on hand February 1, 1888, $1,293,847.19. The penitentiary earnings during the month were $14,723.65, and disbursements a like amount.

The petition alre ady has several hundred signatures.

The position secured for Mr. Henry H. Marmaduke, brother of the late Governor of Missouri, is custodian of the vaults of the United States Treasury. It is a position of responsibility worth $2,000 a year. Mr. Marmaduke has not entered upon the duties, and it is a question whether he will do so until his political disabilities are removed. A bill to accomplish this is pending, and will go through Congress as rapidly as the formalities will permit. Mr. Marmaduke's disabilities were incurred by his course at the outbreak of the war, when he was a cadet in the Naval Academy.

George Ritter, formerly in the employ of the William Barr Dry Goods Company, of St. Louis, from whom he embezzled $1,000, has been brought back from California, whither he had fled, and will be prosecuted by the firm.

No more German in St. Louis schools.

J. E. Prosser, assistant foreman of the St. Joseph Daily News, went to the river to skate a few evenings since. He was last seen on the ice skating, and the supposition is that he fell into an air hole and was drowned. He was about twenty-five years of age.

Henry Ross committed suicide in the Good Samaritan Hospital, St. Louis, by hanging.
The Fourth National Bank of St. Louis has increased its capital stock to $1,000,-000.
The St. Louis Cable & Western railway return for the past quarter shows 44,128 trips made and 1,035,381 passengers carried.
The Merchants' Association of St. Joseph has again inaugurated the plan of getting up excursions from the towns and villages contiguous to St. Joseph. The first in the series will be from Brookfield, on the Hannibal & St. Jo road, which will occur on the 24th inst., to be followed on the 25th by one from Burlington Junction, and on the 26th by one from Bedford, Ia.

The old landmark, Barnum's Hotel, in St. Louis, has been sold to the Meyer Drug Company, who will remodel it and make an immense wholesale drug house of it.
The division encampment of the Sons of Veterans, U. S. A., will take place at Kansas City, June 4 to June 8.
Governor Morehouse will not interfere in the contest between State Oil Inspector Baggot and the Waters-Pierce Oil Company.
The deeds and money in the purchase of the Tyler tract in St. Louis have been exchanged between Mr. Sam Scott, of Kansas City, and Mrs. Tyler, the total consideration being $750,000.
Louis Buelling was convicted at St. Joseph of murder in the second degree for killing his wife last January.
The journeymen carpenters of Kansas City have decided to strike June 1 for thirty cents an hour. They are now getting twenty and twenty-five cents. Of the 1,900 carpenters in Kansas City 700 are members of the union.

Robert Spencer, a pensioner, who was tried recently in the United States Court at St. Louis, for raising a pension check from $6 to $3,000, pleaded guilty and was sentenced to imprisonment for one year in the Kansas State prison.

Considerable excitement was occasioned on the St. Louis Produce Exchange by the failure of Moses Fraley, a prominent bear, a few days since. He settled with his creditors on a compromise.

Fire a few nights ago destroyed the Kansas City Furniture Company's warehouse. Loss on stock, $12,000; on building, owned by Brooks Adams, of Boston, $8,000; fully insured.

Dr. George E. Hayden dropped dead from heart disease in the Brisbane building in Kansas City a few evenings since. He was a well-known physician, published the Farm Journal, owned a livery stable and ran the Berry Printing Company.

Charles B. Willard pleaded guilty at Kansas City to the charge of breaking into the house of Edward M. Weier on February 14, and stealing a large amount of money and clothing, and was sentenced to twelve years in the penitentiary by Judge White.

Governor Morehouse refused to honor a requisition from the Governor of Kansas for the return to that State of the Uhlmans, who now reside in St. Joseph. They are wanted in Kansas for violating the Prohibition law. They have resided in Missouri for four years.

Fire broke out in the factory of the Curtis Manufacturing Company, in St. Louis a few nights ago, and totally destroyed the stock and building, which were estimated to be worth $25,000, and were supposed to have been insured fully.

J. H. Rice, Government contractor, is in St. Joseph and has given orders to have the Eighth and Edmond streets walls of the custom-house torn down, on account of the weakening of the foundation. There has been $50,000 appropriated by Congress for this purpose.

Fire broke out in the Bethel Home, a five-story building situated on the corner of Olive street and the Levee, in St. Louis, a few nights ago, and not less than three, and probably more persons lost their lives by being burned to death.

Rev. B. F. Rice died at his residence in St. Joseph a few days since. He was a Baptist minister. He leaves a wife and seven children. One of his daughters, Maggie, is a Baptist missionary in Brazil. Mr. Rice was born in Buchanan County in 1836. Recently she was pastor of the church at Balcow and Mount Vernon, near Savannah.

A valuable two-year-old filly owned by Thomas Moore, on Noix creek, near Louisiana, died of hydrophobia a few days since. Five months ago the animal was bitten by a rabid dog, and since the occurrence appeared to be in a fearful mood. She gnawed herself so that the flesh was bare to the bone, with the hide hanging in long strips.

The Woman's Missionary Board of the Methodist church for Southwest Missouri meets in Lexington next month, and one hundred delegates are expected to be present. The session will continue about four days. A number of delegates and visitors are expected from Nashville, Tenn.

The second annual session of the Missouri State Board of Anatomy met at Kansas City last week. Fourteen medical colleges have members in the board, nine which were represented at the meeting. The following officers were electe to serve during the ensuing year: Dr. Chas. A. Todd, St. Louis, president; Dr. John W. Vaughan, St. Louis, secretary; Dr. John T. Eggers, Kansas City, treasurer; Dr. Charles H. Lester, Kansas City, first vice-president; Dr. J. W. Heddens, St. Joseph, second vice-president; Dr. Woodson Moss, Columbia, third vice-president.
Annie Stegman, thirty-seven years of age, residing with her husband and six children in St. Louis, committed suicide a few days ago by taking paris green. She had spent a large sum of money belonging to her brother and could not replace it.

There were 375 members initiated during the year, while a total of 89 members are classed as withdrawn, suspended and died. The financial statement shows that the cash receipts were $2,441.55 and the expenditures $2,441.36.

St. Louis, June 29.—A special to the Post-Dispatch from St. Joseph, Missouri, says: Peter Hronek was hanged to-day at 1 p. m., for the murder of his wife on April 17, 1887. The prisoner has borne up bravely and denied any intent to commit the crime. He rested easily last night and arose this morning at six, ate a light breakfast and after religious consolation was conducted to the scaffold, accompanied by his religious advisers. He preserved his firmness to the last, exhibiting only slight symptoms of weakening. After the usual preliminaries the trap was sprung at 1:10 p. m. and in seven minutes Hronek was pronounced dead and the body cut down and taken to the cathedral of St. Peter and Paul. He will be buried by the side of his wife in the Polish cemetery.

The crime for which Hronek was hanged was the murder of his wife, committed April 17, 1887. He had accused her of intimacy with a man living in the same house and had frequently threatened to kill her. On this day while intoxicated he purchased a revolver and went home about 8 o'clock in the evening. Without a word of warning he fired at his wife, the shot taking effect in her breast. He immediately fired a second shot which penetrated her brain. When arrested he declared that he had killed her because of her infidelity, though he later disavowed all knowledge of the murder. Hronek was about thirty-two years old. He was a Bohemian and came to this country ten years ago. Six years after his arrival he sent to Bohemia for his wife whom he had known from childhood and on her arrival they were married at Easton, Missouri. Until within a few weeks of the murder they had lived happily and had a child, a little girl, two years of age, who, since the tragedy, has been cared for by a farmer neighbor of the murderer.

Just about the time when Teemer was disembarking O'Connor, at John Cumberland's, took to the water, and after circling round for awhile started down the course. He pulled very steadily, and so smooth was his stroke that the shell was on an even keel throughout the entire half hour he was out. Both men took a smart walk after leaving their respective boat-houses.

The Senate cattle trade investigating committee met again in St. Louis yesterday. Several witnesses gave damaging evidence against the alleged dressed-beef combine.

In Virginia there are 15 colleges at which branches of the Young Men's Christian association are established, and 1,100 out of 2,000 are members.

Simon Dinningan, of New York, an inmate of the soldiers' home at Hampton, Va., committed suicide Wednesday night by severing an artery in his wrist.

The Mexican cabinet ministers have handed in their resignations, that President Diaz may have full liberty to appoint a new cabinet for the new term, beginning December 1. Many rumors are afloat, though it is probable that the only changes will be war and justice. Lancaster Jones will probably be minister of justice.

Jerry Taylor, a negro, was lynched in St. Helena parish, La., last night for criminally assaulting the thirteen-year-old daughter of Mr. J. C. Williams.

Judge Rucker denies that he sent a challenge to Senator Blackburn.

The acolytes in a Chicago Episcopal Church go on strike because the master of ceremonies is not discharged at their request.

A SAD TRAGEDY.
ONE MAN DEAD AND ANOTHER SAID TO BE DYING.
A Mother Dies from a Shock-A Pistol-Ball Prevents a Lynch- isg.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
ABINGDON, VA., July 23.—The saddest tragedy that ever happened in this community took place last Saturday evening. A desperate man named John Grayson, of Johnson county, Tenn., was in town in company with his uncle and others from his neighborhood. Grayson had been drinking some, and he and another man had ridden through town on horseback with the avowed purpose of going home. Rescending within two and a half or three squares of the east end of Main street Grayson and his companion came up with a wagon from his section of the county and all stopped in front of the colored Methodist Episcopal church and began parleying. Grayson's companion was seen to hand a flask to the driver of the wagon, and about the same time Grayson drew a pistol from his pocket and fired it in the air, and then turned it towards his companion. At this juncture Mr. Liliburn Trigg, a citizen of the town, who was passing on his wav home a square and a half beyond, seeing the danger of Grayson's companion went over to him and, leaving his left hand kindly on Grayson's shoulder, expositulated with him and told him not to shoot. Immediately Grayson turned on Mr. Trigg with the remark: "What the h—I have you got to do with it?" and placing his pistol (a thirty-eight-calibre bulldog) against Trigg's left shoulder-blade fired. Mr. Trigg fell down at once, dragging Grayson off his horse. Grayson sprang to his feet and fled. As he was running, and amidst the cries of a large crowd which had gathered around the scene, in less time than it takes for the telling to "Catch the murderer," "Stop him," the report of another shot was heard in the direction of Grayson's flight. But Grayson went on, and before he passed Mr. Trigg's home the latter's father, who had heard the cries to catch him, and being a constable, ran from his porch to the street to arrest Grayson, who was still in flight, carrying his pistol in front of him at arm's length in a menacing manner. Constable Trigg called on Mr. Samuel Mothner, who was standing in his store door near by, to help arrest the man. Mr. Mothner sprang
the Trigg called on Mr. Samuel Mothner, who was standing in his store door near by, to help arrest the man. Mr. Mothner sprang out, and running up behind Grayson caught him around the arms and tripped him to the ground face-foremost, at once taking the pistol from his hands. Help came to Mothner, and at once it was discovered that Grayson had been shot in the left side at the back. Mr. Litburn Trigg was in the mean time carried home, and his mother when she saw her son being carried in apparently dead was so shocked that it was supposed the excitement caused the rupture of some artery. That night about 1 o'clock she died. Physicians had been called, and were attending the wounded, the slayer, and his victim, but none till just before her death had any idea that Mrs. Trigg was so sorely afflicted. By 5 o'clock the next morning Grayson was dead, the ball with which he had been struck having passed through him and lodged in the abdominal muscles in front, whence it was extracted. Just before dying he made his attendant raise him up, when he asked, "What did that man shoot me for?" His nurse, a colored man, asked him if he didn't know he had shot a man and killed a woman, to which he made no reply, but burying his face in his pillow soon died. His victim still lingers, but at death's door with but a slight chance for recovery, and not aware of his mother's death. Mrs. Trigg was interred to-day. She was esteemed as one of the most fervent Christians in the land.

Such is the high state of the pulse of public sentiment that if Grayson had not died from his wound after Mrs. Trigg's death he would have been lynched. It is not certainly known who shot Grayson, but the general sentiment is his being shot in flight only saved him from a more ignominious ending.

ABINGDON, V.A., July 24.—Mr. Lilburne Trigg, the first victim of the dreadful tragedy enacted here last Saturday evening and reported in yesterday's Dispatch, died today shortly after 2 o'clock. The gloom caused by this deplorable affair hangs heavily over this community and awakens the deepest sympathies for the bereaved family, and the end is not yet.

Mr. Trigg's wife is so overcome with grief, anxiety, and constant watching by her husband, auxiliary, and constant watcher by her husband's bedside that she is now quite ill, though it is hoped not dangerously so. Then, too, news has reached here that Grayson's mother was so shocked at the news of her son's death that her life is hanging by a thread and almost despaired of. In fact, it was rumored that she was dead, but later tidings have shown this to be incorrect.

The Federal courts—Judge John Paul presiding—convened here to-day in special session, the spring term having been postponed for want of funds. The criminal and civil dockets are very large, and the number of persons brought here from all over the district is the largest in attendance upon the sessions of these courts for several years; and while this is true your correspondent remarks that there is seen less drunkenness and disorder on the streets of the town than ever before. An ordinance conspicuously posted about public places and which directs all persons seen drunk or disorderly in the streets to be put in jail and there kept till sober, and then to be fined on conviction, is having a salutary effect.

A Series of Sensational Tragedies in a Virginia Town.

BRISTOL, VA., July 25.—John Grayson, of Johnson county, Tenn., got drunk at Abingdon yesterday, and, drawing a pistol, commenced firing in the air.

Fearing some accident, Lewis Trigg asked Grayson to be more careful. Grayson, with an oath, presented his weapon at Trigg and shot him through the left breast. Grayson then fled up the road, pursued by an excited mob.

As Grayson ran he neared the house of young Trigg's father, who is a constable, and who, hearing the shouts of the crowd, came out to arrest the murderer. Just as he left the house a shot was heard and Grayson fell to the road dead. A moment later young Trigg was brought home seemingly dead. The sight so shocked his mother that she fainted and died in a few minutes. Trigg is thought to be fatally wounded, but may recover.

KNOXVILLE, Tenn., July 26. —The people of Abingdon, Va., are intensely excited over a terrible tragedy recently enacted in their midst. A well-known citizen named Millburn Trigg tried to pacify Grayson, but was himself shot, and so badly injured that he died. Tragedy in Virginia.
ABINGTON. Va., July 25.—On Monday, John Grayson, of Johnson-town, came to Abington, and while drunk drew a pistol from his pocket and turned the weapon toward his companion. Lilburn Trigg, a citizen, seeing the danger, laid his hand on Grayson's shoulder and expostulated with him. Immediately Grayson turned on Trigg and shot him in the left shoulder. Grayson fled, followed by an angry crowd and was finally shot down. Trigg was in the meantime carried home, and his mother, when she saw her son apparently dead, was so shocked that she died. By ten o'clock the next morning Grayson was dead. If Grayson had not died from his wounds he would have been lynched.

Let the Laboring Man Look to His Interest.
As the Norfolk Landmark says, "if men, will only take the trouble to look into this question of tariff taxation for protection they are bound to see that it is wrong. There is no other conclusion possible for the fair and intelligent thinker. It is simply levying a tax on me to pay you or levying a tax on you to pay me as the case may be, and it happens so that through a whole generation the tax rests upon the same class and another class gets the entire benefit; there is no reciprocity and in the nature of things cannot be. The protected capitalist says: "I am a tariff man because I can make more money by it!" "It puts more money in my pocket and therefore I am for it!" The poor man should retort, "And I am opposed to it because it takes money out of my pocket instead of putting it in, and, what is worse, takes it out of mine in order to put it into yours!"

There are thousands and tens of thousands of the latter class to tens and hundreds of the former, and yet, strange that it should be true, those who profit and "make fortunes every year when times are prosperous" are able to so obscure and confuse the thought of the working people that they go on from year to year voting to perpetuate their own hardship; they go on supporting the very methods and systems that are oppressing them."
