CLEVELAND'S HAT.—The Washington correspondent of the Baltimore Sun says that prior to Mrs. Cleveland's departure for Marion, Mass., to become the guest of Mr. and Mrs. Watson Gilder, she invested in a new hat, one that was calculated to stand the wear and tear of travel, and at the same time becoming to her. It was a soft felt hat, drab in color and alpine in style. She wore it for the first time the day the final vote on the tariff bill was taken in the House. It was generally remarked that the hat referred to was the most stylish-looking piece of headgear the young mistress of the White House has worn since she became "Mrs. President." The young ladies of Washington were not slow to catch the style set by Mrs. Cleveland, and the local milliners are having quite a run on the "Mrs. Cleveland hat," as it is familiarly called. At the summer opera, at lawn tennis gatherings, at the open-air concerts in the President's grounds, and whatever fashionably dressed young ladies assemble there will be found the soft felt hat in various colors from the milky white to the deepest crimson. Blonde or brunette can wear one and look well under it, as it invariably gives the wearer a jaunty appearance.

THE AUGUST METEORS.—The August nights from the 8th to the 12th will be enlivened by the display of meteors which are sure to descend through the atmosphere in greater or less numbers. The meteors, as is well known, come from the great meteor zone whose perihelion is on the earth's orbit, and whose aphelion extends beyond the bounds of Neptune, the most distant planet in the solar system. The earth, about the 10th, plunges through the zone, the meteors are set on fire by the concussion of the earth's atmosphere and descend in the form of shooting stars. The radiant point of the August meteors is in the constellation Perseus, and they are therefore called Persids. Perseus rises on the 10th in the northeast about 9 o'clock, and observers who watch the sky in that direction will be rewarded by the sight of several hundred meteors as the hours of the night pass on. Many of them will be brilliant, and as large as stars of the first magnitude, and many of them will leave trails of luminous vapor lasting several seconds.

TRIPLE TRAGEDY.
Sad Consequences of a Tennessee Desperado's Drunken Frenzy.
Sad Consequences of a Tennessee Desperado's Drunken Frenzy.

A Tennessee desperado named John Grayson, with his uncle and two other companions, had been riding rough shot over the town of Abingdon, Va. Grayson, after firing his pistol in the air on Main street, then levelled it in his drunken frenzy at one of his associates. A peaceable citizen, named Trigg, observing the danger of the latter, laid his hand on Grayson's shoulder and begged him not to shoot.

Grayson turned savagely on Trigg, at the same time placing the muzzle of his pistol against Trigg's shoulder and firing. Trigg staggared and fell, fatally injured, dragging Grayson off his horse. The infuriated assassin then turned and fled. A large crowd who had assembled upon hearing the repeated shouts pursued the ruffian with cries of "Stop him!" "Catch him!" "Hang him!" He fired another shot, and when captured was found to have a bullet in his left side.

Trigg was carried to his home bleeding and apparently dead. His aged mother was so shocked at the sight that she died the same night. Grayson expired the following morning.

Killed by a Mob.
KANSAS CITY, Mo., Oct. 10.—John Kirkland of Nashville, Ark., was killed by a mob of citizens at that place. Dr. Chisholm, a prominent physician of the town, had a quarrel with Kirkland about some work done by the latter. A few hours afterward Kirkland met and attempted to assassinate the physician. He failed and was arrested. On the way to the jail the prisoner was seized by a mob of masked men, who took him into the woods and riddled him with bullets.

NASHVILLE, Ark., Oct. 9.—Dr. Chisolm and John Kirkland had a difficulty about some work which Kirkland had done for Chisolm on Saturday, and that night Kirkland waylaid the doctor and fired on him, but without effect. A posse attempted to arrest Kirkland, but he defended himself and escaped. He was captured last night and turned over to the constable, who started with him to the jail a few hundred yards away, but was met by several masked men with Winchester who took charge of the prisoner and told the constable to ride on. They then riddled Kirkland with bullets, killing him instantly. Kirkland was known as a desperate character.

The Washington Gazette says: On Monday a deputy and posse went in search of W. B. Adams and Jno. M. Newton, supposed to have been accessories to the murder of Joshua A. Cox. It was learned that they had fled to the swamps of Blount's Creek, and were armed to the teeth and determined to fight the death rather than surrender. Murder and Lynching. Another horrible affair has happened in our State. It was a double tragedy. Mr. Joshua Cox, living at Blount Creek about 16 miles from Washington, was shot and killed by Thomas Frazier last Saturday night. Frazier attempted to escape but was captured and lodged in jail. That night, a crowd of masked men, took the law into their own hands, went to the jail, brought Frazier out, and riddled him with bullets. There were two other men, Wm. B. Adams and John M. Newton, implicated with Frazier in the murder, but they made their escape. They have been declared outlaws and it is thought that they are hiding around in the swamps near Washington. Disgraceful.
Moore county comes to the front with a most unpleasant affair. Bob McNeill, a young man of a family of good standing in the county, called, last Saturday night, at Shaw's Hotel in Carthage. He asked to see Miss Ida Poe, a young lady stopping there, but she refused to see him. He then went to the parlor, and knocked. Miss Poe, who was in the parlor, not thinking it was McNeill, opened the door; when she did, McNeill caught and closed the door behind her. He then asked, "Why have you gone back on me?" "I have not," she replied. McNeill then drew a pistol, pointed it towards her and fired, the ball penetrating her thigh. He immediately ran out, got into a buggy and made his escape.

Miss Poe is a young lady of pleasing manners and belongs to a family of the highest standing. She is a sister of Mr. Hastings Poe, of Raleigh. The wound though very painful is not very serious.

Every effort is being made to capture the jealous rascal. The CHRONICLE hopes that the attempts will be successful and that the law will punish him to its fullest extent.

RALEIGH, N. C., May 19.—Governor Scales to-day issued his death-warrant for the execution of Stephen Freeman (colored), of Wilmington, who was convicted of outrageous assault. Freeman appealed to the Supreme Court, which affirmed the decision of the lower court that he merited the death punishment. The Governor received a certified opinion of the Supreme Court, and at once issued the death-warrant as the law requires. There is now an application for commutation of Freeman's sentence. The Governor has not yet acted on this. It is a notable fact that Governor Scales will not sentence any criminal to be executed on Friday. General sentiment in this State on the part of judges is against the selection of that day.

Bishop Key has appointed Rev. Frank L. Reid, of this city, presiding elder of Raleigh district of the North Carolina Conference, to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Rev. N. H. D. Wilson. Mr. Reid is editor of the Raleigh Christian Advocate.

To-day a meeting of the State Board of Agriculture was called to be held May 31st.

William Weddington, the negro who murdered Police-Officer Pearce in Monroe last week, has been taken to Charlotte for safe-keeping. It was believed that if he remained longer at Monroe he would be lynched.

The Prohibitionists have perfected their organization at Charlotte, and decided to at once begin an aggressive campaign. They are legally advised that should the city vote in favor of Prohibition it will be in full force and entirely valid.

Governor Scales will be absent from the State the coming week in attendance upon the National Assembly of the Presbyterian Church at Philadelphia. He will preside at some important meetings.

Next week will be an important one in both a religious and political way. There will be one State convention and no less than six district conventions. There will also be the Episcopal conventions of the Diocese of North Carolina at Salisbury, and of the Diocese of East Carolina at Fayetteville. Both begin on the same day—next Wednesday.
Discense of East Carolina at Fayetteville. Both begin on the same day—next Wednesday.

The Prohibitionists have gone right to work here to get up the excitement in the matter of the "wet or dry" election, now so near at hand. They are having outdoor meetings nightly, with music, &c., and seem to be quite enthusiastic. The colored vote is the thing sought for, and a colored orator from Washington is doing the speaking.

A movement is being made to press Hon. T. J. Jarvis as one of the electors at large. A very great number of people desire in some way to bring him into the canvass. People outside the State have no idea of the extreme popularity Jarvis enjoys. One of the brightest men in the State observed to-day that in this respect Jarvis divided the honors with Zeb. Vance. It is learned that the state of Mrs. Jarvis's health renders it probable that Minister Jarvis's early return from Brazil will be necessary.

Though John Newton, who was implicated in the murder of Joshua A. Cox by Thomas Frazier, in Beaufort county, has been captured and is in jail, W. B. Adams, the other man concerned in the crime, cannot be found. He is in hiding somewhere in the dense swamps, it is believed, and is known to be well armed. He is outlawed and is to be taken dead or alive. It was believed at first that Adams and Newton would be lynched as soon as they were captured. Pursuit of Adams is yet in progress. An attempt was made a few nights past to lynch Newton, but the jail was so strongly guarded that the lynchers' plans were abandoned at the last moment.

Some of the papers have put Dr. J. J. Mott, of Statesville, who is one of the delegates to the National Republican Convention from the Eighth district, as a Sherman man. At last accounts he was for Blaine, and there is no reason to believe that his views have changed. The Sherman men are weak and growing weaker. It is said that the State Convention of the Republicans here next Wednesday is apt to endorse Blaine. The attempt to secure such an endorsement will certainly be made. The Sherman men will urge that it is impolitic.

The matter of the construction of the great line of railway from Southport (near Wilmington) to Bristol, Tennessee, is again before the public. So far all the attempts to get at work on this line have been failures. There have been no funds. It is claimed that English capitalists, who have sent an agent over the proposed route, are now ready to put up the requisite money. So far the road exists only on paper.

The greater part of the convicts from the Stokesdale-Madison branch railway have been taken to Haywood county and put to work on Pigeon river, grading the Carolina, Knoxville and Winston railroad.

Six miles of the Winston-Wilkesboro' railroad have been graded. There are 120 men at work at the Winston end and 100 at the Wilkesboro' end. The force is to be increased. The road is to be completed by March 1st.

The "cutworm" is reported to be doing considerable damage to the young corn. It began its work during the cool weather.

Arrangements have been perfected for the holding of a fair at Murfreesboro'.

In Hyde county it is said the curlew bugs have damaged the corn 29 per cent. already.

John Newton, one of those who is accused of complicity in the murder of Mr. Cox at Blount's Creek, and who, with Adams, was outlawed by the officers of Beaufort county. was captured last Friday and lodged in Washington jail. A mob had gathered for the purpose of lynching the prisoner, but the jail was guarded a d the design of the mob defeated. It is thought that Adams, the other outlaw, will be captured soon, as a posse is still after him and is determined to find him if possible.—Reflector.
john-newton-1888-05.A8:
Joshua Cox's Murderers.
RALEIGH, N. C., June 5.—[Special.]—Interest in the murder of Joshua Cox, in Beaufort county, and the lynching of Frazier, his murderer, is revived today. Two men, one named Newton, and Thomas Adams, were concerned in this crime as accessories. Both fled. John M. Newton was captured. Several attempts to lynch him have been made, but failed. Friday the grand jury found a true bill against him for murder, and his trial is to begin tomorrow. Adams is yet in hiding in the great swamps, which are in that section.

FROM A BURNING BUILDING IN KEYSER.
NORTH CAROLINA.
Considerable Property Destroyed-The State
Grange-Election of Officers-
General News Notes.

RALKIGH, N. C., December 15.—A fire at Keyser last night, caused by a defective flue, burned the telegraph office, depot, and warehouse of the Raleigh and Augusta Air-Line railroad, together with all their contents, including the express matter. The total loss is unknown. An employee who was asleep in the telegraph office barely escaped with his life.

An important meeting was held at Newberne last night, at which the question of extending the Atlantic and North Carolina railway was discussed. There is no opposition to the extension. An important letter from the Chamber of Commerce of Charlotte on the subject was read, and the plan of operations was left with a committee of fifteen. It is desired to make this extension either to Charlotte or Concord.

GRANGE.

The State Grange, which has been in session at Kingston, adjourned to-day.

The following officers were elected to serve for the next two years: Master, W. R. Williams; Overseer, N. T. Ridley; Lecturer, S. H. Rountree; Steward, C. L. Rountree; Assistant Steward, H. C. Lassiter; Chaplain, Rev. W. H. Grant; Treasurer, W. H. Powell; Secretary, H. J. T. Ludwig; Gate-Keeper, F. M. Haskins; Pemona, Miss Alpha Haskins; Flora, Miss Nora O. Pitt; Ceres, Miss Annie Henderson; L. A. Steward, Miss G. A. Gilliam.

Resolutions were unanimously adopted instructing the Committee on Legislation, appointed to look after the interests of the farmers during the coming session of the Legislature, to memorialize that body demanding that in the appointment of committees on agriculture only farmers be placed on said committees—those whose leading interest is farming and are actually engaged in agriculture—and asking the cooperation of the Farmers' Alliance in said demand.

The ex-Confederates have just had a reunion, and a very pleasant one, at the town of Monroe.

General W. P. Roberts, State Auditor, is mentioned in connection with the position of Adjutant-General.

John M. Newton, white, who was tried for the murder of Joshua Cox, in Beaufort county, and was convicted of being accessory after the fact, has appealed to the Supreme Court. His bail has been fixed at $15,000, and he is unable to give it.

Material has arrived for a telegraph line on the Georgia, Carolina and Northern railroad, and the wires will be put up from Monroe to Chester.

The contract for the construction of the Williamston and Plymouth railroad has been awarded and work is in progress. The contractor has secured convict labor, under State supervision and control, and fifty convicts are now at work. There are to be 150 in all.

W. J. Boylin and M. A. Underwood will begin the publication at Monroe, January 1st, of a weekly paper, to be known as the Southern Farm.

An extensive enlargement of the Charlotte water-works has just been completed. There has also been an extension of the Duffham water-main to the lively suburb of East Durham, now a railway station.

Very handsome new cars have been put on the Durham, Oxford and Clarksville railroad. A quicker schedule on the North Carolina railroad between Greensboro' and Goldsboro' goes into effect to-morrow.

crops.

Wheat and oats have nearly all been sown. The early sown crops of both look well and the seasons are favorable. Good crops are certainly needed next year, for the farmers have had a hard blow in 1888. They are hopeful, however. Greater care than ever will be paid the crops. This will apply particularly to tobacco.

Only a trifling amount of cotton remains in the fields ungathered. In some sections the picking is completed.

Week after next an architect from the United States Treasury Department will visit Statesville for the purpose of choosing a site for the public building which is to be erected there.

The loss of tobacco barns by fire this season has been smaller than in a good many years. Better construction and greater care have caused a great saving.

The Richmond and Danville Company is finding that the patronage increases daily on its new line from Durham to Keysville. The company has arranged so that passengers will breakfast at Durham and dine at Keysville going north and take supper at Oxford going south.

The working force on the Chowan and Southern railroad is now spread out all the way from Suffolk to Tarboro'. The piles for the bridge over the Chowan river at Tunis are in place. These roads, in the northeastern part of the State, will open a timber country unmatched in the South. The timber interest is already very important. There are already twenty saw-mills near Newberne, which are now cutting 240,000 feet of lumber daily. In Eauafort county fourteen mills are cutting 300,000 feet daily.

So far as now known no election cases will come up at the January term of the Federal Court here. The Republicans have lists of complaints, but have not yet been able to carry out their threats to panish Democrats. None of Quay's promised money has yet come to hand.

Next week the work of putting the state roof on the State Agricultural and Mechanical College will begin.

It now looks probable that the greater part of the troops in the State will be present at the inauguration of Governor Fowle.

UNJUST ATTACKS.

Governor Scales's broad and certainly successful policy in regard to the management of the Atlantic and North Carolina railroad is subjecting him to attacks, entirely unjust, but which do not weaken him at all. Formerly the road was operated as a local affair. Governor Scales realized the fact that the State of North Carolina (that is, the whole people of the State) owns more than half of it. He therefore made it a State road. That is the gist of the matter. The people who desire it again to be a local road attack the Governor, those who hold that all the State is entitled to a voice and share in the management of a road in which the State is so great a stockholder take the Governor's side. It is no flattery to say that Governor Scales is very accurate and just in his conclusions. He is a very safe man.

The last Legislature reduced the annual appropriation to the penitentiary to such an extent as to very greatly cripple that institution, and the present year has been a hard one—in fact, the worst it has yet weathered.

Tarbore's big cotton-factory is about completed. It is proposed to open it December 31st with some ceremonies.

At only two or three points in the State have the negroes celebrated Harrison's victory. Their quietness has caused much comment. They must be rather uncertain as to their status. That is the only reason given for their failure to shout and celebrate. They were never so quiet. They are afraid of each other. Those of Democratic proclivities, or who would vote that ticket, are in mortal fear in some sections of the great black Republican mass.

Many insane people are in jail here and there, for lack of room in the asylums at Goldsboro' and Raleigh. The cost of maintenance of a patient in the colored asylum at Goldsboro' is $118 yearly.

J. F. Oliver's cotton-gin and a quantity of cotton at Warsaw has been burned. Recently his dwelling was burned and also another gin.

joseph-gill-pooler-1888-03-23.A1:
SHOT DEAD BY A THIEF.
JOSEPH GILL MURDERED ON THE LOUISVILLE ROAD.
Killed While Attempting to Arrest Two Negroes in the Act of Carrying off a Sack of Stolen Beef—The Murderers Escape in the Darkness—An Armed Posse Scouring the Woods for Them and the Police on the Look-out—The Coroner Notified.

Joseph Gill, living at the nine-mile post on the Louisville road, about half a mile this side of Pooler, was shot through the wrist and heart and instantly killed in a woods near Butler's avenue and the six-mile post, half way between the Central railroad and the Louisville road, by an unknown negro at 7 o'clock last night. A load of buckshot was fired into the man's body at short range, killing him instantly.

Yesterday the murdered man discovered that a beef had been slaughtered at the point of the killing. Summoning his brother, Jasper Gill, and Henry Heywood, a hunter, the three went to the place where the beef had been butchered and lay in wait for the thieves. The animal, which belonged to the Widow Farrell, had been butchered and the four quarters put in sacks.

Jasper Gill and Heywood were posted not far distant, while Joseph Gill remained near the sacks which contained the beef. Shortly after night fall three negroes came up, and without seeing Joseph Gill they reached down to take hold of the sacks.

"DROP THAT BEEF."

Gill arose from his place of concealment, and called out loud enough for his brother Jasper and Heywood to hear him, "drop that beef."

One of the negroes, who was only a few feet away, emptied the contents of a shotgun into Gill's breast, killing him instantly, and then all three of the negroes ran. Jasper Gill and Heywood were so taken by surprise as they saw Joseph Gill fall, that they did not fire at the fugitives, but hurried to the spot to book after their companion. They found him dead.

He was taken home and the neighborhood aroused. All Pooler turned out to hunt the murderer, Benjamin Rothwell, postmaster, and J. B. Forehand armed themselves, caught the 10:10 o'clock freight train and hurried to Savannah and telephoned Sergt. Killourhy from the depot as soon as the train arrived. The message was received at the barracks at 12:15 this morning, in time to
to Savannah and telephoned Sergt. Killourhy from the depot as soon as the train arrived. The message was received at the barracks at 12:15 this morning, in time to instruct the second night relief of police to watch all avenues, as it was expected that the murderers would try to steal into the city. The Ocean Steamship police were also instructed to vigilantly guard the river front.

Coroner Dixon was notified of the murder by telephone, and Messrs. Rothwell and Forehand notified Sheriff Ronan and Detective Wetherhorn at 1 o'clock this morning.

HUNTING THE MURDERER.

Over twenty men were scouring the woods last night in the vicinity of Pooler, and while suspicion does not rest on any particular party, it is not thought possible that the murderer and his accomplices can escape.

The police will carefully note what negros are missing from the market this morning.

The murdered man was about 27 years of age, and leaves a wife but no children. He has taken an active part in apprehending thieves, and about a year ago arrested a negro for stealing an ox from Mr. Rothwell, and the thief was sent to the penitentiary for two years.

THE MURDERED MAN.

The deceased is spoken of very highly as an industrious man, fearless in the face of danger and commanding the respect of all who knew him. If his murderers are found by the indignant citizens who are now on the lookout for them it is hardly possible that the county will ever be put to the expense of trying them.

If they are not apprehended by daylight blood hounds will be put upon their trail, and they will be hunted down from the place where the murder was committed.
joseph-gill-pooler-1888-03-23.A2:
GILL'S SLAYER AT LARGE.
The Coroner's Investigation of the Shooting at Six-Mile-Post.
Shooting at Six-Mile-Post.

The slayer of Joseph Gill at the six-mile-post on the Louisville road is still at large. Coroner Dixon held an inquest over the remains of the murdered man yesterday. Gill's two brothers, F. M. Gill and Jasper Gill, testified to the shooting as detailed by the MORNING News. They could not identify the thieves or say whether they were white or black. F. M. Gill said that his posse pursued the thieves, firing at them as they ran away.

"Rafe" Bird (colored) testified to seeing two suspicious negroes Friday afternoon, one of whom had a musket. He thinks they were butchers, and he testified that after the shooting of Gill a musket was found near the beef, and he thought it was the one he had seen the negro have during the afternoon. He would know them, he said, if he should see them again.

John Graham who was left by F. M. Gill to watch the beef until he could collect a posse, swore that while he was watching the beef a man came up with a pistol in his hand, examined the sacks containing the meat and went off.

The only new feature in the examination not covered by the Morning News report yesterday was the finding of a hatchet, butcher-knife and butcher's steel, which was omitted by request of those having the search for the murderers in charge, and the fact that Gill's brother and Mr. Haywood pursued the thieves and fired on them.

The verdict of the jury was: "We find that Joseph Gill came to his death from a gunshot wound at the hands of some party or parties unknown to the jury, and we consider it murder."
joseph-gill-pooler-1888-03-23.A3:
BIRD IN THE LAW'S NET.
THE SUPPOSED SLAYER OF JOE GILL BEHIND THE BARS.
Mile Post—A Pooler Posse's Midnight Ride to the Swamp with the Prisoner—His Narrow Escape from Lynching—Bird Tells the Story of His Arrest and Denies the Shooting—Marcus, His Suspected Accomplice, Still at Large.

It begins to look as if there is to be an early solution of the Gill murder mystery. The arrest of Rafe Bird (colored) yesterday morning is the first step in that direction.

Some time last Friday a beef belonging to the Widow Ferrill, daughter of Marion Gill, was found butchered and hidden behind a log in the swamps near Butler avenue, about half way between the Central railroad and the Louisville road, near Pooler. From the best information obtainable Marion Gill had disposed of some cows to Bird, but as the latter had failed to pay for the stock, Marion Gill had agreed with Bird that he would take yearlings in payment. Bird was to bring him a yearling that morning in time to be butchered for market Saturday morning. Instead of doing so Bird and his wife went to Gill's Friday morning, where they killed a lot of chickens for Gill, and where Bird reported that he could not find the yearlings. Gill insisted that he should go out in the woods and hunt them up, but Bird kept making excuses, and finally Gill sent his son to look up his own cattle, and incidentally to keep a lookout for Bird's yearlings. The son discovered the butchered beef in the woods and reported the facts to his father.

SUSPICION RESTED ON BIRD.

Suspicion was at once directed toward Bird by reason of the fact that he had shown no disposition to look for the cattle, but in the later and more exciting incidents of the evening, the suspicion seems to have been dropped.

The readers of the MORNING NEWS are familiar with the facts connected with the Friday night tragedy, when the Gill brothers, Haywood, and their posse took up their station to watch the beef and catch the thief, and how Joseph Gill was shot down.

Detective Wetherhorn at first declined to lend his services and aid in tracking the murderer, but finding that no one seemed inclined to aid in bringing the guilty parties to justice he consented, on a second interview, to do all in his power.

After a full consultation with the citizens of Pooler and with the relatives of the dead
ties to justice he consented, on a second interview, to do all in his power.

After a full consultation with the citizens of Pooler and with the relatives of the dead man he suggested that Bird be sent down to Savannah. The negro had testified before the Coroner's jury to meeting two men Friday afternoon on the railroad track, one of whom had a musket, which he identified as the one found on Saturday in the neighborhood of where the shooting occurred. His statement was to the effect that while he could not recall the names of the two men, he had worked with them in Savannah when he was in the employ of Mr. Andrew McCormick, and he could readily recognize them.

BIRD'S CONFLICTING STORIES.

On Sunday Gill brought Bird to the city and turned him over to Detective Wetherhorn. But Mr. Wetherhorn found Bird's stories conflicting. His description of the two negroes varied in essential details, and the detective soon discovered by carefully watching that Bird was making no sincere effort to find anyone. It was found, too, by the detective that Bird had only been employed three days by Mr. McCormick, although he had created the impression that he had been in his employ for some time. Mr. Wetherhorn found Mr. John Downing, who keeps the time of the hands, and the names of all the men employed when Bird was working for Mr. McCormick were called over in Bird's presence, and while he had said he could not remember the names of either of the two men he saw without hearing their names called he was unable to fix upon any of those on the time book. In fact his conduct was so suspicious that the suggestion was then made to the detective that Bird should be placed under arrest.

On Sunday and Monday Mr. Wetherhorn pretty thoroughly convinced himself that Bird was not trying to find any one. In a consultation Monday evening Mr. Wetherhorn learned that when the butchered beef was found the liver and heart were missing. He was convinced that whoever killed the beef would not take those parts to Savannah, and that they must have been taken to some contiguous cabin for a morning meal. Reasoning on this train, what cabin more probable than the Bird cabin. It was near the scene of the killing. Bird himself had intimated to him that some one might think he was connected with it as it happened so near his house. There was no corroboration of Bird's story of meeting two men, one of whom had a musket.

A STRANGE COINCIDENCE.

It was also a strange coincidence that Bird had found the musket on Saturday. It was suspicious, too, that almost immediately after Joe Gill was shot, Bird, his 12-year-old boy Sam and Henry Marcus, a worthless negro who had been hanging about Bird's place, should come upon the scene and make themselves known, Bird hallooing out not to shoot, that it was him. Putting all these things together, Detective Wetherhorn told the Pooler folks to go back home; that he would keep Bird in town until Tuesday noon, and that they should use their judgment and try to learn from Bird's children if they had had liver on the table recently. The Birds had been living in great penury, and to that degree that they had been known to cook and eat the entrails of the chickees butchered for Marion Gill.

On Tuesday Mrs. Ferrill made an excuse to visit the Bird cabin, taking with her a basket of provisions. Gaining the confidence of a 10-year-old girl of Bird's, she very artlessly told that they had liver to eat, as did old "Rose," an aged negress who made her home at Bird's, but the boy Sam, a lad of 12, seemed to have been posted, and he denied any knowledge of having liver in the house for over a year.

FINDING THE BEEF'S LIVER.

When Mrs. Ferrill communicated this intelligence to her father and supplemented it by saying that as she was coming away from the house she had met Bird returning, Marion Gill, Ben Rothwell, Joseph Ferrill, and Jack Gill mounted their horses and galloped over to the Bird cabin. Bird was immediately taken into custody at about 5 o'clock Tuesday afternoon, and a search of the house resulted in finding a portion of the beef liver in a wash boiler.

Bird was tied and taken to the railroad station, and an effort was made to get him to tell all that he knew about the affair, but he persisted in his original story, with slight variations. Later in the night a larger body of men, armed, made a descent upon the guards, and taking him to the swamp threatened to lynch him if he did not tell the truth. He then criminated a negro

and cries, indeed if he could have heard them from his cabin. It was not in consonance with the negro character to have done this. All this, and the finding of the liver, was to the detective strong circumstantial evidence pointing to a full knowledge of Bird not only about the killing of the beef, but the killing of Joseph Gill.

SUSPICIONS AGAINST BIRD.

It was also suspicious that Marcus, who had so long laid around Bird's house, where there was little or nothing to eat, should leave Sunday when the liver and heart of the beef had evidently been taken to Bird's cabin, and the head and tripe of the beef had been given to Bird for carrying the beef out of the swamp after the killing of Gill.

Detective Wetherhorn says that while he has been keeping a sharp lookout for Marcus, and heard of him being in town Monay, he has thus far been unable to lay dands on him, but that he has such a perfect description of the fellow that he cannot well elude the vigilance of those who are watching for him. Mr. Wetherhorn expects more developments to-day, and it is likely that Sam Bird, the boy, and others, will be put under surveillance, and possibly under arrest to-day.

THE PRISONER'S STORY.

A MORNING NEWS reporter interviewed Bird in his cell at the jail last night. The negro adheres to his statement given before the Coroner's jury, and in concluding the interview where he detailed his experience in the swamp when he was threatened with being lynched, he broke down and wept copiously. He is tall and very black, a type of the thriftless and slovenly negro that is content with wearing cast off clothing, and he is evidently a stranger to daily ablutions. His hair is extremely short even for a negro, and he wears a scattered beard and moustache, both of which are as kinky as the wool on his head. His eyes are neither lacking in luster nor are they bright, but there is a shrewdness lurking in them, although the pupils are large and neither retreating nor staring. He speaks with more than ordinary care and with an intelligent approach to frankness; his phraseology is not a continuation of the African dialect, although he drops into it occasionally as if he would like to be considered more ignorant than he really is. He made the following statement:

BIRD'S STATEMENT.

"My name is Rafe Bird. I was born in Liberty county, and was last owned by Jacob Wise, in Bryan county. My occupation is daily labor. I was married twenty years ago in Bryan county to Hannah Sheftall. We have had thirteen children, eight of whom are dead. We moved to Savannah after the big August storm, in September. I worked here on and off; first for Smith & Kelly, and afterward at draying on the Bay. I worked for Mr. McCormick. Mr. Goodwin, Mr. Heidt and others, off and on. I quit draying fall before last, at which time I was working for Mr. McCormick. I went out into the country, moving to the race track on the Louisville road, and went to farming. I farmed there in 1886. I next moved to the Widow Jones place, five miles from Savannah, on the Louisville road, and farmed there in 1887. This year, in January, I moved to the seven mile post, on the Louisville road, on Mr. Henry Jackson's land, renting a part of the tract to farm it and raise rice, sugar cane, peas and whatever else I could grow.

THE STORY OF HIS ARREST.

I was arrested Tuesday evening about 5 o'clock by Mr. Marion Gill and Ben Rothwell, ticket agent at No. 1, on the Central road. I was at home sitting in the door. Mr. Joe Ferrill was a little ways off with a gun and Jack Gill held the horses. Mr. Rothwell told me that he had a warrant for me and to consider myself under arrest. Then Gill collared me and took me behind the house, and Mr. Ferrill tied me. I made no resistance. I told them that I had never had anything to do with killing the beef and knew nothing about it. That is true. I never even brought any beef to market. I had helped to tote the beef out of the swamp, and I helped tote Joe Gill's body out of the swamp to my house, where it was laid out until the wagon came for it. We did not go to bed that night but Henry Marcus and I slept some sitting in our chairs.

"The beef was killed between my house and the railroad. My house is about one half a mile from the railroad track, and it was about one half mile from my house to where the beef was. I did not see any one go out to watch the beef.

BEEN HUNTING STRAY CATTLE.

"I had been out that afternoon looking for five head of cattle that I had in the swamp. I walked in the direction of the railroad, thinking that as they had not shown up for some four days, that they had been turned over by the railroad. When I reached the railroad, and had walked a
railroad, thinking that as they had not shown up for some four days, that they had been turned over by the railroad. When I reached the railroad, and had walked a short distance, I saw two colored men on the track. One was leaning on a musket and the other was standing by him talking. I was faced toward Savannah, and they were behind me about twenty steps, facing the same way. I knew their faces and recognized them as belonging in Savannah, but I could not recall their names. I said: 'Hello! what are you doing up here? They started toward me, and when they came up they said, 'Pardner what are you doing up here? I said: 'I see staying up here now. Business was too dull in town to make a living. I am up here trying to farm.' It is not strange that I should not remember their names, for I have met two or three men in jail to-day whom I knew and who knew me, and we had to ask each other our names. It was about 2:30 o'clock when I met the two men on the railroad. I told them that I was looking for some yearlings that had been gone some four days, and asked them if they had seen any knocked off by the road. They said they had not. I asked them where they had been, and where they were going.

THE STORY OF THE TWO STRANGERS.

"They said they were going to Savannah. They said that they had been up the road to a turpentine camp where they had been offered $1 per day if they would come up, but when they got there they found differently, and were on their way back home. They had stalled all night Thursday night, they said, at Whitesville, and had been in Dan Martin's turpentine camp, but they did not give the name of the turpentine camp up the road. As we walked along they were a little behind me, part of the time talking to me, and part of the time talking low to themselves. After we had gone about a mile I turned off and took the dirt road and saw no mors of them.

"After walking about a quarter of a mile an the dirt road, or Louisville road, I met Joe Ferrill coming down in a gallop and I stopped him. Ferrill and Marion Gill had agreed to buy a yearling from me, and I was to furnish it, if I could find it, in time to butcher it Friday evening for Saturday's

ing.’ I said to Henry Marcus, ‘let’s go and see what’s the matter down towards the railroad where the holling is.’ He replied, ‘Well, all right. I’ll go with you. “I never killed the beef, and know nothing of it. At 5 o’clock that evening Marcus came home from Parnell’s, where he had been at work, and none of us left the house until we heard the firing. I got up about 5 o’clock that morning, woke Henry and then my wife. I heard the train go by at 6 o’clock and fix the time by that. Shortly after, and without breakfast, my wife and me left home and went to Marion Gill’s and got there about a little after 7. I stayed at Marion Gill’s that afternoon till 1 o’clock, my wife and me butheering fifty head of chickens. Martha Roberts, my next door neighbor, who lives about half of a quarter of a mile from my house, and an old colored woman named Rose knows this statement to be true.”

Bird then went on to detail his visit to Savannah on Saturday and his staying here Sunday, Monday and Tuesday forenoon looking for the two men that he had met on the railroad, so that he could point them out to Detective Wetherhorn, and concluded his statement, in a flood of tears, as to how he had been treated by his captors Tuesday night.

TIED BY HIS THUMBS.

“When they arrested me,” he said, “they took me to station No. 1, on the Central railroad, and tried to get me to tell them about the shooting. I told them I did not know any more than I had told the Coroner. They then took me about 100 yards back of the warehouse and tied my thumbs together and threatened to hang me up by them half an hour at a time until I did tell. I said, ‘Gentlemen, I know nothing about the shooting. I can’t tell any more than I done to you. I didn’t kill the beef.’ They then took me back to the warehouse, where they kept me until very late. It must been long about midnight. It was a good while after the 9 o'clock train passed. They then carried me about a mile out in the swamp, in the woods, and said they was going to lynch me. I begged them and prayed to them all I knew how not to lynch me, and when I saw they were going to kill me, I said, to save my life, I knowed I could show them a man that killed the beef. That it was a colored man named Brown, who lived at the 4-mile hill. They then went and arrested him and carried him to the station. But they let him go for when it come daylight I told them better; that I had been compelled to lie on somebody to save my life."

Further developments in the Gill murder will be awaited with interest, and that the guilty parties are spotted by Detective Wetherhorn seems to be pretty generally believed. There was a rumor that Marcus had been arrested yesterday afternoon, but he is still at large.

Those who examined the beef say that the heart, liver and lights were not with the beef when they found it concealed Friday morning. It is a custom to put the tripe, head, liver, heart and lights in one sack, and the last three articles were not in the sack with the head. Bird's wife denied that Henry Marcus had any clothing there except a worthless pair of pantalons, although Bird told Wetherhorn that Marcus had gone back Monday to his (Bird's) house for his clothing. Bird's wife says Marcus has never been back but is running on the steamer Ethel. She wanted to come down to Savannah yesterday, and Sam, the boy who is in Marion Gill's charge, was permitted to take a message to a friend of Bird's wife, whom she wanted to come down with her, but he pointedly refused and she did not come.

BROWN NO. 2 AGAIN.

Yesterday morning Brown issued from his concealment, and under the protection of the gray headed old minister came to town, where they waited long and patiently in the office of Justice Warring Russell, Jr., for Detective Wetherhorn. But 12 o'clock and 1 o'clock came, and no Wetherhorn. The old preacher could wait no longer, but told Brown to remain, and he left for home. Later in the afternoon the detective returned to the city, and while pretty well satisfied before, he had no doubt that Brown No. 2 was an innocent man and he was permitted to return home.

Marcus is still at large. He is evidently living very low, awaiting developments. Detective Wetherhorn, in an interview with a MORNING NEWS reporter last evening, said that his Wednesday night experience, which included an extra thirty mile drive he had not calculated upon, had so thoroughly tired him out that he was going to rest last night, but that every effort would be made to apprehend Marcus. It was evident to him that Marcus was a thriftless, lazy negro. He had laid out in an open shed at Bird's house, where there was little or nothing but corn bread and chicken entrails to eat, and it was suspicious that when there was plenty in the house to eat, with no talk of arresting Bird, that he should suddenly disappear Sunday, and hide away.

BIRD'S BAD CHARACTER.

The character of Bird, the detective says, is bad. He is an indolent negro, and while Marion Gill had done a great deal for him and let him have the cattle he had never paid for them and never made an effort to pay for them. It was strange, too, that Bird should never mention what Bird's wife had told him.

Bird's wife told the officer yesterday that she heard a shot Friday morning before she and her husband started to Marion Gill's, and that she had said to her old man, "Did you hear dat shot? I wouldn't be sprised ef dat wasn't one of yoh veahlins dun got shot out dah in de swamp." Bird has never made any mention of such an occurrence. When the detective asked her why Bird had not gone out there to see about it, she said they were in too big a hurry to get over to Mr. Marion Gill's to get to work. But the distance from Bird's to Marion Gill's is not over a mile and a half, and Bird's statement is to the effect that he got up at 5 o'clock that morning, woke his wife up and they left for Marion Gill's without their breakfast, right after the 6 o'clock train passed, getting to Gill's after 7 o'clock. The detective says that when he asked her why she did not send Sam to see about the yearling, she replied she never thought of it. The detective's theory is that they had liver for breakfast that morning, and the heart and lights have never yet been discovered.

Detective Wetherhorn says that he feels satisfied that Bird knows all about the affair, and that at one time he was about to make a clean breast of it. That was on Wednesday last, when Marion Gill feelingly alluded to the many charitable and kindly deeds he had done for Bird; that he did not accuse him of shooting his brother; that he did not care for the beef, but that he did want to know who was the slayer of his brother, and he appealed to Bird to tell him what he knew about it.

MOVED BY GILL'S APPEAL.

The appeal seemed to touch Bird, who sat with his head bent, and at the conclusion of Mr. Gill's impassioned pleading for the truth Bird raised his head, and acknowledging the kindness of Marion Gill, started to say, "Till tell you all I know about it," hesitated, looked around at those about him, and then changing his demeanor, said that he knew nothing beyond that which he had already told. His statement made for publication in the MORNING NEWS of yesterday is all that Rafe Bird has had to say since the tragedy with which so many connect him as an accomplice.
Bird, Detective Weterhorn says, got into trouble in Bryan county, where he kept a doggery, and the officers came down nere after him some years ago and took him up there. Bird says that he was indicted for selling liquor without giving bond, and that he got out of it by paying a couple of lawyers $25.
The relatives and friends of the murdered man have relaxed none of their vigilance and are watching every suspicious movement, both in the vicinity of Pooler and in this city, and that Bird's neck was saved in the swamp Tuesday night is due to the presence of mind and considerate judgment of Mr. Haywood, to whom the enraged posse listened, although after finding the liver in Bird's cabin they felt sure they had the right man.
joseph-gill-pooler-1888-03-23.A11:
THE GILL MURDER CASE.
The Pooler Tragedy as Much of A Mystery as Ever. It begins to look if the murderer or
The Pooler Tragedy as Much of A Mystery as Ever.

It begins to look as if the murderer or murderers of Joe Gill have thoroughly succeeded in hiding their tracks. The circumstances of the murder are still fresh in the public mind. Some thief or thieves killed a beef in the neighborhood of Joseph Gill's house near Pooler in April last, and the beef was found concealed near the spot where it was butchered during the day. At nightfall Joe Gill, his brother, and a posse took up their station in proximity to the beef to confront and take into custody the thieves. When they approached Joe Gill came forward from his hiding place and accosted the thieves, when he was shot down, his murderer escaping in the darkness.

Detective Wetherhorn, after two days' investigation of all the surrounding circumstances, arrested Rafe Bird, a negro living near the scene of the murder, and last month Detective Hanley arrested Abram Edy (colored) on the charge of the murder. The grand jury of the superior court, on Wednesday last, after an inquiry, failed to indict either of them, and they have been discharged.

While it has never been thought that Bird was a party to the killing, he was suspected of knowing who killed the beef, and certain suspicious acts on the day of and the day following the murder led to his arrest. It was shown that Bird and his wife did not go to their work the morning of the day the beef was killed as early as was their custom; that Bird was in the habit of going to his work with one Mathis, a negro who was staying with him, and that on the morning of the day the beef was killed he sent Mathis on ahead. That it was the custom of Bird to take his boy with him when he went to work, but on that morning he left the boy at home.

Mathis was arrested by Detective Wetherhorn, but his conduct was so clearly disingenuous that no suspicion attached to him, and he was never committed to jail. He did deepen the suspicion against Bird, however, by relating the incident of two visits from unknown men to Bird's cabin the night of the murder after the body of Joe Gill had been removed to his home near Poolers, and after the excitement had in a measure subsided. It was also learned that the liver of the beef had furnished a meal for the Bird family, and a portion of it was found hidden away in Bird's cabin. Evidence was not waiting to prove that
the liver of the beef had furnished a meal for the Bird family, and a portion of it was found hidden away in Bird's cabin. Evidence was not wanting to prove that when the beef was removed to Bird's cabin after the killing of Gill there was no liver in the sacks containing the beef.

Bird's statements were contradictory, and he claimed that during the afternoon of the day the beef was killed he met two negroes on the railroad near the scene of the killing, one of whom had a musket, and with whom he had worked in Savannah for some time, and whom he claimed he could identify if brought to Savannah. He was brought to the city and the pay roll of the firm he claimed to have been employed by did not corroborate his statement as to the length of time employed, and a close watch on his actions established the fact that he was making no effort to find the two negroes whom he claimed to have met. Further than this it was shown that he had told Mathis in the market that if he could get away he would go further south, or over into Mississippi.

In the light of all these circumstances there was a strong suspicion against him. When the liver was found concealed in his cabin the enraged citizens of Poor took Bird to the swamps, and by threats led him to criminalize one Brown, a negro living some miles further up the road. Brown had no trouble in satisfying his captors that he was not in the neighborhood of the crime and he was released by the posse, Bird taking his statement back when brought out of the swamp and confronted by Brown. Bird was then brought to jail in this city, where he has been kept in confinement until the grand jury this week returned "no bill," and Bird was released from custody.

Another suspicious fact connected with the case was that on the morning following the night of the murder, Bird told Mathis where to look and he would find a gun, which Mathis did, and found the musket which had been fired with fatal aim full in the breast of Joseph Gill.

The theory that Bird knew who killed the beef, that two visits from strange persons had been paid to Bird's cabin, and without inviting them in, but to better conceal their identity from Mathis he had gone to the door and talked in a low tone to one of the visitors, and had gone down the road a part of the way with the other visitor or visitors, all led to the natural conclusion that he knew more of the circumstances than he was inclined to furnish.

Whether the case will rest here depends upon the course which the authorities take in the matter. It is strange that the gun, the hatchet, the canes and the steel found in one of the sacks have never been traced to an owner, although the musket has initials cut deeply in the stock. The rewards offered for the identification and apprehension of the murderer will no doubt stimulate the detectives to renewed effort to track down the guilty man.
joseph-gill-pooler-1888-03-23.A13:
BIRD POINTSOUTTHE MAN
FASTENING JOE GILL'S MURDER
ON FRED ROLAND.
The Assailant of Mannigo Corcivich and the Perpetrator of the Robbery at Five Mile Bend Thought to be the Author of the Pooler Tragedy—Rafe Bird Identifies Roland as the Man He Saw on the Railroad Track with a Musket the Day of the Murder—Officer McDermott's Theory.

The negro Fred Roland, who was arrested in Allendale, S. C., last month for the brutal assault upon Mannigo Corcivich and the robbery of John Cinacavich's store, at the Five Mile Bend, on the Augusta road, on the night of Sept. 17, is thought to be the murderer of Joe Gill, who was killed near Pooler last spring. Roland answers the description in every particular, and Officer McDermott, who is working up the case, is confident that Roland is the man who killed Gill. There have been half a dozen arrests of parties believed to have been connected with the killing, but for lack of evidence they were discharged by the grand jury. Rafe Bird, who was in the employ of Marion Gill, Joe Gill's brother, made the following statement while confined in jail here:

RAFE BIRD'S STORY.

"I had been out the afternoon before the killing hunting some cows. When I reached the Central railroad I saw two colored men on the track. One of them was leaning on a musket and the other was standing by him talking. I knew their faces and recognized them as belonging in Savannah, but I could not recall their names. It is not strange that I should fail to remember their names for I have met two or three men in jail to-day whom I knew and who knew me, and we had to ask each other our names. I asked the men where they were going. They replied that they were going to Savannah. They said that they had been up the road to a turpentine camp, where they had been offered $1 per day if they would come up, but when they got there they found differently, and were on their way back home. We walked down the road, and part of the time they walked behind me and talked low to themselves. After going with them about a mile I turned off to go home and left them. About 8 o'clock that night, when I was at home, I heard one shot, then heard hollering, then heard three shots all
IDENTIFIED THE MUSKET.

Bird recognized the musket, which was found the next morning at the place where the beef was slaughtered, as the one that the man he met on the railroad carried. Bird said that he had worked with the man handling cotton here, and while he could not recall his name, he thought that he could identify him if he ever saw him again. He said that he had not seen the man since leaving him on the railroad track, the afternoon of the murder. He describes the man as a large and tall man, not black, nor yet bright, but between the two.

Officer McDermott, being familiar with Bird's statement as published in the MORNING NEWS at the time of the murder, and also his statement at the coroner's inquest, took Bird to the jail where Roland is confined, and upon being informed that he was there for the purpose of identifying Gill's murderer, he said that he could do so, or at least he could identify the man whom he saw with the musket which was found at the place where the murder was committed.

“DAT'S DE MAN.”

When Roland was brought out of his cell Bird looked at him and spoke to him. Then turning to the officer he said: “Dats de man; I can swear ter it.”

“Didn't we work together at de wharf?” Bird asked Roland.

“Yes,” was the reply.

“Didn't yo' work fur Ryals!”

“Yes.”

“Dats de man, boss.”

“Are you certain?” asked Officer McDermott.

“Dats de man. If it aint, den I'm bline an' don' know what I sees.”

Roland stoutly denied that he killed Gill. He acknowledged to Officer McDermott, however, that he had served twelve months on the chain-gang for cattle stealing at Sandersville, and that his brother is serving a term of several years for the same offense in this county. He said that he was the principal in an organized band here which had been stealing brass from the Central railroad.

Officer McDermott is working the case up, and is confident he will have evidence enough to convict Roland of the murder. Marion Gill, the brother of the murdered man, and also B. Rothwill of Pooler, are positive that Roland is the man from the evidence of Bird and young Butler, who saw the men the afternoon of the killing. Young Corcivich, whom Roland assaulted at the Five Mile Bend, recovered consciousness a day or two ago and said that Roland is the man that struck him. There was a party with Roland, he said, at the time, but he did not interfere. Corcivich says that Roland assaulted him when he stooped down to draw a glass of whisky.

A BATTLE FOR BLOOD.
Outlaws Answer a Summons to Surrender with a Volley—The Entire Gang Killed. Three Citizens Killed.

KANSAS CITY, Mo., Sept. 3.—A special from Paladora, in the public land strip, says that the farmers and herdsmen of that section, who had lost many horses and cattle recently, suspected a band of campers who claimed to be catching wild horses, and, finding evidence of guilt, forty well armed vigilantes surrounded the camp and sent in a committee of six men to demand the surrender of the thieves. The reply of the desperadoes was a volley which wounded one man and two horses. This angered the vigilantes, and firing was at once begun and the outlaws shot down without mercy. They fought desperately and no quarter was asked or given. In twelve minutes the firing ceased and seventeen outlaws were found to have been killed. The vigilantes had three men killed and nine wounded. Two horses were also killed and seven wounded. Sixteen stolen horses were recovered. Not one outlaw escaped alive.
paladora-paladora-1888-09-01.A2:
TWENTY-ONE DEAD.
Report of a Bloody Battle in No-Man's Land.
Report of a Bloody Battle in No-Man's Land.

KANSAS CITY, MO., September 2.—A report has reached here that a battle was fought in No-Man's Land last week between eighteen horse thieves and a force of fifty Colorado settlers, and that all the outlaws were killed together with three of the vigilantes. Several days ago a gang of desperadoes invaded southern Colorado and stole a number of horses, after which they fled to the neutral strip. The settlers at once organized a force to pursue them, and it is supposed that the above fight was the result.
paladora-paladora-1888-09-01.A11:
NO MERCY SHOWN.
Desperadoes Shot in Their Camp.
Seventeen Horse Thieves Killed by Western Farmers.
Paladora, Public Land Strip, I. T., Sept. 1.—For some time past quite a number of horses and cattle had mysteriously disappeared from this and other neighborhood in the strip, being taken from the pastures and picket lines of the settlers and herdsmen.

Suspicion pointed to a band of campers in the brakes of Deer creek, who were there ostensibly for the purpose of catching wild horses, and a strict watch was kept over their camp.

The night following their discovery the camp was surrounded by 40 well armed and mounted vigilants, who sent in a committee of six to demand the surrender of the outlaws and submission to an investigation. The reply of the desperadoes was a volley, which wounded one man and two horses.

This was the signal for the attack and from each projecting peak around the ravine where the camp was located, as fast as the Winchesters could be worked, volleys were poured upon the wretched outlaws without mercy. When they discovered they were surrounded and retreat cut off they fought with desperation, but no living thing could long exist in such a fire and no quarter given.

In twelve minutes the firing ceased and seventeen lawless men lay bleeding corpses or writhing in the agonies of death.

The vigilants had three men killed and ten wounded. Two horses were killed and seven wounded and sixteen horses were retaken and returned to their owners. Several others near the camp were killed and wounded.

The settlers think that at least one gang of outlaws has been subdued.
paladora-paladora-1888-09-01.A15:
A BLOODY FIGHT.
Sixteen Outlaws Instantly Killed by Vigilantes in Indian Territory. Special Telegram to the Statesman.
Sixteen Outlaws Instantly Killed by Vigil- lilantes in Indian Territory. Special Telegram to the Statesman. Denison, September 3.—The press today today gives a meagre account of a battle between a lot of desperadoes and a band of vigilantes Friday morning, on the head waters of the Paladora creek, in the neutral strip, 200 miles northwest of Denison. Your correspondent was fortunate in finding Mr. John Washburn, of Higgins, in Lipscomb county, and learned the following information in information in regard to the fight. Mr. Washburn said: Higgins is the nearest railroad point to the southern portion of the neutral strip, and all the supplies that reach that reach that that portion of the country are freighted across the country. Freighters brought the information Saturday that a battle had been fought between the vigilantes and a band of desperadoes, that vigilants at one time infested the desperadoes, that v
tion was taken in the matter and a vigilance committee was at once organized. Friday morning the committee made a raid upon the camp. The camp fires were burning brightly and preparations were being made for breakfast. A party of three of the vigilantes were sent into the outlaws' camp with an order for an unconditional surrender. The party were fired upon and one of their number killed. Then the fight began in earnest. For about fifteen minutes revolvers and Winchesters were cocked and fired with appalling rapidity. When the smoke of battle had cleared away it was found that three of the vigilantes were killed and several wounded; of the outlaws only one man escaped. Four horses were killed and some half a dozen wounded. Who commanded the desperadoes is not known, but it is supposed that it is the same gang that has been giving the railroads through the Territory trouble in attempting to rob trains. There are seventeen of the outlaws and sixteen of them were killed outright. The vigilantes were commanded by an ex-desperado of Texas, and they were armed with Winchesters, while the outlaws used six-shooters principally, only one of them using a rifle, and he was killed early in the fight. Mr. Washburne says the people of that county are deter mined to rid the county of such men, and propose to take the law into their own hands until the community is rid of them.

The Neutral Strip Battle.
TRINIDAD, Colo., Sept. 4.--A week ago John Jennings and others left Boston, Colorado, in pursuit of horse thieves. In the Neutral Strip the detachment overlooked Billy Cornellius, an ex-marshal of Boston, and one companion, both of them horse thieves, drying their clothing after a rain. The two leaped upon horses bareback and escaped.

Some stolen horses and arms were captured. Part of the detachment returned with these while the rest of the detachment followed the thieves. The pursuing party, reinforced by cowboys from about the Z.H. ranch it is believed, were guided by the flight of Cornellius and his companion to the principal rendezvous of the terrible band of thieves who are a scourge to Southeastern Colorado. It is believed that the reported battle has resulted in the total destruction to the main camp of outlaws though. Here and at Folsom and Clayton this evening there was no particulars, only a meagre report of a pitched battle.

WANT TO LYNCH HIM IN COURT. Tremendous Riot at the Trial of the Ryan Murderer at Parkersburg.
PARKERSBURG, W. Va., Sept. 6.—There is tremendous excitement to-day at the trial of Drake, one of the alleged murderers of the Rev. Mr. Ryan, at Spencer, Roan County. This is the crime for which the citizens of Spencer rose en masse and lynched George and Bob Duffy, Drake's alleged accomplices. On the way from the jail to the court-room this morning the mob tried to drag the prisoner out of the hands of the officers and threatened to lynch him. Threats to the same effect were made in open court after arrival there, and the Judge had to put the prisoner under the protection of a squad of special policemen.

TO BE LYNCHED
is the Alleged Murderer of Rev. Thomas Ryan, if Not Convicted.
Ryan, if Not Convicted.

PARKERSBURG, W. VA., September 8.—The jury trying the case of Perry Drake and Dan Cunningham, for the murder of Rev. Thomas Ryan last fall in Rowan county, are still out. The readers will remember the senational features of the murder; how a band of robbers approached Rev. Mr. Ryan's home in Rowan county, demanded his money, and a battle took place in which Ryan was shot, as was Geo. Duff, one of the murderers; how next day Chess Coon and Bot Duff were lynched, and the consequent excitement in that county. Perry Drake was captured about the same time, but was saved from the lynchers, although one of the men confessed that Drake was the one who fired the fatal shot. He was sent to the Charleston jail. His trial commenced at Spencer last Thursday a week ago and has been of a highly sensational character. The jury went out Saturday, but failing to agree, were sent out again by Judge Fleming with instructions to settle the question of the defendant's guilt or innocence, and they have been out ever since. During the trial Ryan's wife and two daughters testified that Drake was at the house the night of the murder, and standing in the window during the parley. said, "Old man, we have come for your money," and as Ryan reached for his gun, shot and killed him. J. Hunt, one of the attorneys for Drake, being sworn, tried to discredit Mrs. Ryan's testimony by swearing that Miss Ryan had told him that they did not know any of the parties at all. This attempt to question the veracity of Miss Ryan so enraged those present that the judge was compelled to place him under a guard. The failure of the jury to agree last Monday raised indignation to the highest pitch, and the citizens declare if Drake and Cunningham are not convicted, that they well not allow them to leave the court house alive, as they are determined to break up this gang of thieves and toughs at any cost. As a result of the excitement, several encounters have taken place between the opposing factions, and challenges have been made between the hot-blooded friends of both sides.

A Fine State of Affairs.
ADDISON, W. VA., Sept. 17.—The trial of Perry Drake, at Spencer, Roane county, which was begun a week ago last Tuesday, has closed. The jury remained out three days, but failed to agree. Drake stood charged with having been one of the parties who murdered Rev. Ryan last October. S. C. Burdett, who defended Drake, says that the feeling against his client is very strong, and that the case will, in all probability, be removed to Kanawha county for the next trial. The people are very much excited over the matter, and many persons were seen going around the streets of Spencer with shotguns and other weapons threatening to kill Drake if the jury acquitted him.
perry-drake-spencer-1888-09-05.A4: The case of Perry Drake charged as an accomplice in the murder of Rev. Ryan; occupied the attention of our court from last Wednesday to Monday morning; when it was given to the jury. The jury, after being out until Tuesday afternoon, failed to agree. We are informed that there were eleven for conviction and one for acquittal. So endeth for the present a trial which was being watched with interest by many thousand people.—Spencer Bulletin.

Governor Wilson has appointed a number of gentlemen from this State as delegates to the southern immigration convention now in session at Montgomery, Alabama. Among them are Hons. H. G. Davis, Frank Hereford, J. B. Taney, Geo. E. Price and C. B. Hart.

West Virginia is evidently a growing State. It is said that the question of an extra session of Congress will depend upon who gets the certificates in this State. Well, we can settle that right now. The candidates who were honestly elected will receive the certificates, and all the present information points to the democrats as honestly elected.

The mail carrier between Parkersburg and Elizabeth, who disappeared so mysteriously last Monday has not been heard from since. No one appears to have seen him after he left his boarding house on lower Market street, when he said he was going to the postoffice for the mail, which he said he would take on horseback as the roads were too bad for a team. No reason is assigned for his leaving.

Now Ohio and Indiana are in a much worse condition than West Virginia ever was. The disgraceful and lawless White Caps have about captured both States. A party of Baker jurors, including Messrs. J. C. Miller, Jos. H. Hawley, J. C. Wells, M. Roberts and Conrad Miller, accompanied by Prosecuting Attorney Hervey and others, visited the scene of the McWha tragedy on Friday last and were shown over the premises by Robert Patterson, the executor who has charge of the property. The jurors were more than ever satisfied of Baker's guilt, and some are reported as saying all they are sorry for now is that they didn't hang him.—Wellsburg News.

The democrats of Wheeling are prosecuting the illegal voters of the last election as fast as they can catch them. One of the young men arrested is W. H. Lewis, a minor, who voted the Republican ticket, and says he was instigated by some of the Republican managers, whose names he gives. He has been arrested and is unable to give bond for his appearance and is now in jail. It is thought that the men who induced him to cast an illegal vote will furnish him bail and he will then skip, and they will pay the bond out of Quay's honest election fund.

A Charleston telegram says: Three weeks ago Nrs. Matthew M. Ellis died, leaving two small children. She was waited on in her house by her sister, Miss Mary Rumsey, and a few days ago Miss Rumsey and Mr. Ellis were married. Mr. Ellis had received a pension check for $100 a few days before, which he had not drawn, and as one of Mary's stipulations was that he should leave the children with his mother for a while, he started there with them a few hours after his marriage, leaving the check properly indorsed behind him. On returning the next day both Mary and the check had gone, also a former lover of her's named Chas. Hamilton. They are believed to be somewhere in Kentucky, but Mr. Ellis is not anxious to know where as he does not want them.

A correspondent of the Baltimore Sun writing from Tucker county tells of a plucky woman in the following paragraph:

The most celebrated hunters of this section are Bob Eastham, Jule Baker, a woman, and Louis Chidister. There is a law to protect deer, but it is not observed. Out of season venison is called mountain mutton. Jule Baker is the wife of John Baker, and lives near the mouth of Black Water Fork. She can handle a Winchester with the dexterity and precision of Old Leatherstocking, and hundreds of deer and bear have fallen victims to the unerring bullets from her rifle. Bob Eastham says he saw her plunging down the mountain side through six inches of snow one day with two rifles and a bear trap strapped to her back and followed by six dogs. She ran three miles to a point where she thought a deer in full chase would cross, and she got there in time to see her husband kill him. She is a big, black-haired woman, very industrious, with a heart as big as her foot, and she is the mother of seven children. She is not pretty. A few months ago for a silver dollar, she carried a valise, weighing over 100 pounds, seven miles for an engineer. It is said that on one occasion she carried a sewing machine from Grafton to her home, a distance of sixty miles.

CONDENSED NEWS.
The Virginia Republican state convention will be held at Petersburg May 17.

Depositors of the wrecked Metropolitan bank in Cincinnati are to be paid their claims in full.

Business failures during the seven days ended Friday: United States 179; Canada 42, total 221, compared with 243 last week, and 223 for the corresponding week in 1887.

Emperor Frederick was well enough Friday to drive in a half-open carriage with his wife from Charlottenburg to Berlin and pay a visit to his mother, the Dowager Empress Augusta.

The result of the impeachment trial at Frankfort, Ky., is the anticipated verdict of guilty, and the removal of Treasurer Tate from office. His defalcation is now estimated at $204,000.

A young man of Battle Creek, Mich., has taken the glanders from giving a horse a blow in the mouth, a slight abrasion of the skin being made by the horse's teeth. He will probably die.

The Northwestern Railroader, of Minneapolis, Minn., says the cost of the western railway rate war so far has been $15,000,000. The twin cities alone have lost nearly $500,-000 in decrease of business.

New York city employees are in arms against Mayor Hewitt because he refused to declare a holiday on Good Friday. He said it was not a legal holiday, and they say he did it "out of pure cussedness."

The six children of Jacob Krouse, a farmer living near Forest, O., while playing in the woods Thursday, found some wild parsnips and ate them. About midnight they were taken violently sick, and one died in a few hours, The others will die.

The drill used in boring a gas well at Leavenworth, Kan., has penetrated the cavity of an underground river that carries away the loose earth. The drill is now working in the sandstone which forms the bed of the river, which is 1,800 feet below the surface.

A wife beater named Polenski, of Barnesville, Minn., was taken from jail by a mob and a rope placed around his neck to hang him, but he begged so piteously for his life that the mob relented and let him go on a promise of good behavior in the future.

August Hetzke, who whipped his step-son to death in Chicago some months ago, was sentenced Friday by Judge Clifford to the penitentiary for life. He asked for a new trial, having been found guilty at his first trial, and the judge granted the petition provided he would plead guilty, which he immediately did and got the above sentences, thus saving his neck.

ADDITIONAL DISPATCHES.

R. G. Dun & Co., in their review of trade for the week ending on the 30th say: Dullness is the feature in business, but dullness with a hopeful feeling in almost every quarter. The monetary pressure which has almost invariably commenced about this time does not appear, and the dangers which were by experienced bankers apprehended seem to have vanished.

The House Committee on Military Affairs has ordered a favorable report on the Senate bill providing for the erection of monuments at Gettysburg battlefield to the memory of regular soldiers, and donating to the Gettysburg Monument Association the iron fence now surrounding the Lafayette Park in Washington City.

At Atlanta, Ga., on the 30th, Neil Stark shot and killed his brother and fatally wounded Tom Crawley in a quarrel over a nickel game of cards.

RECORDER SMYTH, of New York, on the 30th made public a letter he had received which was marked "personal." The letter said that when a decision favorable to Mr. Jay Gould is rendered, $250,000 in $1,000 bills will be left at the recorder's residence.

HARRY PAINTER and Charles Wilkinson registered at a hotel in Reading, Pa., on the 30th, and were assigned a room together. The next morning they failed to respond to the reporter's call, and on breaking open the door both men were found dead, they having blown out the gas.

GEN. BLACK, commissioner of pensions, has estimated that it will take between $200,000,000 and $300,000,000 to pay all claims for arrears of pensions.

GOVERNOR JACKSON, of Maryland, on the 30th, pardoned the seven Democratic judges and clerks of election who were found guilty in having perpetrated frauds at the polls two years ago. They were sentenced on June 27 last to two years' imprisonment. Governor Jackson said he thought the men had suffered enough for their offense.

It has been ascertained that the total loss of life by the mine explosion at Rich Hill, Mo., was thirty. The state mine inspector is strongly censured by the miners.

The three children of T. S. Richardson, a farmer living near Macon, Mo., were burned to death on the 30th in a straw playhouse in which they were playing.

Almost Lynched by Fellow Prisoners. ROUGH TREATMENT OF A NEGRO CHARGED WITH
Almost Lynched by Fellow Prisoners. ROUGH TREATMENT OF A NEGRO CHARGED WITH ASSAULTING A LITTLE GIRL IN THE COLUMBUS JAIL.

COLUMBUS, OHIO, May 17.—Judge Lynch came very near making an end of Umphreys, a negro who was arrested yesterday for an assault upon a little girl. He was bound over to court, and when taken to jail his identity became known to the other prisoners, who at once attacked him in a vicious manner. After throwing him into a bath tub and nearly drowning him, the prisoners secured a rope, placed it around his neck and dragged him about the corridors, ending the performance by drawing him up free from the floor. The brute would undoubtedly have been strangled to death before the jail officers arrived had not one of the prisoners cut the rope.
