Wanton Murder of a Laborer by a Bailiff. DUBLIN, May 18.—Bailiff Sweeney was escorting to his home in County Tipperary this morning Landlord Lloyd's son, who was drunk, when Lloyd turned to the crowd following and fired his revolver at a laborer, wounding him. Another workman attempted to interfere when Sweeney shot and killed him. Sweeney was set upon by a mob, but escaped. The police pursued and arrested him. They had great difficulty in preventing a lynching. Tender-Hearted Jail Birds.
Columbus, O., May 18.—The negro Umphrey, who is charged with assaulting the little Crouch girl, was taken to jail Wednesday. When his identity became known to the other prisoners they attacked him in a vicious manner. He was first thrown into a bath-tub and nearly drowned. Then a rope was secured and placed around his neck. He was thus dragged about the corridors and finally drawn up free from the floor. He would undoubtedly have been strangled to death had not one of the prisoners cut the rope. The jail officials then put in an appearance and rescued Umphreys.

Growth of Natural Gas Business.

Some idea of the extent of the use of natural gas in Pittsburg, Allegheny and vicinity and the profits of the business may be had from the report of one of the companies just presented. It states that on February 29 the last of the treasury stock had been sold, so that the entire capital stock of $7,500,000 is now subject to dividends. Rents, operating expenses, interest and taxes for the year amounted to 46.65 per cent. of the earnings, or $1,-709,702.74. Monthly dividends of 1 per cent., amounting to $842,626.50, have been paid. The number of house connections made from the lines of the company during the year 1887 was 4,612. A year ago the company contracted to operate the lines of two other companies. The united business of these three companies amounted on March 1 to the supplying of 678 manufacturers and 11,955 dwelling-houses, and, through other distributing companies, the supplying of 113 factories and 10,961 dwellings, or a total of 23,707 contracts.

SALIDA, Col., May 17.—The Leadville express on the Denver and Rio Grande road was derailed while rounding a long curve in Brown's Cañon on Tuesday night. The express and baggage cars were dashed to pieces on the rocks in the canyon and the smoking car partially demolished. The Richmond Dispatch of last Friday reproduces what we said about its classing Col O'Ferrall as an advocate of "protecting" iron ore and coal, and then adds:

"Certainly we did not intend to misrepresent Colonel O'Ferrall's position; and we think the Courier makes a very fine point when it admits that he is in favor of perpetuating the present tariff on iron ore and coal, and opposed to "protecting" those articles. All that anybody means when he speaks of "protecting" coal or iron ore, or any other article, is that he is in favor of a tariff on that article which will "protect" it from foreign competition. We understand Colonel O'Ferrall to be in favor of such a tariff on coal and iron ore, and naturally spoke of him as being in favor of "protecting" those articles. The existing tariff "protects" sumac, manufactured tobacco, iron ore, coal, peanuts, and other articles which Virginians have a deep interest in. We are in favor of continuing that protection. If the Clarke Courier speaks for Colonel O'Ferrall, as of course we have no reason to doubt that it does, then he is not in favor of "protecting" iron ore, nor coal, nor any other article, but of "a tariff for revenue only," and will vote for continuing a protective duty on any article only as a compromise and because the Mills bill provides for such a tax. It seems to us that by necessary implication the Courier condemns Mr. Mill and the Committee of Ways and Means for continuing the duty upon iron ore and coal. However, we simply desire to let our readers know Colonel O'Ferrall's position, and will not discuss any other question."

In commenting upon the above we must state, first, that we did not undertake to "speak for Col. O'Ferrall," who knew no more of our article than the Dispatch did before he read it. But our esteemed city contemporary, on several occasions, mentioned Col. O'Ferrall as being in favor of protection, because of the admission he made to Mr. Butler, and while we readily acquit the Dispatch of purposely intending to misrepresent our representative, we wished to draw its attention to his manly declaration in the main body of his speech for a "Tariff for revenue." To this extent all democrats are willing to go, and statesmanship demands that they shall go no farther, and that the reductions to be made shall be gradual and in proportion to the decrease in our public debt and the annual interest thereon. The Mills bill, of course, is a compromise measure, and public requirement will not be satisfied with the passage of that bill any longer than a mounting surplus admonishes us of the necessity for another reduction in tariff duties. Why, the tax on tobacco was not removed in a lump, but lowered one-half, and the friends of the Mills bill propose to remove the other half, and this part of the programme of the friends of the Mills bill the Dispatch heartily endorses, and it has our approval, although we do not grow tobacco and regard it as a luxury, because every member of one's family does not use it—but every such member feels the need of coal or fuel of some kind, sugar, salt, woolen goods, etc.

The Dispatch cannot successfully maintain that a law is just which would compel the editor of this paper to pay $7 50 extra for every ten tons of coal he might buy in Pocahontas county, merely to help the Dispatch in developing such mines, should it own such properties there.

THE TARIFF DEBATE, which begun in the House on the 17th of April, was closed on Saturday by Mr. Reed, republican, speaking against the Mills bill, and Speaker Carlilse making a masterly argument in its favor. For the first time since the war the democracy, under the inspiration of the brave and admirable message of President Cleveland, took an aggressive position, and although somewhat weakened by the barnacles of expediency that became fastened to its timbers while sailing under the colors of "anything to beat Grant" and similar negative devices, nevertheless a grand sight has been waged and ended, with promises of a glorious triumph when the vote shall be taken. The democracy were thrice armed in this contest, as their cause is a just one, and the sympathies and hearty good will of the unorganized masses is with them. Further consideration of the bill will be laid a side for several weeks.

The republicans of Virginia met in Petersburg on Thursday last, and as was expected, the little bantling Mahone ruled the roost; but some of the fowls declined to keep company any longer with him—although at one time they were proud to crow loudly, "Lead on, Master, we'll follow thee"—whereupon, under the lead of Captain John S. Wise, they withdrew, organized another meeting, appointed delegates to the national republican convention, and adjourned after cheering for Blaine. Wise has promised to make as much noise outside of the convention at Chicago, if he is denied a seat, as Mahone will be able to make inside. If Blaine or Sherman is nominated at Chicago, a democratic victory in Virginia will be won without much effort, but if neither of them is chosen, the rival factions will unite on the person nominated, each one hoping to be made a "big Injun" in the very uncertain event of the republican candidate being elected.

The platform goes on to say that these things can be done "with safety to our industries," and "without danger to the opportunity for remunerative labor," a declaration that will not be gain-said except by those who are endeavoring to rob the public through "trust" combinations. A NARROW ESCAPE FROM LYNCHING.

William Bohen, of Rockaway Beach, who gouged his wife's eyes out, was arraigned yesterday before Edmund J. Healy, of Far Rockaway, and remanded to the Queens County Jail. This step was necessary to save him from the fury of the people at the Beach who were loud in denunciation of his crimes and openly threatened to lynch him if they could lay their hands upon him. After his arrest on Friday he was locked up in the cells at police headquarters. This was soon known all along the Beach and within a short time an angry crowd had gathered. Bohen was only saved from lynching then and there by the subterfuge of Constable Jones, who persuaded the people that the prisoner was not in the little building but had been taken to the jail at Long Island City. Bohen was trembling in his cell until the mob dispersed.

THE GOUGER.

Last week one of the most horrible and fiendish acts ever recorded was perpetrated at Rockaway Beach by a wretch named WILLIAM BowEN, a saloon-keeper at that place. This monster committed an assault on his wife some months ago and gouged out one of her eyes, utterly destroying the organ. The patient but foolish woman's love for her brutal husband prompted her to forgive him, although he had disfigured her for life, and she refused to prosecute. Law and justice must be administered in a very singular manner on Long Is'and, or this felonious assault could not have been hushed up, despite the disinclination of the woman to make a complaint. The Penal Code imposes a punishment of from three to fifteen years' imprisonment for the crime of maiming, and the fellow ought to have been prosecuted by the District-Attorney and received the extent of the punishment. Probably he would have been so dealt with had he not had a liquor saloon and a political "pull."

What is the sequel? Last week Bowen demanded money of his wife, and when she refused him he rushed at her with the savage cry: "Now I'll get your other eye," and thrusting his thumb into the socket actually tore out the remaining eye, and left her hopelessly blind.

The blood curdles to think of the horribly fiendish act, and one can scarcely believe that human nature could be capable of such a crime. What an inadequate punishment is a fifteen years' term of imprisonment for such a monster? Bowen at present lies in the Long Island City jail awaiting the result of his victim's injuries. He may now be tried and convicted. But what voice in the whole community will not declare that the death penalty is as justly his due as if he had murdered the woman he has doomed to darkness for the remainder of her days?

A Wife's Eyes Gouged Out by Her Fiendish Husband.

A Wife's Eyes Gouged Out by Her Friendish Husband.

NEW YORK, August 10th.—Mrs. Kate Bohan of Fairview avenue, Rockaway Beach, lies at her house hovering between life and death. Her husband, Wm. Bohan, who plucked both her eyes out, will be brought before Justice Healy at Far Rockaway today. The unfortunate woman is suffering intense agony, and is under the treatment of Dr. H. Phillo, who said that peritonitis had set in and he was afraid it would reach the brain and soon be followed by death. On the strength of this statement Coroner Cronin took the poor creature's ante-mortem statement. The suffering woman with much difficulty told the Corner the following story:

"William Bohan, my second husband, two years ago plucked my right eye out, and since then has threatened to have the other eye also. When I returned from the hospital two years ago the doctor ordered me to wear spectacles. I had only one eye, and my husband used to hide and break my spectacles. On July 20th he succeeded in gouging out my remaining eye. I think it was with his thumb, but I am not sure. Anyway, I was caring for my grandchild when my husband attacked me. I raised my arm with the baby in front of me, and he put his hand up under my arm and struck me. I screamed, and the cook came in and took the child. Then I felt something on my cheek and could not see. I asked the cook what was on my face, and she answered 'Blood.' 'Oh,' I said, 'I'm done for; my eye is gone.' Then I felt my eye lying on my cheek. I was in such a condition I don't know whether my husband said anything or not. I think I felt something touch my eye when he put his hand on my face."

William Bohan, the beetle-browed Rockaway Beach saloon-keeper who was convicted yesterday of having brutally gouged out his wife's left eye while in a frenzy of anger April 29, 1886, was placed on trial before Judge Garretson and Justices Brandon and Kavanagh in the Queens County Court of Sessions at Long Island City to-day for the second offense of the kind, committed July 31 last, in which he completely deprived his helpmeet of her sight by gouging out her right eye.

Rather than stand the full trial, which, from the weight of the evidence, could be but a mere formality, Bohan pleaded guilty to the charge in this second indictment and on that plea was sentenced to imprisonment for fourteen years and seven months.

Then on the conviction for the first offense, obtained yesterday, Judge Garretson, at 12.30, sentenced Bohan to twelve years and six months.

This makes a total sentence of twenty-seven years and one months. The utmost penalty of the law would have been fifteen years on each indictment, making a total of thirty years.

The case is as peculiarly sad as it is horrible, because of the wifely devotion of the sightless woman and the brutal unconsciousness of the man to the awfulness of his crime.

Mrs. Bohan, who will never see again, was pitifully anxious to shield the beast, but her daughters, Mrs. John Barry, Mrs. John Hoffman and Mrs. John Wiest, together with Mrs. William N. Ferril, a sister of Mrs. Bohan, had no such gentle and sentimental feeling towards the miserable creature who had married their mother and sister evidently with the idea of obtaining her little property.

Mrs. Hoffman was in the dining-room of the Bohans when the infuriated brute committed the second assault, and told often and with graphic simplicity the story of the outrage:

How Bohan had boasted many times that he had poked out one of his wife's eyes and would have the other some day, and how, on July 31, 1888, while this grown-up and married daughter of Mrs. Bohan by her former husband sat on her mother's knee, Bohan rushed across the room, and, taking the wife's head between his hands as in a vise, thrust his thumb into her right eye and gonged out the eyeball so that it hung on her cheek.

After his sentence, Bohan broke down and wept. He was allowed to see his wife for a moment and clumsily tried to caress her. By advice of his counsel he deeded to his wife his share in their joint property at Rockaway Beach, but afterwards in another moment of brutal frenzy, he demanded the deed, that he might tear it up. Finally he let it stand. He will be taken to Sing Sing to-night or to morrow.

SHE LOVES HIM YET.
Mrs. Bohan Attempts to Shield the Brute who Blinded Her.
The little courtroom in Long Island City was crowded with men and women yesterday afternoon and the eyes of all were turned with a fascinated horror on a burly, brutal-looking fellow, who scowled at them in return. He was William Bohan, and he was on trial for gouging out his wife's eyes. He looked capable of the crime, horrible as it is. His square jaws were thickly covered with stubby black beard and his closely-cropped hair seemed almost to touch his little, furtive eyes, so low and narrow was the retreating forehead. Clad in a flannel shirt and an old suit of dark clothes, he sat with his lawyer on one side of him and a constable on the other. So great was the prejudice against him, excited by his crime, that it was with difficulty a jury could be obtained, and even the judges on the bench—Garretson, Brandon and Kavanagh—could scarcely conceal their disgust.

Across the courtroom and behind the prisoner sat his wife, a large, kindly-faced, motherly-looking woman, with her two married daughters and her married sister beside her. She wore a green veil as a bandage across her face, and sat with the patience of the blind hour after hour without moving. When her husband testified she turned her sightless face towards him and listened in an eager, intent way to what he had to say. Her daughters would now and then say something to her against their savage father, but she would only rock herself backward and forward and answer deprecatingly, trying to shield him.

The story of the terrible assault has been told in the World. Bohan kept a low groggery at Far Rockaway. On the night of April 29, 1886, while drunk and quarrelsome, he tore out her left eye. He was arrested, but she pleaded for him and he escaped. He declared many times afterward that he would "have her other eye." On the night of July 30, 1888, he kept his word. He accused her of having driven his brother away earlier in the evening. Then he rushed at her and deliberately thrust his right thumb into the corner of her eye and gouged it out so that it lay on her cheek. The agonized screams of the poor woman, who fell to the floor in a paroxysm of pain, frightened him and he fled. He was arrested and confined in jail without bail. The grand jury found two true bills against him, one for each offense; and it was for the first offense that he was on trial yesterday.

Mrs. Bohan, who was the first witness, was led to the stand by two court officers. She walked slowly, her groping gestures awakening overwhelming sympathy in the hearts of all who saw her, and rekindling the fierce horror for the brutal wretch who robbed her of sight. Her kindly face wore a troubled look and she turned to the judges before she was well seated and asked tremulously:

“Do I have to testify?”

“You have to tell all you know and answer truthfully all the questions put to you,” said Judge Garretson, gently. The troubled look grew deeper.

“Can you see me, Mrs. Bohan?” asked District Attorney Fleming.

“No, sir; I can’t,” she replied, sadly.

“Perhaps if you lift your veil you can see?” continued the lawyer, alluding to the green bandage about her eyes. She removed it, and a murmur ran round the courtroom, which the judges themselves were too affected to check. Even Bohan winced, and turned his head aside that he might not look upon those pupilless sockets. The poor woman waited patiently till she was told to put the bandage on again, when she did so.

“How did you lose your eyesight?” asked the lawyer.

“William put up his hand in the dark, and I ran against it, sir,” she replied, with a pleading tone in her voice.

“Do you mean to tell me that this was done accidentally?” exclaimed Mr. Fleming indignantly.

“It just happened this way, answered Mrs. Bohan, earnestly, turning her sightless face appealingly toward the jury. "On April 29, 1886, William and I were living together at Rockaway Beach. William was in bed that night and I took some money out of his pocket and went into the next room. William wanted the money, and he followed me into the room. There was no light, and William was groping about in the darkness when his finger happened to go into my eye. I have not been able to see out of it since." Here she paused a moment and then, as if fearing she had not laid sufficient emphasis on the innocence of her husband, she added earnestly: "It was an accident, and he wasn't to blame."

When she heard the voice of her husband's lawyer, how quickly and readily she answered, and how relieved she appeared, and how the troubled look passed out of her face! The questions sounded like the most exquisite irony.

"Did you and your husband ever quarrel?" asked the lawyer.

"Oh, no! We got along very well together. I never made any complaint against him," she replied.

"He did not intentionally assault you?" he continued.

"Indeed, no, sir," she answered promptly. "He just put up his hand in the dark and I ran against it. It was quite as much my fault as his."

The daughters next testified, and one of them—Mrs. Barry—told how she had seen the blood on her mother's cheek just after the assault, and how she had heard her father say he would give her a mark that she would take to her grave. She also heard him say he would pull the other eye out. Mrs. Hoffman, another daughter, heard her father threaten her mother.

Mrs. Mary Farrell, a sister of Mrs. Bohan, gave the strongest evidence. She was heart and soul against the prisoner, and she evidently wanted to see him punished for his sickening crime. She said: "I have seen that man," pointing to Bohan, who scowled back at her from under his lowering black brows, "strike his wife many times, and more than once I have heard him threaten to injure her. I heard him say once. 'Do you see those cedars out there? I will swing you yet.'"

Bohan himself was put on the stand, and he seemed to feel the universal execration that looked out from the hundreds of eyes bent on him. He kept his head down most of the time and talked in a low tone. He never raised his eyes from the floor, except now and then to glance furtively at the jury.

"Did you ever strike your wife?" asked District Attorney Fleming.

"Yes; I often struck her," was the unabashed reply. "And I have hit her in the face, too; bnt her eyes were put out by accident. I
"Did you know that your wife went to see ex-District Attorney Downing to take proceedings against you?"
"She didn't take no proceedings," replied the prisoner sullenly. When I was arrested and taken before Justice Healy I was discharged."

A ONCE PROMINENT CITIZEN OF WYOMING HANGED FOR HORSE STEALING.

Chicago, Sept. 15.—A dispatch from Bismarck, Dak., says: A man named Wise was lynched for stealing horses in the Turtle Mountains on Wednesday. Wise was at one time a prominent citizen of Wyoming, and during his residence in that territory was prominently mentioned for the legislature. Private advices from the scene of the lynching are to the effect that Wise was overtaken by several settlers who had missed horses. He was en route to Manitoba, and it is believed that many of the animals which have been missed in that vicinity of late were taken by him across the border. He was overtaken in a ravine and at first showed sight, but was forced to throw down his rifle and surrender the horses. Then he was driven to the nearest tree and lynched. Wise came from Pennsylvania, where it is said his family still reside.

Berlin, Sept. 15.—A sham fight took place yesterday at Muenchberg. The emperor himself took part in the contest and handed his troops in a masterly manner. The opposing forces presented a splendid spectacle. The battle ended at noon. The emperor delivered the usual criticism on the movements of the troops. In the afternoon his majesty entertained thirty-one guests at dinner.

Minneapolis, Minn., Sept. 15.—Under order of the court the entire stock of shotwhee, Cleriwhe and Lotham, the suspended wholesale dry goods firm, was sold yesterday. The stock had been invoiced at $421,000. Wm. Lindke, of St. Paul, bid 80 per cent for the stock in bulk, and it was knocked down to him. The sale will net the creditors some $25,000.

MADRID, Sept. 15.—The queen of Spain has awarded the decoration of the golden fleece to the Duke of Edinburgh.

LONDON, Sept. 15.—It is reported that the czar and czarina have declined to receive Queen Natalie of Servia.

AN ANTI-SLAVERY SOCIETY.
Cardinal Lavigerie has formed an anti-slavery society in Paris. The committee includes many prominent persons.

A CONFLICT WITH STRIKERS.
PARIS, Sept. 15.—A conflict has taken place at Pierre Buffiere, in the department of Haute-Vienne, between striking workmen and the military. Several persons were wounded, and a number of the strikers were arrested.

DEATH OF A GERMAN PRINCE.
VIENNA, Sept. 15.—Prince Johann-Adolph of Schwarzenburg is dead. He was eighty-nine years of age. His death occurred in Bohemia.

PARIS, Sept. 15.—The French government has ordered that gunboats proceed to the West Coast of Africa for the purpose of pursuing vessels engaged in the slave trade, especially those which fly the French flag.

Buried by a Cave-in.
ONE MAN TAKEN OUT DEAD AND ANOTHER LIKELY TO DIE FROM HIS INJURIES.

SEYMOUR, Ind., Sept. 15.—While Wm. Vondehren and a number of assistants were at work last evening in the bottom of a sewer excavation 9 feet deep, the quicksand gave away, and the sides of the ditch fell in, burying Vondehren and one of his assistants, Arthur Orrell, under about 8 feet of clay. Vondehren was extricated, but terribly injured and is dying. Orrell was suffocated before he could be rescued. The others escaped with slight injuries.

Irish-Americans Visit Gen. Harrison.
CHICAGO, Sept. 15.—About 500 members of the Irish-American Republican Club went to Indianapolis this morning to pay their respects to Gen. Harrison. They will reach that city about 9 o'clock this afternoon.

A Stock Broker Falls.
NEW YORK, Sept. 15.—The failure of C. M. Ward was announced on the stock exchange. He has no outstanding contracts on the exchange.

AN EXPRESS TRAIN WRECKED AND PASSEGERS AND
CREW HAVE A NAMBOW ESCAPE.
CHICAGO, Sept. 15.—A dispatch from East Saginaw, Mich., says: Fire has been running in the woods of Northern Michigan two weeks, and although several towns and much valuable property have been threatened no serious losses have resulted up to this time. A disaster is reported on the Saginaw, Tuscola and Huron Railroad, resulting from forest fire. An express train, while running 20 miles an hour, ran on a place of track beneath which the ties had burned. The engine, express, and baggage cars, and two coaches left the rail, ran along the ground about two lengths of the train, and the engine then turned over in the ditch. The engineer, driver, and express messenger were thrown clear of the wreck and escaped with bruises and burns. The fire on the track immediately communicated to the coaches, and the passengers and crew barely had time to run through the train and escape by the run coaches before every particle of woodwork in train was burned.

A DAKOTA LYNCHING.
A Horse Thief Strung to a Tree in the Turtle Mountains.
BISMARCK, Dak., Sept. 15.—A man named Wise was lynched for stealing horses in the Turtle mountains on Wednesday. Wise was at one time a prominent citizen of Wyoming, and during his residence in that territory was prominently mentioned for the legislature.

Private advices from the scene of the lynching are to the effect that Wise was overtaken by several settlers who had missed horses. He was en route to Manitoba, and it is believed that many of the animals which have been missed in that vicinity of late, were taken by him across the border. He was overtaken in a ravine and at first showed fight, but was forced to throw down his rifle and surrender the horses. Then he was driven to the nearest tree and lynched.

Wise came from Pennsylvania, where it is said his family still reside.

MAGGIE GAUGHAN'S SLAYER CAUGHT Sixty Miles From Chicago BY PURSUERS ON A HAND CAR.
The Mulatto Confesses His Terrible Crime—Farmers Try to Lynch Him—Taken Back to Chicago—An Exciting Hunt in the City.

CHICAGO, Feb. 28.—When Zeph Davis, the bullet-headed mulatto murderer of little Maggie Gaughan, left the body of his victim in the boot heel factory in State street yesterday afternoon, he boarded a freight train on the Wabash road and rode as far as Forest, a small station about sixty miles south of Chicago. He reached that place about 3 o'clock in the morning, and entered the depot, where he lay down to sleep. He did not wake up until 10 o'clock. In the mean time Marshal Martin kept a close watch on the sleeper. At 10:15 o'clock Davis arose and started south on the track. At 11 o'clock Marshal Martin received official information of the murder, and a minute description of young Davis. The fellow was now out of sight. Summoning three men, the Marshal leaped upon a hand car, and started after the fugitive at a lively clip.

While on the way the pursuers picked up large patches of fur which the negro had ripped off the collar of his overcoat in the hope of concealing his identity. Two miles from the depot the man was seen standing in the middle of the track, about half a mile away, and upon the only knoll in the long stretch of prairie. When he saw the hand car bearing down upon him, Davis struck across the country as fast as his legs would carry him. The Marshal and his men were close behind him, however; and after a hard run of nearly a mile the murderer, who was exhausted, fell face downward upon the prairie. Marshal Martin pounced upon him.

"Where's your warrant?" asked Davis.

"Here it is," replied the Marshal, pushing the barrel of a six-shooter under his nose.

On the way back to the station Davis confessed that he had killed the little girl, but stoutly insisted that he had not assaulted her. The depot was crowded with excited farmers when the Marshal drew up to the platform on the hand car. There was a rush made to seize the mulatto, but the officer finally succeeded in landing his prisoner in the baggage room of the depot, where he was shackled.

At 4% o'clock Davis was hustled into the smoking car of the evening passenger train to Chicago. He sat in the forward seat, with Marshal Martin at his side. Before the train started Davis raised the window and expectorated among the farmers who for three hours had been clamoring to lynch him. Quick as a flash one of the heavily booted grangers drew a long knife and made a lunge for the negro. The blade shattered the window pane, but missed the fellow by the merest scratch. The train then pulled out.

When it reached the Twenty-second street station in this city at 6:30 o'clock Davis was hustled out of the car and driven in a close carriage to the Central Station. If he had alighted at the Polk street depot, where an immense crowd was awaiting his arrival, he would have been lynched in short order. At the Central
at the Folk street depot, where an immense crowd was awaiting his arrival, he would have been lynched in short order. At the Central Station he made a clean breast of his crime.

He said he thought he was boss in the factory. When Maggie came to work in the morning she refused to obey one of his orders and he threw a hatchet at her. "She ran to the closet to get a bucket to hurl at me," he continued, "and then I closed in on her and hit her with the hatchet until she fell. She did not cry, but fought like a wildcat all the time."

Davis asserts that he is but 17 years of age, but he appears much older. If he can prove that he is under 18, he will escape the gallows.

After John Wheeler of the signal service of the Desplaines street station thought he saw Davis run into Meridian street from Union street, early this afternoon, he sent in an alarm to his station, and a few moments later fifteen other policemen were searching every nook and corner bounded by Madison, Meridian, Union, and Desplaines streets. The news that the murderer was penned in the block created intense excitement, and soon 5,000 men and boys were ransacking the tumble-down dens in the district. Beds, barrels, and boxes were overturned, and the colored inmates of the houses driven into the streets. Two negro boys, who bore a striking resemblance to the murderer, were nearly killed before they could prove their identity. The hunt lasted until 2 o'clock, when the news of the capture of the murderer at Forest dispersed the mob.

CALENDAR OF CRIMES.
The Black Murderer of Little Maggie Gaughan Caught.
CHICAGO, Ill., Feb. 29.—Seph Davis, the young mulatto who murdered fifteen-year-old Maggie Gaughan Monday morning, was brought back from Forest, Ill., where he was captured. He confessed the murder, but denied having criminally assaulted the girl. He says he was alone in the store when Maggie came in Monday morning. After she had stood by the stove some time, he told her to go to work. Some words passed between them, and, becoming angered, he picked up a hatchet with which he had been splitting wood and threw it at her.

"I was not very close to her," continued Davis, "and it hit her glancing, cutting her forehead and hand, which she had thrown up. Then she began to strike at me and fought me with her nails. I hit her again on the head and she then ran toward the little closet. I followed her. There was a pail standing in the closet and she picked it up and threw it at me. That made me madder than ever, and I hit her again and again over the head with the hatchet.

"She then fell to the floor and I saw she was dead.

"This frightened me," continued the murderer, "and I kicked her body into the furthest corner of the closet. I then went in the next door and got some warm water in which I washed the blood off my hands. When I went back to the shop

"What was your object in covering up the body with the sacks of leather?"

"Well, I wanted to hide it until night, then I was going to draw what money was due me and leave town. When I heard Mr. Green say that he intended to order some coal I became frightened, for I knew it would be put in the closet, and the body would be found.

"I was afraid to leave the shop for dinner, and when Mr. Green sent me on an errand, I thought I could get back before her body was discovered. When coming back I saw the patrol wagon and crowd in front of the door, and knew the body had been found. I hid until evening and then got on a freight train and rode to Forest, where they caught me."

During his recital of his horrible crime Davis preserved a stolid countenance, and not once did he express a feeling of regret for his flendish work. His only anxiety appeared to be for the future, and several times he asked what punishment could be meted out to him for his crime. Before being locked up he said again and again that he had not criminally assaulted his victim, and he had killed her because her refusal to go to work had made him mad. Davis claims to be but seventeen years of age, but he appears to be two or three years older.

ZEPH DAVIS' DOOM.
The Murderer of Maggie Gaughan Sentenced to be Hanged.
CHICAGO, Ill., April 3.—The jury in the case of Zephyr Davis, the young negro who murdered Maggie Gaughan, last evening returned a verdict of guilty and fixed the penalty at death by hanging. The condemned murderer did not blanch when the fatal words were pronounced. He stood with his arm lightly leaning on the wooden partition dividing him from the twelve men who had pronounced his doom, chewing a wad of paper quite vigorously, an amusement he had kept up most of the afternoon. The usual motion for a new trial was then formally entered by Mr. Arney, of the defense, and Davis was taken away to his lonely cell by the deputy sheriffs.
